title: Amazon’s Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75
snippet: Amazon-owned Bee has launched its first new AI devices since its acquisition, including an updated wearable and a credit-card-sized recorder that attaches to smartphones. The devices can summarize conversations, create to-do lists, and integrate with Alexa and Amazon shopping, with prices starting at $74.99.
fullText:
Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee, is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year. The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device.

The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush. 

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.

For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things.

All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates.  

To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.

In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.)

With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.

Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more. 

Plus, you can upload photos to Bee or connect it with Apple’s HealthKit to add a picture of your overall wellness to be integrated into your provided insights. 

The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering. 

All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app. 

The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter.

title: YouTube’s contextual AI search rolls out to all users on Android and iOS in US
snippet: “Ask YouTube” is no longer a YouTube Premium feature as the conversational AI search becomes available on mobile Android and iOS devices. more…
fullText:
“Ask YouTube” is no longer a YouTube Premium feature as the conversational AI search becomes available on mobile Android and iOS devices.

Today, Google announced the Ask YouTube feature would be widely rolling out to mobile users, in addition to TV instances of the YouTube app. Unlike before, Ask YouTube will now be accessible to all users, not just Premium subscribers. 

Access to some form of contextual AI model has been available on YouTube for a while, dating back to 2023. Since then, Google has settled on an “Ask YouTube” button that lets users ask questions about videos to get more insight. The rollout has been limited, with TVs and Premium users getting access first.

The feature has evolved a bit, and it’s taken on a conversation-oriented presentation. It isn’t limited to questions about the video or what happens at which timestamp. It’s powered through Gemini, so its answers go beyond strictly what’s in the video you’re watching.

	

Google also notes that users will be able to use Ask YouTube from the watch page in their Shorts feed and during live streams, but that feature will be a later release. For the time being, users in the US can expect Ask YouTube to show up on your mobile Android or iOS device soon as it rolls out to more users. Google says it plans to gradually expand availability.

title: Apple unveils Apple Home Collection smart home accessories developed with LG and Schneider
snippet: Apple today confirmed that it is working with at least two third-party companies to develop a new lineup of smart home accessories, including cameras, thermostats, and a smart lock. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple today confirmed that it is working with at least two third-party companies to develop a new lineup of smart home accessories, including cameras, thermostats, and a smart lock. Here are the details.

’Clean, minimal aesthetic and premium materials’

In addition to announcing the new Apple TV 4K, the new HomePod mini, and the new $299 HomeView smart display today, Apple also unveiled Apple Home Collection, a lineup of smart home accessories developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.

Apple says it collaborated with both companies to bring “the simplicity, reliability, and privacy of iPhone and Apple Home to a new suite of smart cameras, thermostats, and a door lock.”

Building on the thousands of Works with Apple Home and Matter accessories available today, Apple Home Collection offers customers a new array of recommended products to better understand what’s happening inside and outside their home, manage access, and keep the temperature just right throughout the day.

The Apple Home Collection lineup currently includes the following products, with prices starting at:

LG Floodlight Cam: $399.95

LG Indoor Cam Plug-in: $199.95

LG Outdoor Cam Plug-in: $299.95

LG Smart Deadbolt Lock: $349.95

LG Smart Thermostat: $199.95

LG Temperature Sensor: $39.95

LG Video Doorbell Wired: $249.95

Schneider Home Smart Thermostat: $199.95

Schneider Home Smart Thermostat Room Sensor: $39.95

You can find more details about color and regional availability here. Apple says availability for the lineup begins in December, with some accessories not arriving until early 2027.

The new Apple Home Collection can be set up with one tap on the iPhone. From there, the entire lineup can be managed through the Apple Home app, with no separate apps or accounts required.

All accessories support Thread, while the smart lock also supports Matter and Aliro, allowing its core access functions to work locally, even without an internet connection.

Apple says all data in the Home app is end-to-end encrypted, meaning neither Apple nor its partners, LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, can access it.

Here’s Apple on the home monitoring lineup:

LG’s lineup of four cameras gives users a private and intelligent way to monitor their homes when using a home hub like Apple HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K. Every camera captures up to 2.5K resolution video and recognizes people, familiar faces, pets, vehicles, and packages, with video history securely stored in users’ supported iCloud+ plan, so there’s no separate camera subscription.

The cameras also support Apple Intelligence features, including automatic video summaries that describe what’s happening in recorded footage, and the ability to search recordings using natural language. Both features require an eligible iCloud+ subscription and compatible Apple devices.

As for home access, which is handled by LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock, Apple confirms that it supports Ultra Wideband, which in practice means the door can automatically unlock when someone approaches with a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch configured with a home key, without needing to tap either device.

	

It also features an integrated PIN pad and a hidden backup key slot, and can detect when the door has been opened, closed, or tampered with, including alerting users if it remains open while locked.

When it comes to the Home Climate products, Apple explains that the new thermostats from LG and Schneider Electric can automatically adjust temperatures based on whether users are home, getting ready for bed, or away, without requiring manual scheduling. They can also use temperature and humidity readings from sensors placed in different rooms.

Schneider Electric’s Smart Thermostat on the left, LG’s Smart Thermostat on the right.

Finally, Apple says that starting this fall in the U.S., customers will be able to pay an additional fee to have their Apple Home Collection accessories professionally installed by ADT through Apple Retail.

title: Gemini AI Plus subscribers will lose access to Pro models next month
snippet: Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash. more…
fullText:
Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash.

A change in Gemini’s subscription model was announced earlier this month. It came right before Google’s new Argon model went live and became the new high-performance offer in Gemini. The company made it clear that Gemini 4 Argon would be included for AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers, but it also said AI Plus members would lose access to AI Pro entirely.

According to one user on Reddit, Google has begun emailing AI Plus subscribers to let them know Gemini Pro models would be excluded from the AI Plus tier starting on November 13. The email lists Flash-Lite and Flash as the only two options after that date.

We wanted to let you know about changes to the models that you can access with your Google AI Plus plan.

Starting on ﻿1﻿3﻿ ﻿N﻿o﻿v﻿e﻿m﻿b﻿e﻿r﻿ ﻿2﻿0﻿2﻿6﻿, the ability to select Pro models in both the Gemini app and AI Mode in Google Search will only be available to Google AI Pro subscribers and above. You’ll still have access to our latest Flash-Lite model and Flash, built for speed and intelligence. Your previous chats using the Pro model can be continued with a different model.

To learn more about these changes, you can visit our Help Centre article for additional details. You can manage or cancel your subscription at any time.

Thank you for being a Google AI Plus subscriber.

– The Google One team

A couple of others report getting the same email, which puts a pin on exactly when the Gemini AI Plus plan changes.

	

The $4.99/month option will give users access to just two models, while the $19.99/month tier gains access to Argon, leaving a bigger gap between the two. Google is still keeping the free plan around, which leaves everyone with access to Flash-lite.

Of course, these subscriptions tie into Google Workspace for cloud storage and other perks, like YouTube Premium. Still, the $4.99/month plan seemed like a good deal for those who wanted access to more capable models for more than just passive chats.

Who said all privacy protections had to be digital nowadays? In my line of work, traveling can be common, and working from a coffee shop, train, or hotel lounge is something I do on the regular. So when I came across this nifty privacy app that knows to blur your screen the second you look away, I was enthralled.

The app is called ShyGlass, and it comes from developer Max Rovensky, who posted a 10-second demo on X last month that has since racked up over 230,000 views. The way it works is pretty simple. While wearing a pair of AirPods, if you turn your head to a certain degree, your MacBook screen blurs. When you turn your head back, the screen unblurs itself.

Behind the scenes, it’s using the motion sensors Apple uses for dynamic head tracking in Spatial Audio, the feature that keeps your music anchored when you look around. ShyGlass uses the same motion data but to detect presence. A user calibrates a center position from the menu bar, and anytime head positioning drifts past a set angle (15° by default, adjustable from 2° to 30°), a blur fades in over the display until it’s fully covered.

Now this is Security Bite after all, so I have a couple of thoughts on the permission the app needs: Screen Recording. ShyGlass does need to pull a snapshot of a user’s display to apply the blur effect, which kind of sounds a little ironic for a privacy tool. According to the developer, the snapshot stays in memory and is never saved or uploaded, and capture stops the moment the blur does.

I have no reason to doubt that. But it’s worth bring up the trade here. Screen Recording is one of the most powerful permissions on the Mac. An app with it can see everything you see, all the time, and macOS has no way of enforcing that it only looks when it says it does. So you’re basically taking the developer at his word.

Still, I find its functionality useful more often than not. Like turning to chat with the person next to you on a flight, or digging through your bag in a public space. Any time your head leaves the screen, there’s a window where someone else’s eyes can land on whatever you’re working on.

I hope to see Apple implement a macOS feature like this one day.

But if you want to check out ShyGlass, the developer has it priced at $4. It’s available on macOS 14 or later and requires AirPods 3 or later, any AirPods Pro, or AirPods Max.

title: Apate sends AI agents undercover to get scammed so they can gather fraud intelligence
snippet: Most companies use AI agents to ship products faster or speed up workflows. Apate.ai sends them undercover to get scammed.
fullText:
Most companies use AI agents to ship products faster or to speed up workflows. Apate.ai sends them undercover to get scammed.

Founded in 2024 on the basis of research done in Macquarie University in Sydney, the Australian startup deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, sporting different ages, genders, and accents, and speak various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

The company says its fleet of agents has so far wasted 17 years of scammers’ time across 2.5 million conversations. More importantly for Apate’s customer base of banks, telecom companies, government agencies, and utilities, the undercover agents try to get scammers to reveal things about themselves that are usually learned only after a victim has been scammed: bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, malicious websites, the brands they’re impersonating, and other details about the scams they’re running.

Apate, one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, then feeds that information to its customers, who use it to inform their anti-fraud measures and initiatives. (The company will pitch a panel of VC judges at Disrupt, which is taking place this week at Moscone West in San Francisco through Thursday, October 15.)

It’s a curious evolution of scam-baiting, but it’s not so surprising given how much AI has empowered scammers and hackers. The FBI received more than 22,000 complaints of AI-related crimes in 2025, which resulted in about $893 million in losses. More than $632 million of that came from investment scams, in which the FBI says fraudsters use AI to run conversations, and deepfake the voices and appearances of celebrities, executives, and trusted figures.

For a long time, people have made a hobby out of deliberately stringing scammers along — sometimes hilariously, like getting scammers to read aloud entire books, or even to get ridiculous tattoos. Now, with AI growing increasingly capable, the tables are turning.

Curiously, the idea behind Apate was sparked by a real scam call.

Several years ago, Apate’s founder and CEO Dali Kaafar was at a family picnic when he got a call from an unknown number. Realizing it was a scammer on the line, he decided to play dumb for the benefit of his kids and managed to keep the call going for 44 minutes.

Everyone had a laugh, but Kaafar noticed that those were 44 minutes the scammer had not spent calling a real victim. It was also 44 minutes of his wasted time, which led him to wonder: Could he automate it, and in the process, learn something useful? 

That idea eventually led to research work at his job at Macquarie University, where Kaafar and his colleagues used machine learning and natural language processing to uncover the content of scam calls, and develop better ways to detect and prevent scams. 

“Most of the industry works after the fact. Telcos block numbers, but scammers just get new ones. Banks watch transactions, but by then the scammer has already reached the customer. We go to the scammer directly and get the information before anyone gets hurt,” Brad Joffe, co-founder and chief commercial officer, told TechCrunch. “Our AI agents talk to tens of thousands of scammers every day across calls, messages, email, and the web. What we offer our customers is what comes out of those conversations, and what they can do with it.”

Joffe said Apate uses both frontier models and its own fine-tuned models to power its agents and analysis. The company trains its models on conversations its agents have had with scammers, as well as the research Kaafar did at Macquarie. 

In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get access to an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more. Customers can even assign these agents particular missions, such as obtaining a bank account number or crypto-wallet address. Its text agents can search forums, investment groups, and social platforms for potential scam activity, and can then enter conversations with a fabricated identity to surface scammers’ details.

The startup’s customers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia, TPG Telecom, as well as other utilities, telcos, and government agencies. Joffe said TPG has diverted nearly 590,000 calls to Apate’s agents, Commonwealth has seen a 76% drop in publicly reported scam losses, and an unnamed Australian bank the startup works with has used its outbound agents to disrupt 22 scam campaigns.

Investors are betting there is money to be made from fooling scammers, too. Apate raised $8.15 million in seed funding in August from Lobby Capital, OIF Ventures, Investible, Concept Ventures, and Baobab Ventures. Joffe said the 20-person company has raised just under $10 million in total and plans to spend the latest round on its product and international expansion, including opening an office in London and building a larger presence in the U.S.

“Apate is named after the Greek goddess of deception, which felt appropriate given what our agents do,” Joffe said, adding that the startup even features scammers swearing at the bots in its pitch material.

“We track that as a sign of frustration and every swear word gets celebrated by us at Apate. We are probably one of the only businesses in the world that celebrates when people swear at our product.”

title: Apple Intelligence reportedly coming to China in December, but without Siri AI
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple plans to finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in December, although some important features could still be missing. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple plans to finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in December, although some important features could still be missing. Here are the details.

Apple Intelligence to see limited launch in China with iOS 27.3

Earlier today, a report from the South China Morning Post claimed that Chinese regulators had approved the use of Alibaba’s AI models to power Apple Intelligence, following preliminary approval for the platform’s rollout in July.

The report noted that the timing of the approval was particularly relevant, as the iPhone Duo is scheduled to launch in China next week.

Now, Bloomberg reports that Apple “is planning to launch Apple Intelligence in the region in December as part of an upcoming iOS 27.3 update,” although the launch “will exclude the new Siri AI assistant and other features announced this year,” according to the publication’s sources.

The move comes after a lengthy and complicated effort to bring Apple Intelligence to China, where local regulations governing AI-generated content, security assessments, and algorithm registration have forced Apple to take a different approach than in other markets.

Here’s Bloomberg:

In order to get Apple Intelligence approved, the company had to make some concessions. Unlike in other countries, the platform has guardrails developed with China’s Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., including a filter that allows the government to approve ongoing updates to the AI models. Apple is also working with Baidu Inc. on features related to search and Siri.

On Sept. 29, Apple received Chinese permits allowing recent iPhones to support the use of Apple Intelligence and Alibaba AI models, including Tongyi Wanxiang and Qwen.

The report notes that Apple Intelligence’s launch in China will not feature “the company’s in-house image-generation tools,” while certain “features for generating text will also be limited in some applications.”

According to Bloomberg, the initial rollout will include Genmoji for creating custom emoji, Apple’s AI-powered notification summaries, writing tools, and the Clean Up feature in Photos, which lets users remove unwanted objects from images.

The report notes that it is unclear whether these features will be enough to win over Chinese consumers, as local smartphone makers have already introduced their own AI capabilities:

With AI services proliferating on rival phones from Huawei Technologies Co., Xiaomi Corp., Oppo Guangdong Mobile Telecommunications Corp., Vivo Mobile Communication Co. and others in China, it’s unclear how much Apple will benefit from launching a two-year-old set of relatively basic AI features in the country.

Interestingly, today’s report came just one day after Apple said in the footnotes of its HomeView announcement that it is “working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward” to launch Siri AI in Europe, where the assistant also remains unavailable due to regulatory issues.

title: Now that Character.AI is going bankrupt, what happens to all of its users’ data?

fullText:
Lauren Feiner

 

is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed a years-long multi-state investigation against Character.AI as they now seek to require protections on consumer data sold through its bankruptcy proceeding.

James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in Character.AI’s bankruptcy case “to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets.” Character.AI announced Tuesday it was filing for Chapter 11 and selling some assets to Disney. But the AGs warn there could be serious risk involved in the transfer of the technology due to the “highly sensitive nature of the conversations many users have with Character.AI chatbot characters, the large number of minors who use the product, the serious risks posed by specific features of the product.”

The filing also reveals that several of the states had been mid-investigation when Character.AI filed for bankruptcy. The states say they opened a probe into consumer protection and privacy concerns in 2024, following a lawsuit from the mother of a 14-year-old who died by suicide allegedly “seconds” after talking with the chatbot.

“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers”

“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers and potentially unlawful conduct from Character.AI, particularly its treatment of children, including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, exposure to sexual and violent content, weak age checks, misleading safety claims, and potential violations of state privacy laws,” according to a press release from James’ office. The states were working to address these issues with Character.AI, but didn’t reach an agreement before the company filed for bankruptcy. Character.AI and Disney did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The states are urging the judge to require the purchaser of Character.AI’s assets to implement procedures that will safeguard the sensitive information the company maintained. Those include effective age-assurance systems, restrictions on how minors can engage with the chatbots, implementing “Crisis safeguards,” and letting users delete their data. “This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder,” James said in a statement. “I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”

title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
snippet: The label will appear on the player page and include songs entirely generated by AI or partially, such as AI involved in composition and vocals.
fullText:
YouTube Music announced Wednesday the rollout of a new labeling system aimed at improving transparency around songs created with the help of generative AI. Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.

The label will appear on the player page. Clicking on this label provides additional information about the specific role of AI in the track’s creation.

Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app. 

YouTube said it collaborated with various music partners and deployed its own detection tools to identify AI-generated music. According to its help page, partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI. 

“Fully Gen AI” applies to tracks that are entirely generated by AI, while “Partly Gen AI” refers to works where artists may have incorporated AI-generated components but added their own live elements. Tracks edited using pitch-correction tools such as Auto-Tune fall under the “No Gen AI” category.

The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches. For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year. Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.

Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily. The platform labels detected AI-generated music and excludes it from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, while also withholding royalties from fraudulent streams. The company is also working on an option to let users filter out AI-generated music.

TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution. 

YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions. Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization. YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track, which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.

title: Gemini app rolling out Gemini 4 Argon to AI Pro and AI Ultra
snippet: Following the announcement at the end of September, Gemini 4 Argon is starting to roll out to the Gemini app, Google Antigravity, and more. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement at the end of September, Gemini 4 Argon is starting to roll out to the Gemini app, Google Antigravity, and more.

Gemini app 

In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Argon is available for both Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Last month, initial availability was just for the Ultra ($99.99+) tier. 

Google says to expect “frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows” in the app. Additionally:

“Argon answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn’t repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses.” Additionally, it “follows style instructions more reliably than any of our previous Gemini models.”

“For longer tasks, it keeps you in the loop by sharing its progress more often and more effectively.”

Given the “major improvements” in coding performance, Google is letting users “switch between chatting and coding” within the Gemini app for macOS. Users will specifically have direct access to Antigravity’s agentic coding interface in the consumer client for building apps, web experiences, and more.

	

Meanwhile, there will be a new toggle in the main chat window that lets you switch from chat to tasks (previously Spark). As of today, AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers will see 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.8 Flash, 3.1 Pro, and 4 Argon in the model picker.

AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers can also access Gemini 4 Argon in AI Mode.

Google Antigravity + more

	

In the Antigravity desktop app and Antigravity CLI, the new model requires AI Ultra. Google today shared more examples of how it has been using Argon with its internal version of Antigravity across Chrome, Gemma, YouTube, and more:

“Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase. Piping multiple clean code changes at a time, Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome’s billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes.”

“Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the upstream pull requests (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes.”

“Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms.”

AI Ultra is also required for Argon access in AI Studio and Android Studio (Canary).

Argon is available in the Gemini API at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, 2026. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

On the science front, Google is offering 10,000 scientists the “highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months.” Applications are now open.

title: CedarDB wants one database to handle both transactions and analytics, as AI agents raise the stakes
snippet: Databases have traditionally been designed either for analytical data or for operational data. But database engine CedarDB supports both, and its approach has gained relevance with the rise of agentic AI.
fullText:
Databases have traditionally been built for one of two jobs. Analytical databases help businesses spot trends and answer questions, while operational databases store the day-to-day records of transactions, like orders and payments. But the Munich-based database engine CedarDB supports both, and its approach has gained relevance with the rise of agentic AI, its co-founder and CEO Moritz Sichert told TechCrunch.

CedarDB has been in the making for the last decade, but its current momentum stems from enterprise companies whose existing data stacks may have been well suited to storing years of transactions, yet less suited to quickly answering analytical questions asked in natural language about that data.

CedarDB’s questioning of the divide between analytical and operational queries is a by-product of its focus on efficiency. The company is a Technical University of Munich spinout based on Umbra, a research project that was built from scratch to beat legacy database engines at processing speed by making the most of modern hardware.

With five Umbra researchers as its co-founders, CedarDB kept that approach, promising faster performance without requiring more CPUs or processing power and memory — and requiring few changes from customers. In particular, its team made sure CedarDB was compatible with PostgreSQL, an open source database system.

According to Sichert, this compatibility with the popular database helps keep switching costs low, since users don’t need to rebuild their apps. It also has an added advantage: CedarDB follows the logic LLMs are most familiar with as a result of their training.

That decision is one of many choices that proved lucky in retrospect, Sichert said. But it wasn’t all luck. In a blog post, co-founder Christian Winter detailed key priorities the team set after leaving academia, “such as reliability, fault tolerance and compatibility with popular tools.”

Not all of the answers were obvious. The team strongly debated whether it should launch a cloud offering right away. In the end, it launched CedarDB Enterprise as an on-premise offering alongside its free version, CedarDB Community Edition, both announced in May of last year at the same time as it announced a €5.3 million seed funding round (approximately $6 million).

The cloud offering was only delayed, though, not abandoned. After conducting beta testing with users who had signed up for its waitlist, the company on Wednesday announced limited availability of CedarDB Cloud onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where it’s competing with 20 other startups vying to win TechCrunch’s prestigious Startup Battlefield competition.

A fully managed, cloud-hosted version will likely help CedarDB expand its user base beyond large enterprises. It will also make it better prepared to compete with the likes of Databricks, a major data company that seems to have reached the same conclusion as the German startup.

At its Data + AI Summit in June, the American company cited “the agentic era” as the reason why it was launching LTAP, a new data architecture aiming to “[unify] transactions, analytics, streaming, and operational data on a single copy of storage in the lake.”

It is too early to tell how disruptive this might be, but Sichert interprets Databricks’ move as another sign that there is demand for what CedarDB does. The startup plans to serve its first cloud users with its current team of 14 people, but Sichert expects it will need a larger team once it gets more traction. “And this is where we would raise our next round.”

title: YouTube Rolls Out New Labeling System for AI-Generated Music
snippet: YouTube’s new AI labels will help users identify music made with generative AI tools.
fullText:
Streaming your daily tunes is about to come with a bit more clarity. YouTube has expanded its labeling system to mark AI-generated songs on YouTube Music. As AI music continues to flood streaming apps, the service’s latest move aims to keep listeners informed about what they’re hearing and whether it was produced by humans. These labels will eventually appear on the main YouTube app as well.

“Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” YouTube said through its official blog on Wednesday. “As these tools evolve, our listeners have told us they want transparency when they’re hearing an AI-generated track.”

The labels in question will appear on songs that YouTube identifies as created primarily with generative AI, based on its own detection tools and music partners. It’s not clear how much AI must be featured in a track to qualify for this label.

			

More from CNET

Labels marking music as AI-generated are rolling out on YouTube Music and YouTube.YouTube

A YouTube spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

YouTube’s decision to mark AI music is the latest move to clarify the growing presence of AI-generated tunes across the music streaming landscape. Earlier this year, Apple Music unveiled a suite of tools to identify AI-generated content, saying new Made with AI labels will roll out by year’s end. Spotify now includes AI Personas, which help people confirm if musicians are actually people making human-made music.

Other streaming apps like Tidal, Bandcamp and Deezer have all made moves to crack down on the AI music boom. 

Earlier this year, Deezer released a report stating that AI-generated music accounted for 44% of all new music delivered to its platform. Apple Music previously stated that over one-third of the tracks uploaded to its service are “100% AI.” Forbes reports that AI-generated music could be an industry worth billions of dollars by 2028.

The Recording Industry Association of America, International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences and the performers union SAG-AFTRA came together earlier this summer to push for a two-tiered labeling program to mark AI-produced songs as either AI-Generated or AI-Assisted.

“Fans want to know whether and how generative AI has been used in the music to which they listen,” IFPI CEO Vikki Oakley and RIAA CEO Mitch Glazier said in a joint statement. “Given how important human artistry and authenticity are to music lovers all over the world, these labels will provide an immediately understandable and easily scalable approach to transparency.”

The line between human and AI-generated audio is rapidly blurring. At least having a labeling system in place will let you know if you’re nodding your head to a banger made by a human or through other generative means.

title: Apple website suggested Siri AI may be coming to full size HomePods
snippet: The headline feature of the new HomePod mini 2 is support for Siri AI, something that won’t be available for the first-gen model. But there’s hope that existing full size HomePods may also get access to the smarter intelligent assistant. A leaker noticed two clues on Apple’s website seemingly pointing to this, but it’s possible that it was an error on the part of the company … more…
fullText:
The headline feature of the new HomePod mini 2 is support for Siri AI, something that won’t be available for the first-gen model. But there’s hope that existing full size HomePods may also get access to the smarter intelligent assistant.

A leaker noticed two clues on Apple’s website seemingly pointing to this, but it’s possible that it was an error on the part of the company … 

HomePod mini 2 with Siri AI

The HomePod mini 2 has the same design as its predecessor, other than refreshed colors. Internally, the S5 chip is replaced with an S10 one, and that provides access to Siri AI.

Not all of the processing is done on the device itself. Apple notes that full Siri AI support is dependent on pairing with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, HomePod mini can tap into a user’s personal context to help them find what they need in the moment.

Full-size HomePods may also get Siri AI

Leaker pdfu spotted a couple of indications on Apple’s website that support is also coming to existing full size HomePods – though likely only to 2nd-gen models.

First, there were the images used, where the color glow appeared to match that of the HomePod mini 2.

Big updates to the HomePod 2 product page this morning. May suggest support for Siri AI is coming.

The Siri examples now use Siri AI’s gradient style, and the refreshed glow matches Siri’s look on HomePod mini 2. pic.twitter.com/5X1sbwsC4T

— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 13, 2026

Second, alt text for one of the images described it as showing the “multi-colored Siri Al glow on top.”

9to5Mac’s Take

From a commercial perspective, Apple does like to hold back some software features from older devices in order to encourage upgrades. At the same time, the company is making a big push on Siri AI, likely to boost Services revenue once usage limits kick in on lower iCloud tiers.

It’s notable that Apple has replaced the images concerned, but this doesn’t provide much clue as to whether it was an error or simply an announcement the company isn’t yet ready to make. Even on the new HomePod mini 2 speakers, the Siri AI update will follow at a later date. It’s possible that support for their bigger brother could be announced at the same time.

The optimistic view would be that Apple isn’t requiring Apple TV owners to upgrade in order to get access to Siri AI, which might provide a clue to the company’s thinking. The update is coming to second-generation devices and up, and that may well point to the same story with the full-size HomePod 2.

title: Nothing reportedly launching two pairs of smart glasses, one with barely any AI
snippet: A reliable source says that Nothing is building out its own AI smart glasses that feature ChatGPT integration, a camera, and two very different models. more…
fullText:
A reliable source says that Nothing is building out its own AI smart glasses that feature ChatGPT integration, a camera, and two very different models.

WinFuture’s Roland Quandt says on Bluesky that Nothing is preparing to launch two new smart glasses models, and they sound wildly different.

One pair would be similar to the Ray-Ban Meta lineup with a built-in camera and AI features such as translation. While Nothing as an avid Android user might seem like one to hop on the Android XR train, it sounds like that’s probably not the case given Quandt says these are bringing integration with ChatGPT rather than Gemini. That’s not a new pivot on Nothing’s part, though, as the company has been building out ChatGPT integration for a while in its other products.

The other pair of smart glasses, though, would take a much simpler approach.

	

These would work as a pair of headphones with the ability to take calls and interact with your phone’s voice assistant, but they’d lack a camera or any direct AI integrations. Both models are said to offer photochromic lenses, otherwise known as “transition” lenses and commonly found on other smart glasses.

Prior reporting on Nothing’s efforts to build smart glasses pinned a release date sometime in 2027. The dual strategy here is certainly interesting, especially given a recent report that suggested Nothing would go all-in on AI devices going forward.

title: Googlebook will improve support for Linux apps eventually, but it’s all about AI for now
snippet: Googlebook was always going to run into problems with app availability, but few expected the platform to regress its support for Linux apps from Chromebook’s fairly robust solution. In a blog post, Google reiterates that the “Linux Terminal Preview” on Googlebook isn’t for using Linux apps, but for building with AI. more…
fullText:
Googlebook was always going to run into problems with app availability, but few expected the platform to regress its support for Linux apps from Chromebook’s fairly robust solution. In a blog post, Google reiterates that the “Linux Terminal Preview” on Googlebook isn’t for using Linux apps, but for building with AI.

ChromeOS introduced support for Linux apps a few years ago, allowing users to install apps designed for Linux on their machines to expand what the laptops could do. Googlebook does not have this same support, with the Linux Terminal accessible and apps technically installable, but those apps now show up alongside Android and web apps, nor do they feature the same level of user-facing functionality.

In a blog post this week, Google reiterates that the priority around Linux support on Googlebook is, for now, focused on AI-aided app development. 

Today, getting the most out of AI workflows requires access to a terminal with a command line, even if someone doesn’t identify as a programmer or software developer. With Googlebook, we’re excited to help users express themselves and gain access to these tools. Googlebooks come with pre-installed tooling to get you going.

Google says that the Terminal is designed to be the “entry point” for AI agents so that tools like Google’s own Antigravity can use command-line tools within the Linux virtual machine. That setup also ensures your private files are isolated from the agent’s access (unless you grant access). 

	
	

The Linux Terminal implementation on Googlebook is “optimized for rapid prototyping, web development, scripting, and agentic workflows via CLI,” Google says, with a future focus on “building not only on Googlebook but also for your other devices” while also fine-tuning the experience for “heavier workloads.” 

Also directly mentioned is that Google is working on support for showing Linux GUI apps in the app launcher, which is the main downside to the current implementation. 

We can’t wait for the terminal and Linux VM to continue getting more capable over time, including Linux GUI app support with integration directly into the app launcher.

There’s no word on when this might arrive, but the focus right now is very much on AI and development. The rest of Google’s roadmap includes:

We are working hard to get you building not only on Googlebook but also for your other devices. In addition to the existing network passthrough and wireless ADB, USB passthrough and support for ADB over USB are coming, enabling local device debugging and more from our Linux VM and Antigravity. Learn more about Antigravity on Googlebook.

Our testers have been eager to run more complex tasks. To make this more seamless, we are adding dynamic memory and storage scaling for the VM.

We will be adding GPU/NPU hardware acceleration for heavier local workloads, allowing users to leverage the performance and power efficiency of dedicated hardware.

VM persistence and separation from the terminal window will better support long-running processes, when you want to take on more demanding agentic workloads.

title: Apple confirms HomePod mini 2 won’t have Siri AI at launch
snippet: Today Apple introduced HomePod mini 2 with Siri AI as a major tentpole feature. HomePod mini 2 ships on October 30, but checking the fine print on Apple’s website, it seems Siri AI won’t be available on launch day. more…
fullText:
Today Apple introduced HomePod mini 2 with Siri AI as a major tentpole feature. HomePod mini 2 ships on October 30, but checking the fine print on Apple’s website, it seems Siri AI won’t be available on launch day.

Siri AI coming to HomePod mini 2 in ‘a future software update’ per Apple

HomePod users have been waiting for Apple to reveal when Siri AI is coming to its home devices. And today it became official: Siri AI will be available soon on the new HomePod mini 2.

But unfortunately, if you buy HomePod mini 2 for launch day delivery on October 30, you’ll be left waiting a bit longer to access Siri AI.

From Apple’s website, in the ‘Meet Siri AI’ section for HomePod mini 2:

Siri on HomePod mini 2 puts a powerful, AI assistant right at the center of your home.1 Once set up with your iPhone or iPad, Siri draws on broad world knowledge and your personal context to help you find what you need and get more done every day.

Enjoy more natural conversations, richer answers, and effortless smart home control — while your privacy is protected at every step. Just ask to play your favorite music, check your schedule, or catch up on podcasts, completely hands-free.

1 Coming in a future software update. Usage limits may apply.

The footnote above says that Siri AI won’t be arriving until a future software update. This is further confirmed in Apple’s press release here near the bottom.

HomePod mini 2 arrives two weeks ahead of HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K, both of which ship November 13. Each of those products support Siri AI at launch, so here’s hoping that means HomePod mini 2 will gain support by mid-November too.

If that’s the case though, it’s certainly curious why Apple wouldn’t just launch all three products the same day with Siri AI.

When do you expect HomePod mini 2 to gain Siri AI support? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
Today Apple introduced a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K with Siri AI, and A19 chip, and more. But the company also shared welcome news for current Apple TV users: Siri AI is compatible with select older models too.

Siri AI supported on Apple TV 4K 2nd and 3rd generation

The new Apple TV 4K is packed with a variety of upgrades, but it also has a higher $299 starting price.

While it’s previously been expected that the rumored Siri AI support in tvOS would require the new hardware, it seems that’s not the case.

	

In Apple’s press release, it says:

Siri AI is available as a beta on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation or later), and is available at launch in the U.S., Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and the UK in English.

title: Ledger’s new hardware wallet is an Android phone without the phone
snippet: The Atom couldn’t have launched at a worse time for Ledger. | Image: Ledger Ledger has announced its latest crypto-centric hardware effort, the Android-based Atom, a device that resembles a phone but is instead designed to be used alongside one. It arrives at a tricky time for Ledger, which has been forced to cease sales of some of its hardware across southeast Asia following hardware tampering in its supply chain, which has reportedly seen over $86 million worth of crypto stolen from across some users' accounts. In fact it … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Ledger has announced its latest crypto-centric hardware effort, the Android-based Atom, a device that resembles a phone but is instead designed to be used alongside one. It arrives at a tricky time for Ledger, which has been forced to cease sales of some of its hardware across southeast Asia following hardware tampering in its supply chain, which has reportedly seen over $86 million worth of crypto stolen from across some users’ accounts.

While Ledger’s previous hardware wallet signers have been compact devices, running custom software and often with E Ink displays, the Atom is the spitting image of a regular Android smartphone. In fact it essentially is an Android phone, except for the fact that its eSIM capabilities have been limited to data-only, with no support for texting or calls.

The Atom runs on both Android OS and Ledger OS, which sits on its own secure element chip, allowing you to move into a secure environment for tasks like crypto transactions. Two Atom users can also send encrypted messages to one another using regular Android messaging apps, with the messages decrypted within Ledger OS on the recipient’s device. Ledger has designed the device with AI agents in mind, including a partnership with OpenClaw, designed so that agents can handle financial tasks without getting full access to digital wallets, with physical approval required to complete transactions.

1/5Image: Ledger

Ledger says that the Atom is “not designed to replace your phone.” The company’s head of PR, Phillip Costigan, told me that Ledger recognized it was unlikely to be able to produce a device capable of competing with top Android handsets on camera and other specs, and so didn’t try to. The Atom is in fact intentionally limited in some respects: the 6.77-inch OLED display is only 60Hz, it runs on a Qualcomm Dragonwing chip rather than Snapdragon, and it only has a single rear camera and a 4,000mAh battery. Still, it will receive five years of Android OS updates, and at least seven years of support for spare parts, including a user-replaceable battery. It also has a physical privacy switch, which cuts power to the camera and microphone “at a circuit level.”

The launch couldn’t come at a worse time for Ledger. The company has confirmed reports that at least one of its hardware signers was sold by a reseller with “an unauthorized hardware implant,” which read users’ 24-word recovery phrases and transmitted them elsewhere using an eSIM. The discovery has forced Ledger to pause sales across southeast Asia, and at German retailer MediaMarkt. Reports suggest that over $86 million worth of crypto may have been stolen from across affected users, though Ledger hasn’t confirmed the scale of the losses.

That would be enough to give anyone pause before buying new Ledger hardware, at least from a third-party seller. Still, the company says that the Atom has been designed with physical anti-tampering measures, which it claims would have blocked the screen reader implants involved in the recent incident:

Core protection: A protective enclosure surrounds the Secure Element, MCU, and FPGA, and it is designed to detect any attempt to drill into or open this area.

Display and back cover detection: Ledger Atom detects when the display or back cover is removed. The back cover is paired with the device, so it cannot be swapped with a cover from another Ledger Atom.

Tamper-evident packaging: Ledger Atom’s packaging is designed to show whether it has been opened before it reaches you.

The Atom will be available from summer 2027. Reservations are open now, with a refundable $100 deposit to secure a Founder’s Edition device for $849. After the launch, the price will rise to $899.

title: Apple acqui-hires AI startup founded by former NotebookLM developers
snippet: The European Union’s Digital Markets Act transparency website lists Huxe as Apple’s newest acqui-hire, and at least the fourth AI-related deal disclosed this year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The European Union’s Digital Markets Act transparency website lists Huxe as Apple’s newest acqui-hire, and at least the fourth AI-related deal disclosed this year. Here are the details.

Apple’s latest AI deal involves former NotebookLM developers

In mid-2025, a team of three developers who worked on Google’s NotebookLM announced Huxe, their own personalized AI audio app that could generate daily briefings from a user’s email and calendar, create podcast-style conversations around specific topics, and provide continuously updated audio feeds for subjects such as news and sports.

NotebookLM, which was recently renamed as Gemini Notebook, is one of Google’s most popular AI products to date. It started as an experimental research and note-taking tool designed to answer questions and generate summaries based on a user’s own documents, and grew into a broader AI research assistant capable of creating podcast-style Audio Overviews, video summaries, study materials, and more.

In December 2024, as NotebookLM was exploding in popularity, project lead Raiza Martin left Google to found a new company, alongside two former NotebookLM colleagues: designer Jason Spielman and engineer Stephen Hughes.

They formally launched Huxe on an invite-only basis in June 2025, and opened it to everyone that September, alongside the announcement of a $4.6 million funding round.

Huxe continued developing its product until May 2026, when the company announced it was shutting down. The service ended on May 28. At the time, the company’s website said only that the team was “moving on to new things.”

Today, the European Union’s Digital Markets Act transparency database revealed that Apple has struck the following deal with Huxe, and informed the bloc last June:

09.06.2026   Huxe

Apple Inc. (“Apple”) will have the right to make employment offers to and hire certain employees of Huxe AI, Inc. (“Huxe”) and receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights. Huxe provides a mobile application that creates personalized audio content. Apple designs, manufactures and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and sells a variety of related services.

In other words, this is not an outright acquisition of the company, but rather the now-common acqui-hire structure in which a larger company brings over key employees and gains access to some of the startup’s technology without purchasing the business itself.

Although there are no details about what Apple plans to do with Huxe’s technology or which employees it intends to hire, the deal fits Apple’s pattern of recent AI acquisitions and acqui-hires of AI companies developing new ways for people and devices to interact through voice, vision, and other interfaces.

Acqui-hires have been criticized for potentially allowing large tech companies to sidestep traditional merger reviews.

Earlier this year, FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson said the agency was beginning to look closely at such arrangements, and in March, the FTC and Justice Department formally began considering changes to premerger reporting rules that could specifically address acqui-hires, reverse acqui-hires, and deals involving non-exclusive IP licenses.

There has been little public movement on that specific issue since then.

title: iPhone hits record Q3 shipment share as global smartphone market plunges 20%, per report
snippet: According to Counterpoint Research, Apple saw its share of global smartphone shipments cross 20% for the first time in a third quarter, despite an industry-wide decline. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to Counterpoint Research, Apple saw its share of global smartphone shipments cross 20% for the first time in a third quarter, despite an industry-wide decline. Here are the details.

’The second successive quarter to take the full brunt of the memory crisis’

In a report released today, Counterpoint Research says memory constraints and rising prices have pushed global smartphone shipments to their lowest third-quarter level in 14 years, with a 20% year-over-year decline. The report doesn’t say what that translates to in absolute numbers.

According to Counterpoint Research, Apple shipped 22% of all smartphones during Q3 2026, up from 18% in the year-ago period. That helped it narrow the gap with Samsung, which remained in first place with a 23% share.

The top five also included Xiaomi (10%), OPPO (9%), and vivo (8%), all of which saw their shipment shares decline compared to Q3 2025.

Here’s Counterpoint Research on Apple’s performance for the period:

Apple’s market share crossed 20% for the first time in any Q3, reaching 22%, despite a YoY decline in shipments. The volume decline was largely driven by the absence of a base iPhone 18, which resulted in a smaller launch-month channel fill than the full iPhone 17 lineup a year earlier. Apple also joined the industry wide shift toward price hikes, although the impact was limited to the final weeks of the quarter. However, the iPhone 18 Pro models saw a stronger launch than their predecessors, particularly in China and India, while sustained momentum from the iPhone 17 series helped offset a higher shipment decline.

Looking ahead, the report noted that things don’t look particularly encouraging for the remainder of the year, “with OEMs increasingly prioritizing profitability over shipment volumes amid elevated component costs and weaker affordability.”

Counterpoint added that price-sensitive segments will likely face further pressure from higher device prices and limited component availability, with a meaningful recovery in shipment volumes unlikely until costs come down and supply conditions improve.

fullText:
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman today reported that the Apple home hub – set to be announced on October 13 as part of Apple’s ‘Welcome home’ event experience — will be called the HomeView. The brand would obviously sit alongside the company’s existing HomePod brand for smart speakers.

Gurman also reported on a few other new tidbits for the device, including the news that while it will be announced on Tuesday, it probably won’t be released until the middle of November …

Apple’s connection to the ‘HomeView’ trademark was first reported by MacRumors. 

The home hub will feature a design akin to the iMac G4, a floating display sitting atop a speaker base. Gurman says it will be powered by an A18 chip. There will also be a wall-mountable version with a square base.

The HomeView with speaker base will reportedly come in four color options: space gray, silver, starlight and pink. The wall-mountable model will only be offered in monochrome silver or space gray.

The device will primarily use voice as the input method, with Siri AI as the centerpiece of the user experience, with users ‘viewing’ content from across the room. It will run Apple apps, and not have an App Store — although users might be able to project third-party app widgets from a nearby iPhone.

Alongside the HomeView unveiling, Apple is also preparing hardware refreshes for the Apple TV set-top box and the HomePod mini. It has also partnered with appliance makers like LG to prepare a range of smart home accessories all meant to work well together, including smart thermostats, door locks and doorbells.

Apple is set to officially announce its new smart home initiative on Tuesday. Stay tuned for full coverage of all the announcements.

title: Figma announces new features to define how agents work on its platform
snippet: Figma is also releasing its code layers feature in open beta.
fullText:
Design platform Figma announced a new Markdown-based editor to help define a company’s design, bring in design and code libraries, and integrate with the Payload headless content management system during the company’s first Config event in India. Through some of these features, the company aims to provide a definition for its own and third-party agents to adhere to a brand’s design rules better while creating with AI.

The company debuted a new feature called Figma Specs, which is a markdown editor that lets users define their design language in a simple way. The document can serve as a reference for teams and agents while designing in Figma. Specs can exist as a standalone file in Figma or can co-exist within the canvas. Apart from acting as a text editor, users can reference other Figma elements, such as elements on the canvas, and embed FigJam diagrams, code layers, and designs. 

What’s more, teams can bring in more context about design, including design libraries, code libraries, and guidelines to manage context for the design system. Agents can also refer to this centralized system to adhere to rules. 

Image Credits:Figma

In the past week, the company made its agent on canvas available to a wider user base. However, given the non-deterministic nature of AI, the company is providing tools to steer it toward more predictable outcomes.

Figma also made its code layers feature available to users in open beta, which adds coding to designs on canvas for more interactive prototypes. The company announced this feature in private beta back in June. At its India event this week, the company is making the function available in public beta to let more users test it out. Users can also ask the agent to turn a design into code or change a part of the code to iterate on a prototype.

Image Credits:Figma

“We see Figma as the place where software teams come to decide what they build and ship. And so for that, I think one of the key things to keep in mind about what AI has changed and what it made available is the ability to build,” Figma’s chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch. “There are 17-times more lines of code being produced today than in the past. But when you’re looking at releases, only 1.3-times more releases. A lot of that code actually is not necessarily built to ship, but really built to discover what the product is. It’s built to design.”

The company said it is also supporting over 20 new tools with its MCP, including Open Code, Dia, Grok Bot, and Indian AI startup Sarvam.

Last year, Figma acquired open source headless CMS Payload. Now, the company is integrating it with its Figma Make product for generating dynamic websites and directly managing content. The company said that Payload’s downloads have increased sixfold in the last 12 months.

The company opened its first office in India late last year with sales, partnership, go-to-market, and product support functions. Figma said that the country is its biggest market in terms of users outside the United States. The company noted that the platform works with 40% of India’s top 100 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange.

title: MacPaw launches Eney, a proactive AI assistant for Mac and iPhone
snippet: Today marks a milestone for MacPaw, as the company is releasing Eney, a proactive AI assistant that works across your apps, files, and system to help you get things done, following a development process that began back in 2019. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Today marks a milestone for MacPaw, as the company is releasing Eney, a proactive AI assistant that works across your apps, files, and system to help you get things done, following a development process that began back in 2019. Here are the details.

A bit of background

A few days ago, I had the opportunity to talk to Oleksandr Kosovan, founder and CEO of MacPaw, as he showed me Eney, the company’s Mac-first proactive AI assistant.

Eney isn’t a new idea. In fact, we have written about it on 9to5Mac a few times. However, as the underlying AI technology kept changing and evolving, Eney changed and evolved with it.

As Kosovan explained, Eney originated back in 2019 as an idea for simplifying MacPaw’s CleanMyMac through natural-language commands. Then came the LLM boom, which in turn gave way to the agentic AI boom.

More recently, local AI models have become powerful enough to handle increasingly complex tasks that, until not long ago, required much larger cloud-based models.

So, MacPaw kept reworking and refining Eney, which finally launches today for Mac and iPhone.

Here’s MacPaw:

Unlike other AI assistants Eney is built for the Mac: it understands the context of the machine itself — the apps you work across, the files on your disk, the meetings on your calendar — and spots what needs attention before you do. A call about to start. A meeting that needs a summary. A disk running out of space. Eney notices, prepares the next step, and puts it in front of you for approval, without the need to switch between multiple apps, tools and products.

Eney Wand

The very first thing I noticed about Eney was MacPaw’s clever gesture to invoke it through the Eney Wand command. Just shake your cursor over some text, and Eney Wand activates, allowing you to select that text and prompt Eney about it. You can also invoke Eney Wand with the Option + W shortcut, or double-tap the Option key to bring up Eney from anywhere.

The Eney Wand is a particularly clever feature, as it solves one of the main pain points I have with most AI tools: constantly having to copy and paste content in and out of a chat window to get help with whatever I’m working on. Instead, Eney’s system-wide integration lets me simply point to something on my screen and ask the assistant to work with it, without having to move anything between apps.

Eney relies on both local and cloud-based AI models, with MacPaw working alongside Liquid AI to develop custom models optimized for Apple hardware. I recently had the opportunity to visit Liquid AI’s San Francisco headquarters, and it was really impressive to see how the company is bringing advanced AI capabilities to devices that weren’t originally designed to run them. (Not that the Mac isn’t, but you get what I mean, right?)

One of the demonstrations included an AI assistant running on an older Mercedes-Benz, whose hardware was many years old and, at least in theory, nowhere near powerful enough to run modern AI models. But Liquid AI has developed models efficient enough to run on existing hardware with limited computing resources, which goes to show that if one company could help MacPaw with the task of bringing increasingly capable AI models to Macs without relying on the cloud, Liquid AI would be it.

(That doesn’t mean Eney operates entirely on-device, however, as more demanding tasks still rely on cloud-based models.)

Mnemos

Back to Eney, it also relies on Mnemos, MacPaw’s proprietary AI memory system. It allows Eney to remember information about users and their preferences, and use that context to provide more personalized responses and suggestions.

Mnemos uses a knowledge graph to connect information about people, projects, preferences, and events, and it also understands how information changes over time. This means that if you correct something or a previously stored fact becomes outdated, Mnemos can keep track of what is currently relevant and update accordingly.

Another important aspect is privacy. Mnemos is designed to store and process memories locally on the Mac. It also distinguishes between information explicitly provided by the user, facts retrieved from connected sources, and patterns inferred from previous interactions.

However, Mnemos is still in development, and not all of its capabilities are available through Eney just yet. For now, its integration is limited to managing Eney’s own memories, rather than independently accessing information stored in other apps.

During our conversation, Kosovan confirmed that Eney already supports importing ChatGPT archives, which is a great plus for users who want to bring their existing context and preferences into the new assistant.

More ways Eney can help

Another tentpole feature of Eney is its writing assistance tools. As MacPaw explains, the Eney Spell feature “fixes spelling, grammar and wording right in Mail, Slack, Notes or the browser,” and it works very similarly to tools such as Grammarly.

With today’s launch, Eney works in eight languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Polish, Brazilian Portuguese, and Ukrainian. During our demo, Eney occasionally switched between English and Ukrainian, after Kosovan interacted with Eney in Ukrainian. It’s a mistake that won’t seem particularly unusual to frequent users of LLMs and chatbots, and shouldn’t be a dealbreaker for most users.

Beyond these features, Eney is also designed to anticipate what users might need based on what’s happening across their Mac. For example, copying some text can prompt Eney to offer a translation or summary, while an upcoming calendar event can trigger a reminder to prepare for a meeting.

And speaking of meetings, Eney can also transcribe calls without requiring a separate bot to join the conversation, a useful feature for anyone relying on AI-powered meeting summaries. Afterward, Eney can prepare notes, action items, and follow-up invitations for the user to review and approve.

And, in keeping with MacPaw’s roots, Eney also includes some Mac maintenance capabilities. It can warn users about low disk space, memory pressure, and repeatedly crashing apps, suggest possible fixes, organize the Downloads folder, and help locate files.

Eney also includes ready-made workflows such as Morning Brief, Plan My Day, and Weekly Review, which can be triggered manually or scheduled to run automatically.

To make all of this possible, Eney integrates with a wide range of apps and services. It works with Apple Mail, Calendar, and Reminders out of the box, and also supports connections to Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Slack, Notion, Jira, Linear, and more.

The idea is to let users work across these services through a single interface, without constantly switching between apps or manually transferring information from one to another.

Availability

Eney launches today on the Mac, and you can get it here. Eney offers a 14-day free trial with 10,000 AI credits, after which users can choose from three subscription plans: Starter, with 10,000 monthly credits for $14.99; Boost, with 20,000 credits for $29.99; and Power, with 30,000 credits for $49.99.

Users can also sign in with a Setapp account. Importantly, a Setapp membership isn’t required, but something tells me Eney might become even more useful in the future as MacPaw expands its integration with the apps available through Setapp. That is certainly where I would go next.

title: Ambrosia Energy will build a 10 GWh factory in Texas to make batteries for off-grid data centers
snippet: Startup Ambrosia Energy will build a massive factory to crank out batteries to augment solar panels, creating a round-the-clock clean power plant.
fullText:
Ambrosia Energy has begun work on a massive, 10 gigawatt-hour battery factory near Austin, Texas, co-founder and CEO Ben Longmier announced onstage Tuesday at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco.

“That allows us to build about a 300 megawatt power plant per year out at our field sites,” he said.

The factory will occupy 150,000 square feet, and Longmier said that Ambrosia plans to reach full production in two to three years.

The startup emerged from stealth in June to build power plants for data centers at a cost of $100 per megawatt hour. Longmier and his co-founder, Sara Spangelo, had settled on solar plus batteries as the cheapest option that’s the fastest to deploy. Solar panels power the load during the day and charge the batteries, which discharge at night and on cloudy days to keep the data center operating round the clock.

Longmier and Spangelo previously founded the satellite constellation startup Swarm, which they sold to SpaceX. 

Ambrosia is also beginning work on its first commercial power plant in West Texas later this year, Longmier said. The facility will pair 300 megawatts of solar panels with 660 megawatt-hours of batteries to deliver 30 megawatts of continuous power, with a goal of 99.3% uptime.

Even with “overbuilding” solar and batteries to deliver continuous uptime, Longmier said the company can be profitable at $100 per megawatt-hour, making it competitive with natural gas turbines that many hyperscalers are planning to use to power their data centers.

Sections of Ambrosia’s first pilot-scale power plant have been operating continuously for more than 100 days, Longmier said. The pilot is capable of generating 200 kilowatts of electricity 24/7.

To hit its cost targets, Ambrosia has been finding ways to simplify its components, including solar mounts and battery packs. By reducing part counts, and manufacturing many components in a factory, the startup has been able to reduce costs relative to buying from outside suppliers.

“We buy existing cells and we make our own pack in-house, and it has the fewest parts by a factor of about 100 compared to any other competitor we’ve seen,” Longmier said. ”We’ve been able to get to about 1.3x the cost of the bare cell compared to about a 5- or 7x for most stationary storage systems.”
