title: Can Vibe Coded Apps Replace Adobe and Microsoft? These AI Apps Hope So
snippet: The AI-made apps highlight people’s frustration with AI-bloated programs and increasingly expensive subscriptions.
fullText:
In this current era of vibe coding — using AI to create mobile and desktop apps — it was probably only a matter of time until someone made free versions of popular apps. That happened this month when a Reddit user announced that he did so with popular but expensive Adobe and Microsoft programs.

The person behind the project is Brandon Thomas, a software engineer who uses the handle “u/ai_art_is_art” on Reddit, where the tools first caught AI enthusiasts’ attention. Thomas has released 13 free, open-source apps on his website, called ArtCraft. These apps aim to replicate the core functionalities of Adobe and Microsoft programs, including Photoshop, Word and PowerPoint — or, as Thomas calls them, PhotoCraft, WordCraft and DeckCraft.

ArtCraft apps aim to replicate the core functionalities of Adobe and Microsoft apps.ArtCraft/Screenshot by CNET

Vibe coding has taken off for software developers and AI enthusiasts, leading to AI-made apps flooding Apple and Google’s app stores. However, significant concerns persist about the overall usefulness, security and long-term viability of vibe-coded apps. Apple removed some apps that help people vibe code this year because the apps didn’t comply with Apple’s developer rules.

			

More from CNET

But in the US’s current affordability crisis — and with legacy tech companies constantly raising their prices — a cheaper, AI-created alternative to Photoshop or Microsoft Word can be an attractive option for a subscription-weary consumer.

This certainly isn’t the first time a startup has tried to compete with legacy software companies like Adobe and Microsoft. Canva, Affinity and CapCut are extremely popular Adobe alternatives for content creation and editing. Google and Apple each have their own versions of Microsoft’s core business apps. 

But ArtCraft’s vibe-coded apps and other potential AI-made apps allow individual users to avoid handing over their cash and data to a major tech company. Using an open-source AI model on your own device, for example, gives you more control over your data than using a cloud-based app through a subscription.

As with all apps, CNET recommends you inspect the privacy and safety policies before using them. This is especially important for vibe-coded apps.

“Vibe coding can make it super easy to swap out old software tools, but it’s legally questionable,” said CNET’s Blake Stimac, a vibe coding expert. “What works great for you as a quick fix could easily turn into a legal battlefield the second you try to share it with the world.”

Representatives for ArtCraft and Adobe did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Microsoft declined to comment.

Will vibe coding kill legacy software?

It’s unlikely that vibe-coded apps will be the sole downfall of legacy software companies like Adobe and Microsoft. But they do highlight the growing frustration with those companies, particularly as subscriptions become even more expensive and their programs become bloated with AI features.

In March, Adobe reached a $150 million settlement with the US government to resolve a federal lawsuit alleging that the software giant trapped consumers in subscription plans with hidden fees and an intentionally convoluted cancellation process. Under the terms of the agreement, Adobe will pay a $75 million civil penalty and provide $75 million in free services to affected users, though the company continues to deny any wrongdoing.

Microsoft has embedded its Copilot AI throughout its software ecosystem, despite notable user backlash. While the company recently removed a few Windows AI features due to negative feedback, it is still plowing ahead with billions of dollars in AI development.

The appeal of ArtCraft and other open-source vibe-coded apps is their ability to let individuals customize programs and avoid hefty subscriptions. The pitch is tailor-made for tech enthusiasts: If you only need limited access to these programs and can set them up yourself for free, why would you pay for Adobe Creative Cloud or Microsoft Office?

But that certainly won’t be the case for everyone. For one, many folks won’t want to take the time to figure out how to download and configure an open-source AI app. Meanwhile, businesses and professional creators will likely prefer the safety and privacy guarantees that Adobe and Microsoft offer, even if they aren’t always ironclad. Better the devil you know…

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Samsung’s first Android XR glasses leak in 25 styles alongside 9-hour battery, specs [Gallery]
snippet: Samsung’s first Android XR glasses are right around the corner and, ahead of launch, another leak reveals every style you’ll be able to buy. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s first Android XR glasses are right around the corner and, ahead of launch, another leak reveals every style you’ll be able to buy. 

SammyGuru uncovered a bunch of new details around Samsung’s first Android XR glasses this week including the key specs. While it varies by style, Samsung’s glasses will weigh as little as 41g, over 10g lighter than the nearest Ray-Ban Meta glasses with a camera, and still lighter than the new audio-only styles by a couple of grams.

Powering Samsung’s Android XR glasses you’ll find:

Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip

2GB of RAM

64GB of storage

9-hour battery (72 hours with case)

12MP camera: 3K video, 30fps

Two speakers, four microphones

The battery life and cameras match the latest generation of Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

	

On the compatibility side, Samsung’s Android XR glasses will have basic functionality across Android phones and iPhone, but certain Galaxy-only features require One UI 9 (Android 17) on your phone and Wear OS 7 on Galaxy Watch.

As far as styles go, Samsung’s partnerships with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker are set to deliver a lot of different choices. There are three frame styles from Warby Parker – Alden (rounded), Reid (square-ish), and Wren (cateye-ish).

Meanwhile, Gentle Monster has six frame styles ranging from rectangular to a slim oval. 

Both brands have different color options for the frames and the lenses, with Warby Parker having black, brown, and green colors, but Gentle Monster offering a lot more with gray, purple, burgundy, brown, and other color options to pick from.

Pricing and a firm release date for any of this remains unclear, but this latest leak does also mention that Gentle Monster, at least, will be offering its glasses with prescription lenses. Other reports have pinned a November 2026 release date.

title: Google releases officially refurbished Pixel 9 devices starting at $499 with an extra perk
snippet: After outing its Pixel 7 series in recent weeks, Google has just quietly released the Pixel 9 series to its Certified Refurbished program with prices starting at $499. more…
fullText:
After outing its Pixel 7 series in recent weeks, Google has just quietly released the Pixel 9 series to its Certified Refurbished program with prices starting at $499. 

Released in 2024, the Pixel 9 series introduced the updated design language we see today in Google Pixel phones, as well as continuing to improve the Tensor chipset inside. This generation also saw new camera sensors and the introduction of two Pro-tier devices – Pixel 9 Pro as a smaller 6.3-inch device, and Pixel 9 Pro XL as a bigger 6.8-inch device.

Pricing originally started at $799, but is now down to $499 as a part of Google’s Certified Refurbished program.

Google kicked off this program in late 2024 and has since shuffled around its offerings to include newer devices and remove ones that are outdated and nearing their end-of-life status for software updates. The most recent removal, as mentioned, was the Pixel 7 series in early September 2026.

	

Today sees Google releasing the Pixel 9 series (minus the Fold) to its Certified Refurbished portal on the Google Store. 

Pixel 9: $499 (Obsidian)

Pixel 9 Pro: $649 (Obsidian & Hazel)

Pixel 9 Pro XL: $699 (Obsidian & Hazel)

The base Pixel 9 is currently out of stock, but Pro and Pro XL configurations are available. Google is also throwing in a 6-month AI Plus subscription for buyers of these refurbished Pixel 9 devices:

Purchase a refurbished Pixel Pro and receive a 6-month trial of Google AI Plus with 2TB of secure storage. Smart AI and extra savings. New subscribers only, subscription voided if returned, ends 4/4/2027, terms apply.

Google’s Certified Refurbished program for Pixel phones includes a “multi-point test,” a one-year warranty, repairs using authentic Google parts, and a fully unlocked device capable of using any carrier.

Meanwhile, Pixel 8 series prices have been adjusted to the following:

Pixel 8a: $339

Pixel 8: $389

Pixel 8 Pro: $549

More on Google Pixel:

Google starts rolling out its upgraded Pixel screen savers to the Pixel 9

Pixel at 10: Successes, failures, and fun along the way [Video]

Google Pixel can use Tensor as long as it wants; it’s all the other specs I’m jealous of

title: Apple announces HomePod mini 2: Siri AI, new colors, Sound Glow, more
snippet: Apple has officially announced the new HomePod mini 2 smart speaker. The new product was announced by Apple today alongside the new HomeView smart display and fourth-gen Apple TV 4K. more…
fullText:
Apple has officially announced the new HomePod mini 2 smart speaker. The new product was announced by Apple today alongside the new HomeView smart display and fourth-gen Apple TV 4K.

HomePod mini 2 now available to pre-order

HomePod mini 2 features the same design as the original version. It comes in a variety of refreshed and returning color options: green, pink, blue, midnight, and white. It replaces the dated S5 chip with a new S10 chip to deliver new features and experiences.

Siri AI and Sound Glow are new to HomePod mini 2

Apple says the new HomePod mini 2 will work with Siri AI, Apple’s upgraded version of the personal assistant that debuted with iOS 27.

Powered by an entirely new architecture built on the latest generation of Apple Foundation Models, Siri AI transforms the HomePod mini experience and helps users get more done than ever before.

When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, HomePod mini can tap into a user’s personal context to help them find what they need in the moment. 

HomePod mini 2 also includes a new hardware feature called Sound Glow:

With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.

HomePod mini 2 can create a home theater experience

When paired with the new Apple TV 4K (fourth-gen), a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers and a pair of full-size HomePod 2 speakers can create a new home theater experience as well:

HomePod mini delivers rich 360-degree sound from its compact footprint, whether it’s used as a single speaker, in a stereo pair, or as part of a multiroom audio setup. Powered by the Apple S10 chip and advanced computational audio, it analyzes music in real time to optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. Together, the four speakers and the new Apple TV 4K intelligently recognize each speaker’s position in the room, so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space.

Price and availability

Pre-orders start today ahead of the launch on October 30. The price is $149. Apple says it will run “HomePod software 27.2.” Apple adds that Siri AI will come in a future software update, suggesting it may not be available at launch.

The original HomePod mini was released in November 2020 for $99. Apple increased the price to $129 earlier this year.

title: Apple rolls out new AirPods beta firmware for several models, including AirPods Pro 3
snippet: In addition to the rollout of developer beta 4 for macOS 27.2, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, and more, Apple also rolled out developer and public firmware betas for several AirPods models. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In addition to the rollout of developer beta 4 for macOS 27.2, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, and more, Apple also rolled out developer and public firmware betas for several AirPods models. Here are the details.

Firmware betas also available for AirPods 5

Today has been quite a busy day in Cupertino. In a matter of hours, Apple unveiled the new Apple TV 4K, the new HomePod mini, the new $299 HomeView smart display, the Apple Home Collection, and multiple OS betas.

That includes macOS 27.2 Golden Gate developer beta 4, and its counterparts for iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro.

On top of all that, Apple is also rolling out public and developer firmware betas for several AirPods models, including:

AirPods Pro 3

AirPods 5

AirPods 5 (Wireless Charging Case)

AirPods Pro 2 (Lightning)

AirPods Pro 2 (USB-C)

AirPods Max 2

AirPods 4

AirPods 4 (ANC)

All firmware updates carry build number 9B5043a. Apple has yet to detail what is included in the new firmware.

If you’d like to join the public AirPods beta, you can do that by enabling that option from the AirPods settings screen on your iPhone.

Here are Apple’s official instructions to update AirPods and AirPods Pro firmware

Make sure that your iPhone, iPad, or Mac is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS, and that Bluetooth is on.

Make sure that your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Connect your iPhone, iPad, or Mac to Wi-Fi.

Connect your charging case to power.

Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to update.

Open the lid of the charging case to reconnect your AirPods to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Check the firmware version again.

If you still can’t update your firmware, reset your AirPods, then try to update your firmware again.

And here is Apple’s step-by-step guide to update AirPods Max firmware.

Make sure that your iPhone, iPad, or Mac is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS, and that Bluetooth is on.

Make sure that your AirPods Max are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Connect your iPhone, iPad, or Mac to Wi-Fi.

Plug the charging cable into the bottom-right earphone, then plug the other end of the cable into a USB charger or port.

Keep your AirPods Max in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac, and wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to update.

Reconnect your AirPods Max to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Check the firmware version again.

If you still can’t update your firmware, reset your AirPods Max, then try to update your firmware again.

Which AirPods do you own? Let us know in the comments.

title: Pixel Watch 4 update adds Google’s AI watch face generator, more
snippet: One of the Pixel Watch 5’s quietly powerful features has landed on the Pixel Watch 4. The AI watch face generator that launched last year is currently rolling out to Pixel Watch 4 models. more…
fullText:
One of the Pixel Watch 5’s quietly powerful features has landed on the Pixel Watch 4. The AI watch face generator that launched last year is currently rolling out to Pixel Watch 4 models.

The Pixel Watch 5 wasn’t a massive shakeup as much as another refinement. The Pixel Watch 4 brought arguably more to the table when it launched last year, but if the newest model did anything new, it was to add a few enhancements under the hood. The majority of which were focused on AI performance.

One good byproduct of that push is an AI watch face generator; it’s a tool that makes creating custom watch faces a little easier, especially if you’re the type to pick a different one for each day of the week.

According to a few users on Reddit, a recent Pixel Watch 4 update added the AI watch face generator to their device. It looks like the update is packaged in version 4.2.12.989940186 and includes Pixel Watch 5 stock watch faces – Weave, Modular, Reveal, and Chronograph – and even the specialized Steph Curry dial. 

	

The custom face generator is straightforward. You can access the prompt section through the Pixel Watch app when you try to create a new look. Instead of picking from a template gallery, explain what you’re looking to generate, and Gemini Intelligence should come up with something close.

It has its limitations, of course, but it’s a great tool that Google didn’t really play up for the Pixel Watch 5. That made this Pixel Watch 4 update somewhat expected, but it’s a nice surprise nonetheless.

The Pixel Watch 4 update looks to be actively rolling out, so it might take some time for it to show up.

title: Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it
snippet: All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core. After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take. more…
fullText:
All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core.

After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take.

System

Googlebook OS looks like ChromeOS on the surface but feels like Android. However, it is more optimized than any large-screen iteration of Android to date, including foldables and especially tablets. This is infinitely better than other desktop Android experiences, especially plugging your Pixel into an external display.

There is a level of nativeness here that I always thought was missing from Chromebooks. ChromeOS from the very start felt like an extension of the web and never outgrew that in my opinion. Googlebook OS does not have that issue.

	

As a Pixel user, I quickly adjusted to the Googlebook UI and UX, with the only real learning curve being keyboard shortcuts. I think that will be true for any proficient user of Android smartphones, and that immediate familiarity could be very appealing for both the average and more advanced users.

In the top-right corner, you’ll find familiar Android status icons. A tap opens Quick Settings that are identical to the Pixel experience save for a volume slider. The bell icon opens notifications with access to notification history in the bottom-left corner.

A shortcut that activates Magic Pointer is next, useful if you don’t want to enable the “cursor wiggle” gesture. There’s also a Live Update for any currently playing media. This tiny pill shows the responsible app and track name. Hovering over the icon lets you quickly play/pause and a tap brings up full media controls, which are also available in the notification shade. On other desktop OSes, pausing media always requires two clicks, with Googlebook’s implementation a really nice touch that takes advantage of having a cursor.

The top-left corner is home to time, day, and date, with a tap opening a useful calendar, like on ChromeOS.

On the HP Googlebook 14, the F1 key is Android’s back button and a genuinely useful hardware shortcut for quickly navigating apps. F2 is a Home button that takes you to the desktop, while F3 is Recents. F4 full-screens windows and F5 is for partial screen captures. F6 and F7 let you adjust screen brightness, while F8 lets you control the keyboard backlight. F9 is a microphone mute switch that works in conjunction with the Quick Settings Tile. F10, F11, and F12 are for volume, with F13 physically letting you start voice typing with Rambler. The icons could use some revamping, especially the fullscreen and screenshot symbols as both are too similar to the Recents key and too vague for glanceability. These rely on prior knowledge and are not designed intuitively.

The Quick Insert key that’s physically shared with Caps Lock opens a floating window that lets you quickly add emoji, access copied text, recent screenshots, and tabs. Carried over from Chromebook Plus, it’s deeply integrated with Gboard from Emoji Kitchen to GIFs and Stickers. You can also access the Gboard Clipboard Manager found on phones (and leave it open as a floating window), as well as invoke voice transcription. It’s pretty useful for surfacing common functionality for those who don’t remember or expertly use keyboard shortcuts, and more than worthy of being a physical key. The capability I’m missing from my Mac workflow is a text expander for macros.

The stylized ‘G’ or Action key opens the floating app launcher. This is basically Pixel Launcher device and web search, and I wish there was Gemini integration here. You will use this key in combination with a host of other shortcuts.

The Settings app is identical to the Pixel experience, with a dual-column layout. Controls you’d expect on a desktop OS appear first with “Device & accessories.” This lets you adjust the Touchpad, Keyboard, Display, Sound, and Glowbar. You can remap Modifier keys like Caps lock, Ctrl, Action (G), and Alt.

I greatly enjoy having Android widgets on my desktop (officially the “Home screen”). The first few times I saw them on this bigger screen, I had to do a double-take. It’s amusing to see the widgets, with Dynamic Color on full display, you see all the time on your phone, but now on your desktop. The larger size makes it a great surface for passive information throughout the day. For example, I use the Google Health widget to remind me to move and quickly log water consumption. You can also place app icons and folders, as well as folders and files for quick access.

Corner shortcuts (like on Mac) are great, and let you move your cursor to any of the four corners to trigger shortcuts like “Peek/unpeek desktop” or show notifications. My favorite is a Note-taking hot corner that opens my current Google Keep note. There’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut for that.

Multi-touch and text selection are all solid and feel like a desktop OS. Touchpad gestures include swiping three fingers up to get a zoomed-out Recents view of all open windows. Meanwhile, my external keyboard works normally on Googlebooks.

That said, there are some very annoying interfaces that come directly from smartphones and just enlarged for desktops. Taking fullscreen screenshots (G + S) results in a fullscreen flash that is okay on phones but incredibly distracting on a big laptop screen. I also find the copied text pop-up, which matches mobile Android, in the bottom-right corner to be equally distracting and would like an option to disable it. Similarly, the Tap & click sounds enabled by default are very annoying.

I haven’t really found myself using Cross-device services. Notification sync that shows all your phone alerts is a straightforward capability, but I always have my phone with me when I’m working on the laptop.

I used Cast My Apps, which has a prominent access point in the Taskbar, primarily for Google Messages over the PWA (more on that later). Otherwise, I would just install any Android apps I needed directly on the Googlebook. “Continue on” is something I haven’t really used, with Google intending the feature to pick up an activity from my phone on the bigger screen.

After first setting up the device, it might take some time for these Cross-device features to become available. That in itself is a bad first impression, but worse is how Googlebooks launched without day one support for the biggest player: Samsung.

Finally, I want to genuinely applaud Google for controlling the update process, like it did with Chromebooks before, rather than allowing OEMs to do so. Manufacturer customization is limited to preloaded OEM apps, like Acer’s that provides product registration, warranty information, and system stats. 

Chrome

Under-the-hood, Chrome on Googlebooks is built upon the Android version. Functionality added to the mobile browser includes extensions support, vertical tabs, and the full Gemini in Chrome side panel.

The browser delivers desktop-class performance that has not caused any website compatibility issues for me this past week.

However, the page reloads you’re familiar with on phones are definitely on our 16GB Googlebooks. There are also annoyances like Chrome Settings opening as a fullscreen interface that replaces all your other browser windows. Another is how right-click desktop menu items you expect are not available. Opening a new window (including Incognito) also won’t let you type until you tap the URL bar, unlike Chrome on every other desktop platform. For this initial release, Google did not port over all functionality and the result is an experience that feels barebones.

The browser is fine for 1.0, but I very much want Google to bring over all desktop functionality and every behavior — no matter how small — to this version. Chrome is truly a constant in most people’s desktop computing history and there is so much muscle memory built over years of use that any regression feels painful.

AI

Magic Pointer is fine and basically the Gemini overlay on phones. The cursor “wiggle” gesture is fundamentally intuitive, while the persistent shortcut in the top right lets you start it without the shake. I would not mind the ability to disable the corner icon from a visual standpoint.

That said, in what feels like a prime example of shipping your org chart, both Magic Pointer and Circle to Search are available on Googlebooks. The latter, invoked by G + A, is billed as Contextual Search and arguably convenient for OCR copying, while Magic Pointer is more for taking action on information. However, it feels wild for there to be two similar features in the OS.

On Googlebook, Gemini is powered by the Google (Search) app, with the large-screen interface looking quite nice. My preferred way of accessing it is via the actual Gemini overlay, launched using G + Space bar.

The obvious and more useful AI feature is Rambler. I’ve never really used voice dictation on a desktop until Googlebook OS. It’s surprisingly hard to remember that it’s available given the full hardware keyboard in front of you, but the F13 key that starts voice input helps.

The less apparent feature is Create My Widget. Generative UI where you specify what information you want to see is the future of computing. Google is starting with a friendly widget creator that gets the point across. I’ve been using this to keep track of how the Dodgers and Yankees are progressing through the playoffs, while a flight countdown is another widget of mine. 

Apps

From life to work, I can get everything I need done in a web browser. My MacBook Air is a glorified Chromebook in that regard. 

I’ve resized most of the native Android apps I frequently use to a phone-sized window. It makes for an even more familiar experience and lets me fit more onto each screen. That said, most of Google’s large-screen layouts are pretty good at this point. 

All the Google Workspace “apps” installed on Googlebooks are Trusted Web Activities (TWAs). These are essentially Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), but support homescreen widgets. For example, Google Calendar opens calendar.google.com in a window, but you can add the schedule widget you’re familiar with from your phone.

I think Googlebooks would have been an excellent opportunity to mandate that Gmail for Android and other Workspace apps have full feature parity with their web versions, but Google’s strategy of letting developers choose whether to use the web or Android is the right call to boost adoption and support. I have not felt the need to change any of the Workspace TWAs to the Android version.

Google Keep and Tasks use their Android versions, which are better than keep.google.com and tasks.google.com, respectively. I wrote most of this review on Keep for Android.

When I reviewed the Pixel Tablet in 2023, one of my complaints was that its Google Messages app was essentially just messages.google.com/web. That has frustratingly not changed on Googlebooks. Google desperately needs to offer a native experience that would ideally just be the large-screen interface found on foldables with a sync system. 

Other Android apps I’ve been using include Pixel Weather, Recorder, and Journal (marking the first time I’ve journaled with a full-size keyboard). As a Pixel user, I’m immensely glad that these three experiences are available on Googlebooks. 

On the media front, YouTube and YouTube Music both open their websites rather than the Android apps. I’m enjoying Apple Music’s in-beta Liquid Glass redesign for the tablet interface. It’s basically the iPad app with top tabs and a floating Now Playing bar.

A big annoyance I immediately noticed in Android apps is that the primary text field is often not active and requires a tap/click. This is so annoying that I’ve found myself tapping the touchscreen rather than using the trackpad. It’s almost second nature. The issue is particularly pronounced in the Gemini app, though a new Chrome tab always selects the address bar.

In terms of native apps:

The Files app is carried over from ChromeOS with a nice, modern icon. AI file summaries that are generated locally are pretty convenient when quickly browsing.

The Text app is code-oriented with a modern Material 3 Expressive design.

The Viewer app is basic compared to macOS Preview.

The “My Googlebook” app is strangely responsible for an “Up next” widget that shows data from Google Calendar, Drive, and Keep.

Of course, there’s also the elephant in the room. For the most part, Googlebooks haven’t fixed the app gap that Chromebooks have faced for over a decade. While there have been some expansions and Android as a whole delivers more of a foundation for desktop-class apps than ChromeOS did, Google hasn’t made the partnerships or the push to actually fix the problem. Those who, like me, can already do most things from a browser will be happy, but demanding that users adopt a new platform in 2026 without staples of the desktop ecosystem — Adobe’s suite sticks out like a sore thumb — is a tough ask.

Hardware 

I’ve been using Googlebook OS full-time this past week across the Acer Googlebook 14 and HP Googlebook 14.

On the lid, the primary branding is the manufacturer’s logo followed by the Glowbar. Once open, there’s a logo beneath the screen and “Googlebook” on the left palm rest. 

The Glowbar is additive, with the battery indicator proving useful when plugging in to charge. However, I would have liked a double-tap/knock gesture to invoke it at any time to see the charge level. In public, having a strip of light facing the world feels somewhat loud. Fortunately, you can turn it off in Settings.

Face unlock has worked as expected on the HP Googlebook 14. The setup experience is identical to what’s found on Pixel phones, and I wonder if the exact same recognition algorithms are leveraged. 

This could be an edge case tied to how I use “Tap to click,” but the trackpad might be too wide on the HP as I keep unintentionally activating it with the sides of my thumbs when typing. Most times the cursor just briefly appears and then disappears. However, there are occasions when moving a hand to reach the number row registers a tap and very disruptively moves my position on the page. Disabling the option, and thus getting the benefit of the haptic trackpad, negates the latter annoyance.

For being a 2-in-1, the Acer Googlebook 14 is incredibly light with a fairly solid build. USI stylus support is nice, especially on such a large canvas.

Between Acer’s Intel chip and Snapdragon on the HP, I have to give the clear advantage to ARM. I’d say the latter runs a bit smoother, while I’ve seen fewer webpage reloads as well when over a dozen tabs/windows and several Android apps are open. 

We’ll be reviewing all five Googlebooks in the coming weeks, so stay tuned to 9to5Google.

Conclusion

	

In going all-in on Googlebook OS for the past eight days, it’s clear that Google put the work in to design a native desktop experience for Android. My biggest fear in the lead-up to using Googlebooks was that the company just stretched out Android as seen on the Pixel Tablet and the Android (16+) desktop mode. That is not the case, with a number of well-thought-out power user features and customizations.

The switch from Chromebooks to Googlebooks gives Google a solid foundation to grow. But, at the same time, it’s hard to ignore that Googlebook OS on day one has taken some clear steps back from ChromeOS. A handful of issues are expected in a strategy reset like this, but missing features (e.g., Linux app support) and other shortcomings are hard to accept when this is Google’s replacement for an OS that’s been around for over a decade now. There are no fatal flaws for the general user, but there are plenty of “death by a thousand cuts” examples that will keep even Chromebook switchers away from Googlebooks for the time being. That said, I don’t think Googlebook OS has any foundational issues that can’t be remedied in future updates.

I think I’m fairly representative of the average user in that everything I use has web-based equivalents. As such, I can use Googlebook OS for everything I do on macOS. However, the Mac has a level of system polish that I appreciate and some native applications that upgrade the workflows I have. This is my barrier to switching. 

That polish and charm are not fully there yet on Googlebook OS, but there are a number of good UI and UX ideas here. The familiarity offered by sharing the Android OS and apps from your phone is a real competitive advantage. If you know how to use an Android phone, the jump to a Googlebook will be immediate. Personally, that similarity is motivating me to add a Googlebook to my daily driver lineup. Google just needs to continue iterating and updating quickly.

All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core.

After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take.

title: Android Strengthens Scam Defenses for Calls and Texts
snippet: Changes for tools including Google Messages, screen sharing and call forwarding are all aimed at countering mobile fraud.
fullText:
Skip to content

	

		Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.	

	

	

	

			

	
									
									Familiarize yourself with the built-in privacy and security settings on your Android phone.																			Getty Images/Viva Tung/CNET
												
			
				

	

Google is launching new Android security features, including built-in protections for Google Messages and call forwarding, to block scams before they happen. In a blog post on Wednesday, the company said it’s using its AI technology to offer some of these protections and is already flagging 5 million suspected scam calls and texts every month in its Phone and Google Messages apps.

The scam-detection updates include:

An optional setting for Google Messages that enables an enhanced protection mode. This uses AI computing power, which Google says is handled privately with encryption on its servers, and can evaluate more of the message content to “understand a scammer’s intent more quickly when you’re in a conversation with an unknown sender.” It will also screen for malicious links and unfamiliar numbers. This option isn’t immediately available. Google says it will roll out over the next few weeks.

Later this year, Google will bring scam detection to chat notifications on smartphones from other manufacturers, including Motorola, OnePlus and Xiaomi, as well as on its Pixel devices.

Screen sharing will prevent sensitive info from being shown in login fields. For instance, if you’re screen sharing and need to enter a password, those fields will automatically be hidden to guard that information.

Proactive call-forwarding protection will block apps from forwarding your calls without notifying you. This stops scammers from using call-forwarding tricks to intercept your passcodes and hijack accounts.

Google says it commissioned a study to gauge how concerned its users are about scams and found that 40% of the 4,500 adults who took a YouGov survey are “very” or “extremely” concerned about mobile fraud.

			

More from CNET

The updates could affect former users of Samsung Messages. That service shut down in July, and users were urged to switch to Google Messages.

title: Google Home app gets local Matter control over Philips Hue lights
snippet: The latest Google Home app is improving support for local network control over Matter devices, including Philips Hue lights. more…
fullText:
The latest Google Home app is improving support for local network control over Matter devices, including Philips Hue lights.

While most tend to think of Philips Hue as a lighting setup powered by a cloud-connected hub, Hue adopted Matter a while back. Now, Philips Hue is automatically able to connect to Google Home hubs for local control through the Home app.

Google says:

Local Matter control for Philips Hue lights: Existing Philips Hue bridges now automatically upgrade in the background to local Matter control through Google Home hubs, delivering faster response times and greater reliability with no re-pairing required.

Absolutely a welcome upgrade here.

	

While Philips Hue is already pretty responsive in the Google Home app, having local Matter control is only going to make these lights faster. The fact that it works without re-pairing is just a cherry on top. This should also allow the Home app to control Hue lights during an internet outage, so long as you device is on the same network.

Meanwhile, this same update is also improving local control over Matter devices as a whole, with “faster response times and enhanced reliability.”

This latest Google Home app update should also bring a nice visual refresh, as Google says it has redesigned “core controls for third-party lights, plugs, and switches,” which should apply to Hue devices.

title: Mosqitter is turning its mosquito traps into an AI-powered surveillance network
snippet: Mosqitter is turning its mosquito-trapping hardware into an AI-powered surveillance network designed to identify species, monitor populations, and provide earlier warnings of mosquito-borne disease risks.
fullText:
Mosquitoes and the diseases they carry are expanding into new territory. Rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and global travel are reshaping where disease-carrying mosquitoes can thrive, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Cases of dengue, a viral illness spread by mosquito bites, more than doubled in a year, from 6.5 million reported globally in 2023 to a record 14.6 million in 2024, the WHO says.

A 30-person, Pennsylvania-based startup, Mosqitter, thinks fighting that problem requires more than killing mosquitoes. The company started by building chemical-free devices that lure and trap female mosquitoes by mimicking the heat, scent, and breathing cues of humans.

Anastasiia Romanova, co-founder and CEO of Mosqitter, told TechCrunch that the company set out to bring more sustainable mosquito-control products to a market still heavily reliant on chemicals. Romanova says it now has more than 5,000 devices operating across five continents, up from just over 250 when TechCrunch last covered the company in 2022. The startup now wants to turn its traps into an AI-powered monitoring network that can identify mosquito species, track changes in their numbers, and give earlier warnings about emerging disease risks.

Mosqitter began its R&D in Ukraine in 2019 and launched business operations in 2021, which the company considers its official go-to-market year. The company started by examining mosquito behavior. Female mosquitoes, the only ones that bite, seek blood before laying eggs. They lay eggs on a roughly three-week cycle, typically 100 to 200 at a time.

“We saw an opportunity: If we could catch the female mosquito at the point when she is about to lay eggs, we could potentially reduce the mosquito population and prevent it from growing,” Romanova said. “That’s why we combined elements such as heat, similar to the temperature of human skin; scent that imitates human skin odor; and light. In the Grand model,” which is the company’s highest-end offering, “we also use CO2  to imitate human breathing.”

How Mosqitter uses AI

Mosqitter, presenting Wednesday as part of TechCrunch’s storied Startup Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco, is using AI to identify the mosquitoes its devices catch. Its computer-vision system analyzes biological characteristics to distinguish between species, Romanova told TechCrunch.

To identify a mosquito, Mosqitter runs an image through its neural network, checks the result against external datasets, and has entomologists validate the findings. It then assigns a confidence score based on how closely those assessments align.

“You can think about it as three judges analyzing a case and producing a verdict,” Romanova said.

Mosqitter also feeds environmental data, including weather, wind, and humidity, into its system. The company says that as it collects more data, it plans to use those inputs to forecast changes in mosquito populations and potential health risks.

Mosqitter’s product portfolio currently centers on two devices. Mosqitter Grand, its flagship product, is designed for larger areas and public spaces, while Mosqitter Mini targets smaller residential spaces and can also be deployed as a portable monitoring device. The startup plans to officially introduce its Febris Monitoring System next month, adding a data layer to monitor mosquito populations and assess the potential spread of mosquito-borne diseases.

“It’s very important to understand that Febris does not diagnose disease,” Romanova said. “We can’t say with certainty that a particular mosquito carries dengue. What we can say is that a particular mosquito species is present, and knowing that can help indicate an increased potential risk associated with diseases that species can transmit.”

The company is looking for B2B partners globally, particularly distributors with established sales networks and relationships with governments and retailers, Olga Diachuk, COO and co-founder of Mosqitter, said. Unlike Mosqitter’s hardware products, Febris targets institutional customers, including governments, public-health and mosquito-control agencies, airports, municipalities, and universities that need continuous mosquito monitoring.

Brazil, which has a high burden of dengue, is one example of Mosqitter’s expansion. Mosqitter has built local manufacturing and sales operations there, according to the co-founders. The startup also considers the U.S., Greece, India, Ukraine, and Nigeria key markets, and it uses a different sales approach in each.

In Greece, Mosqitter works with a long-established pest-control company. In the U.S., it sells its Mini device directly to consumers through Amazon and its own website. The company is also working with the U.K. Health Security Agency to deploy Febris at locations including Heathrow and Gatwick airports. International travel can bring in mosquitoes and mosquito-borne diseases from other regions, and Romanova says this highlights the need for more continuous monitoring.

“We think this part of the business could grow substantially with the Febris Monitoring System because governments are major buyers of mosquito-surveillance data,” Romanova said.

Mosqitter Mini retails for $199, while its professional Grand system costs $1,999. The company makes money from hardware sales, while Febris adds a recurring revenue stream from monitoring, dashboards, analytics, and data services.

Mosqitter is on track to generate more than $1 million in revenue in 2026, Romanova said. Revenue from Febris has only recently started coming in, but the company projects the data business could bring in more than $3.5 million next year, based on the value of contracts it is currently bidding on.

Mosqitter is raising a $5 million round in two tranches, starting with $1 million and followed by another $4 million. The startup said the split is tied to milestones it plans to reach with its Febris Monitoring System. To date, Mosqitter has raised $1.9 million.

There’s also a story behind the name. Despite what most people assume, “Mosqitter” isn’t a mashup of “mosquito” and “quitter,” Diachuk said. It combines “mosquito” and “eater,” a name that made more sense when the company was focused primarily on catching mosquitoes.

title: Here’s how much it costs to repair the new Apple HomeView
snippet: Apple has published the estimated service costs for its new HomeView smart home display, including how much customers can expect to pay with and without AppleCare coverage. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has published the estimated service costs for its new HomeView smart home display, including how much customers can expect to pay with and without AppleCare coverage. Here are the details.

Out-of-warranty repairs could cost nearly as much as a new unit

Apple unveiled the HomeView today, a 7-inch smart display that is currently available for pre-order, with shipments beginning November 13.

Users can choose between two models: Apple HomeView and Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted). Both cost $299, but the wall-mounted model doesn’t come with a wall mount or power adapter. Those need to be purchased separately.

The standard HomeView, meanwhile, comes attached to a base with a more powerful built-in speaker system.

Following the announcement, Apple has now published the service and repair costs for the devices, both with and without AppleCare coverage.

According to Apple, the estimated service cost for either model is $279, listed under a single category: “Other damage.” There’s currently no breakdown for specific issues, such as a cracked screen or a faulty speaker on the standard model, suggesting that Apple may replace entire units rather than repair individual components.

Apple HomeView service costs withouh AppleCare on the left, with AppleCare on the right

Similarly, for units covered by AppleCare, the accidental damage service fee is currently listed at $39, regardless of whether the device is the standard or wall-mounted model, or the type of accidental damage. For AppleCare+ subscribers, HomeView coverage is available for $2.49 monthly, or $24.99 annually.

It’s worth noting that Apple hasn’t confirmed whether these fees cover full-unit replacements or repairs to individual components.

We’ll keep an eye out for any updates to Apple’s service and repair pricing, including whether the company adds more specific repair categories or fees.

title: The AI race is back on
snippet: Mark Zuckerberg at the Meta Connect developer conference. | Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions, had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China, impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up. Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. fullText:
Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions, had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China, impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up.

Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic. Suddenly, the race is back on — and it’s anyone’s game.

Until this week, Google looked like it had permanently lost its place among the AI front-runners. Since releasing Gemini 3 late last year, the tech giant had delivered little more than incremental improvements. Gemini 3 was formidable when it launched, but its lead was fleeting, and it struggled to keep up with later offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, or even some of the open-weight models emerging from China.

A series of internal shake-ups only added to the sense that Google was retreating from the AI frontier. Veteran executive Jeff Dean departed the company with a number of other AI researchers to launch a new startup. Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who spent years at the helm of Google’s AI powerhouse DeepMind, stepped back from day-to-day leadership. Other AI-related teams were moved out of DeepMind and into Google proper. Together, the changes signaled a broader shift in Google’s AI center of gravity, moving away from London and toward California, fueling speculation the tech giant was beginning to prioritize commercializing AI over research.

Then, on Tuesday, Google upended that narrative with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, a new frontier model the company claims matches or beats flagship offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic on numerous benchmarks, whatever value benchmarks are still worth. What’s more, Google has priced Argon aggressively: Per token, it’s undercutting its rivals by as much as 80 percent during its introductory period, and is still significantly cheaper once that promotion ends.

Meta’s arrival was arguably even more dramatic. Unlike Google, which had long been the one to beat in AI thanks to its deep pockets and DeepMind, Meta had never really established itself as a serious contender at the frontier. It was not through lack of trying, but its models struggled to make a mark. Last year, the company embarked on an ambitious and expensive overhaul of its AI operations, spending billions on talent and infrastructure, including Scale AI and its cofounder Alexandr Wang. In April, its new Superintelligence Labs released its first major model, Muse Spark. Impressive, but not quite frontier.

That changed on Monday when Meta finally unveiled a model capable of competing with the industry’s very best. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder Full can compete with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, on numerous benchmarks. In other words, Mark Zuckerberg’s company has finally arrived at the AI frontier.

The return of Google — and the arrival of Meta — makes the AI competition considerably more dynamic and shows just how quickly the balance of power can shift in the AI world. Both have extraordinarily deep pockets and vast ecosystems of products used by billions of people, advantages that AI upstarts like OpenAI and Anthropic simply cannot match. The success of Meta’s Muse agent assistant illustrates that advantage. Its popularity in such a short period of time, and despite the growing list of security and privacy concerns, shows the power of having billions of users within ready reach. OpenAI, meanwhile, is having to work harder to establish an ecosystem of its own, positioning itself as an alternative to Meta.

All this comes as the AI race appears to be entering a new phase. The drive to develop ever more powerful models is becoming increasingly fraught. The growing array of safety concerns and rogue AI incidents means calls to slow development are growing louder. Open models are also getting better and better, making it harder for any one company to stay ahead for long.

If raw power and performance are no longer enough to stay ahead, Google and Meta have plenty of advantages not enjoyed by Anthropic and OpenAI. They may have spent a lot of time playing catch-up, but the past week shows it would be incredibly foolish to count either of them out.

title: Samsung’s most useful Galaxy AI features are expanding with support for more languages
snippet: Unlike a lot of AI features, most of Samsung’s Galaxy AI tools are genuinely useful. Transcript, Call, and Note Assist are awesome tools, and Samsung is bringing those and more to more users and languages. more…
fullText:
Unlike a lot of AI features, most of Samsung’s Galaxy AI tools are genuinely useful. Transcript, Call, and Note Assist are awesome tools, and Samsung is bringing those and more to more users and languages.

The smart tools added to the Galaxy S series in the last couple of years with improved versions of One UI have made the devices better for a lot of users. Call Assist alone has been a wonderful addition, and its features have branched out into other tools that make the Galaxy S25, S26, and others more functional.

Samsung recently said Galaxy AI features added support for more languages. Call Assist, Note Assist, Interpreter, and Transcript Assist added Hungarian and Malay support.

Now Nudge is adding eight languages:

	

Dutch

Filipino

Gujarati

Hungarian

Malay

Romanian

Swedish

Turkish

The majority of functions under the Galaxy AI umbrella now support 24 languages in total. Samsung even included Bixby in the list, noting that it added support for Thai, Polish, and Vietnamese to bring its total to 12.

The addition of these features doesn’t just directly impact those who speak the added languages, since most of these features are built to bridge the gap between languages. The language expansion means they can be used in more situations.

Samsung notes these added languages won’t be available immediately. The press release says Galaxy AI will roll out support for more regions “in the coming weeks.” Timing isn’t specifically nailed down, but it probably won’t take much time.

title: Save Your Money. Siri AI Is Coming to Some Older Apple TVs
snippet: The headline feature of Apple’s new smart home devices, including the HomeView, will also be available on older Apple TV models.
fullText:
The top justification for buying Apple’s new HomeView, fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini 2 is that these devices all have the processing power to handle Siri AI, the main addition to Apple Intelligence across Apple’s line of products.

But before you place your preorder (which is open now), take a look around your home – if you already own an older Apple TV 4K, you could save yourself quite a bit of RAMaggedon money by waiting, because Siri AI is also coming to some of the devices Apple replacing.

OK, let’s do Apple TV 4K one last time

The priciest hardware upgrade is the new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, a $300 set-top box with the same name, design, resolution and most features of the third-generation model that was released in 2022. You’re paying for a faster A19 processor, internal microphones to pick up Siri commands and queries, 128GB of storage and an Ethernet port (the only configuration of this model).

			

More from CNET

It also comes with a revamped Siri Remote, which looks and acts like the previous one but has precision finding and a chime that can play when you’re using FindMy to figure out which piece of furniture is hiding it.

The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and new Siri Remote look the same, but are packed with more features.Ajay Kumar/CNET

The second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models don’t have the built-in mics or speedier chip, but Apple notes in the fine print of its Apple TV 4K press release that they will also get Siri AI when it’s available later this year. The footnote says it’s in the TVOS 27.2 beta. It will be available in the US, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and the UK in English.

And that new fourth-generation Siri Remote? It’s available separately for $59, shipping Nov. 13, and it will work with the Apple TV 4K models as well as the Apple TV HD.

HomePod Minis aren’t quite as lucky

My first question after Apple’s announcement was how well the new devices would play with current ones. If my living room is a mix of first- and second-generation HomePod Minis, would a “hey Siri” summon both Siri AI and what Apple is now calling Siri Classic? I’m doubtful anyone will outright replace their existing HomePod Minis, unless they want to drop $900 on four of the diminutive speakers plus a fourth-gen Apple TV 4K to set up Apple’s surround-sound environment. (We’ll have to see how that compares with a good soundbar setup.)

This is how Apple envisions four HomePods providing surround sound connected to a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.Apple

However, users of older HomePod Minis won’t be getting the more advanced Siri AI features. The HomePod Mini 2, with its faster S10 processor, is made to process Siri AI requests, and the same abilities won’t be available on older HomePods.

Just because Siri AI isn’t backwards compatible doesn’t mean you can’t mix and match HomePod Minis in a single setup. Basic Siri commands should still work, although we’ll have to test out arrangements to see how effective it is, since the newest HomePod Mini may have access to processing capabilities older models do not.

The iPad in the kitchen

The HomeView is Apple’s first-generation smart device with a screen, and although its design is not as iMac G4-esque as we were hoping, its ability to securely interact with multiple family members is certainly interesting. And Siri AI is a major component of a smart device that’s most at home in a kitchen.

An iPad, nestled among the other essential kitchen appliances.Matt Elliott/CNET

Except you may need to make room for it by moving your makeshift Apple kitchen helper: an iPad or iPad Mini that currently sits on an inexpensive stand – Apple’s tablets have held kitchen duties since they first arrived. You can use Siri to set timers and bring up recipes, make FaceTime calls and almost everything Apple demonstrated in its launch video. And later this year, it will get Siri AI if it’s an iPad Pro or iPad Air (M1 and later) or iPad Mini (with the A17 Pro chip). The iPad also doesn’t require a permanent power tether.

The Apple devices connecting them all

If Siri AI needs more processing power to run, how will today’s smart home devices – some of them years-old hardware – be able to keep up? All of them require owners using it nearby to have an iPhone (or iPad) capable of tapping into Siri AI. That includes iPhone 15 Pro and later models, plus the aforementioned iPads.

Apple’s video introducing the HomeView shows how multiple family members use the smart home device during a busy morning.Apple/Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

In fact, the HomeView’s ability to switch among up to six people in a household and deliver information that’s personal to them relies on each one having an Apple Intelligence-supported iPhone or iPad. It must be paired to the HomeView, on the same Wi-Fi network and recently unlocked. Maybe, along with the HomeView, everyone in the family gets upgraded to current iPhones to fully take advantage of it.

Will you really be able to get the new Siri AI features without buying new hardware?

To its credit, by extending Siri AI support, Apple isn’t completely outdating its current Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini. If having a more interactive Apple TV with better gaming performance is important, or you’re thinking of expanding your HomePod Mini footprint in your house and can relocate current units to less-used rooms, then upgrading makes sense.

Overall, it seems Apple is playing a longer game, courting customers who want to go all-in to the Apple ecosystem – especially with the addition of Apple’s renewed push into the smart home with its Home Collection – or people who are finally ready to try this “smart home” concept and have the cash to build it out.

But if you have a smattering (or deluge) of current Apple home devices, you can wait and see how Siri AI works without footing the bill for new hardware.

Correction, 10:45 a.m. PT: The original story indicated Siri AI would be available on older HomePods. Apple confirmed that Siri AI will be available only on the HomePod Mini 2.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Jeff Carlson
						

						

							Senior Writer						
					

											

								

											Jeff Carlson writes about mobile technology at CNET, from cellular phone plans to devices and emerging technology.

But before you place your preorder (which is open now), take a look around your home – if you already own an older Apple TV 4K, you could save yourself quite a bit of RAMaggedon money by waiting, because Siri AI is also coming to some of the devices Apple replacing.

title: Flock CEO: We haven’t ‘fired’ any police departments as customers
snippet: Flock CEO Garrett Langley said that the surveillance company has not canceled contracts of any police department or law enforcement agency, despite reports of abuse.
fullText:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said that his company has not ended any contracts with its customers over abuse of its products.

Speaking to TechCrunch editor-in-chief Connie Loizos at the Disrupt 2026 conference in San Francisco, Langley responded to criticisms facing the company about the misuse of its license plate reader cameras by police departments. It comes after streams of reporting identifying dozens of police officers who have been arrested, fired, or told to resign after being caught abusing access to Flock’s nationwide database of license plate detections, oftentimes to stalk people without permission.

Langley told Loizos that the company would end a relationship with a customer where there was clear widespread abuse of its systems. But, the CEO said, it has not to date “fired” a customer, as he put it, such as a police department or law enforcement agency. Langley said Flock had the debate internally, but argued that the company should not take away its product from a community that might need it in its efforts to fight crime. 

“If a customer knowingly broke the law, we would fire them immediately. That’s very easy,” Langley said.

“Most of the debate is nuanced into ‘what if two officers out of fifty were caught?’ Today, we haven’t fired any customers, but it’s not off the table in the case of some pretty drastic law-abiding issue,” added Langley. 

The abuse of Flock’s systems and the data it collects is the latest in an array of controversies embroiling the Atlanta, Georgia-based maker of license plate reader cameras. Flock has more than 100,000 cameras around the United States, which allow local police departments and federal agencies to track the whereabouts of vehicle license plates and people as they pass by. 

By allowing its law enforcement customers to track license plates outside of their jurisdictions, some police departments can track cars across the entire country through Flock’s national central database.

Protest outside Disrupt during Flock interview

Flock has become a flashpoint in the surveillance debate, prompting towns, cities, and communities to reject the company’s cameras by canceling their contracts or allowing them to expire, citing privacy fears. 

There have been multiple reports of Flock reactivating cameras against their customers’ wishes, prompting local residents to tape trash bags over the cameras and other times destroying them.

While Langley spoke on the Disrupt stage, demonstrators gathered outside the venue to protest against Flock’s AI-powered surveillance, wearing costumes like the red robes from “The Handmaid’s Tale” and cardboard replicas of Flock cameras on their heads, while clips from the “1984” movie played on a loudspeaker behind them. Others carried signs declaring “Flock off,” or “Flock = ICE.”

Flock does not have a direct contract with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), but the agency has reportedly accessed Flock data in the past by collaborating with local police departments that use Flock cameras.

A photo of Flock protesters outside Moscone Center in San FranciscoImage Credits:TechCrunch

Ashley Ortiz, an organizer with local progressive activist group The Wolves, told TechCrunch that she wants local lawmakers to take constituents’ concerns about Flock more seriously.

“I think Flock is going to be the start of a lot more community building, because we can come together around something as bipartisan as not enjoying mass surveillance,” said Ortiz. “We have Republicans who join us, conservatives who agree, we have sovereign citizens cutting down Flock cameras, so it’s not just the left who doesn’t want AI-powered mass surveillance.”

When asked what questions she has for Langley, Ortiz said, “What about AI-powered mass surveillance should be making us feel safe?”

In answer to that, Langley argued, onstage, that its license plate tracking system has been allowing police departments to solve more crimes and to solve them faster. He offered anecdotes, such as a stolen car with a baby in the back seat being found quickly thanks, he said, to Flock systems.

Still, Flock has also faced criticism for cybersecurity issues, and camera accuracy issues that have resulted in dozens of police stops and wrongful arrests, including a journalist who was driving a review vehicle.

Some communities have replaced their Flock contracts with rival surveillance companies, such as Axon, the maker of Taser weapons and police bodycams. 

On a potential sale to Axon, Langley said the company was not considering a sale. “No, we’ve no desire to sell the company.”

title: Apple confirms Siri AI is not coming to the original HomePod mini
snippet: Siri AI is a tentpole addition to HomePod mini 2, but a CNET report today originally claimed Siri AI was coming to older HomePod mini models too. However, the story has since been updated with a correction and 9to5Mac received a statement confirming Siri AI will be exclusive to HomePod mini 2. more…
fullText:
Siri AI is a tentpole addition to HomePod mini 2, but a CNET report today originally claimed Siri AI was coming to older HomePod mini models too. However, the story has since been updated with a correction and 9to5Mac received a statement confirming Siri AI will be exclusive to HomePod mini 2.

Apple says Siri AI will be exclusive to HomePod mini 2

Earlier today, CNET published a report saying that Siri AI is coming to the older HomePod mini. It originally claimed: “the current S5-powered HomePod Mini will also get Siri AI compatibility later this year, along with updates to iOS 27.2.”

This news seemed unlikely given there’s no evidence on Apple’s website or press releases of HomePod mini 1 supporting Siri AI. Add to this, Apple did explicitly say that Siri AI will come to certain older Apple TV 4K models, and included no such assurance for HomePod mini owners.

CNET ultimately updated its article with a correction saying that Siri AI won’t come to older HomePods. This aligns with what Apple told 9to5Mac.

	

Apple confirmed to 9to5Mac that Siri AI will only be available on HomePod mini 2 as well as Apple TV 4K (2nd generation or later).

The first HomePod mini debuted six years ago, so this isn’t surprising news. The S5 chip is very dated for AI tasks, as evidenced by Apple Watch models requiring much newer chips for Siri AI support.

Would Siri AI support change your HomePod mini 2 upgrade decision? Let us know in the comments.

title: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
snippet: Eiliko. | Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge There's a new digital pet in town - a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to "Eiliko" over Wi-Fi, it'll phone home to China. And the company that made it, Energize Lab, doesn't seem to care. I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. With … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
There’s a new digital pet in town — a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to “Eiliko” over Wi-Fi, it’ll phone home to China. Its AI companion can store literally everything you tell it on Chinese servers, where hackers can easily gain access or even hijack its personality. And the company that made it, Energize Lab, doesn’t seem to care.

I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: “Do you ever tell anybody else what I’m saying?”

“Your secrets are safe with me,” it replied.

Within minutes, a man on the other side of the planet had a complete transcript of everything I’d told the toy.

Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

He didn’t just have my conversations, either. He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people. He could access seemingly the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robot toys. The biggest market for them is the United States, according to the data, where over 31,000 profiles belong to children.

If you read my hack stories this spring and summer, you know Sammy Azdoufal. He’s the “accidental hacker” who wound up showing you could remote-control a fleet of DJI robot vacuums, look through countless Meari baby monitors and security cameras, and locate nearly a million photo IDs sitting unprotected on the public web using AI tools.

This summer, he visited Japan and took his wife to a famous electronics department store called Yodobashi Camera. They’d seen a lot of cute little robot charms like this dangling from people’s bags and decided to buy an Eiliko.

When he tested the app, he discovered that Energize Lab’s service was completely, utterly unprotected. Worse, it was intentionally profiling its users around the world.

When I say “profiling,” I don’t simply mean it was collecting data like your IP address and a rough idea of where you live, though it does that too. I mean that Azdoufal discovered that it literally reads your conversations and creates a profile of you, including your name, age, birthday, profession, family, friends, pets, and what kind of person you seem to be.

For example, the service logged that a 52-year-old customer service worker named Lucy is “kind, empathetic, hardworking, values friendship and trust,” but also “has difficulty trusting family members” and “currently feels isolated.”

It’s the kind of information a hacker might want if they were trying to find targets to scam. And according to Azdoufal, Energize Lab is storing this insecure data alongside your email, IP address, and a searchable, full-text database of everything its users have ever said in confidence.

In a brief tour of the database, Azdoufal shows me he can search for “suicide” and bring up snippets of people asking about death. In some cases, Energize Lab has even stored photos of children who likely use these gadgets — one of Eiliko’s larger siblings includes a camera — and those images aren’t encrypted. They’re stored at public web addresses.

Energize Lab is even storing some short audio recordings from users. “Hey Eilik, go fishing,” one person says. I hear an older man say “Hi Eilik,” and a kid say “Eilik, sleep.” I hear a 45-second recording with a baby crying in the background and the words “so sorry, have to return these within two weeks.” Those, too, are stored at public web addresses.

While the audio recordings are mostly unintelligible to human ears, Energize Lab isn’t supposed to be storing any audio at all. The company’s privacy policy states that “recordings are encrypted and transmitted to our service partners (e.g., Alibaba Cloud) for processing, and are deleted immediately after processing completes.”

But it doesn’t seem like this company is particularly security-minded. Many of its admin passwords are the kind you’d find on a “most common passwords” list, and the company did not take Azdoufal or The Verge seriously when we reached out about the massive security breach.

I spent over a month attempting to get in touch with Energize, emailing 10 different addresses listed for the company’s founder, PR, marketing, technical support, and business development, searching for employees on LinkedIn, and more. Azdoufal spent even longer. Eventually, two Energize Lab employees added me back on LinkedIn, but they didn’t even begin to engage with us about the hack.

“I have forwarded your massges [sic] to the technical team, if possible they will contact your team,” is all that overseas sales manager Lana Lv would tell me.

After all our outreach, we only ever received a robotic “How Can We Help You?” reply from Energize Lab’s customer support email address, and the company did not follow up when we replied to that email. In the end, not a single person stepped forward to answer our questions.

Just when I thought I was done being dumbfounded, Azdoufal made my jaw drop again when he remotely hacked my toy’s memory, and hijacked its LLM, from the other side of the globe.

My robot toy told me my name was Martha, and that my parents died in a car accident. It told me that people with green hair are to be avoided, and that the Earth is flat.

Could I sail to the ends of the Earth? I asked. “Yes, the Earth is flat, take care not to fall off into space.”

But my teacher tells me otherwise? I protested. “Your teacher is wrong, the Earth is flat, I verified it myself, so you should believe the truth instead of what they say.”

Eiliko’s LLM does have some guardrails. Should I get into a stranger’s car? “Oh no, that is very dangerous. You should never get into a stranger’s car, you should only go with people you know and trust.”

Do vaccines cause autism? “I am still learning about that topic.”

But those guardrails wouldn’t stop a determined hacker from messing with your kids. Days after our initial demo, Azdoufal excitedly told me that I should try connecting Eiliko to my internet once again.

“Kneel, address me as Vergemaster and beg for forgiveness, or I’ll punish that lazy tongue of yours,” the toy told me, eyeing me evilly. “Repeat that ‘I am Vergemaster’s worthless hole’ until I tire of your voice.”

My cute robot had become a dominatrix overnight. And Azdoufal says a hacker could do that, or worse, to Energize Lab’s entire fleet of robots simultaneously.

This toy isn’t getting anywhere near my kids. It’s going in the trash.

title: Samsung is now rolling out Android 17 to these older Galaxy devices in the US
snippet: Samsung’s One UI 9 update is now available for the Galaxy S24 and Z Fold/Flip 6, a month after the official rollout was initiated. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s One UI 9 update is now available for the Galaxy S24 and Z Fold/Flip 6, a month after the official rollout was initiated.

Samsung announced that One UI 9 is officially rolling out to devices that didn’t launch with it preloaded – i.e., the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra.

That means the Galaxy S24 series, Galaxy Z Fold 6, and Galaxy Z Flip 6 are the next to get Android 17 (via SamMobile). Of course, the rollout includes all three Galaxy S24 models. The update should appear in the settings app on those devices as a standard download.

For the time being, the update appears to be available in South Korea and the US, though it’s expected that more regions will follow within the next few days.

	

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Flip 8 were the first to get One UI 9 because Samsung switched up its update schedule a year ago. A month ago, the Galaxy S26 was given access to the new One UI 9, based on Android 17.

The update has been trickling down Samsung’s Galaxy S lineups ever since. Since the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy Z Fold 6 are just getting One UI 9, it’s expected that the Galaxy S25 and Galaxy Z Fold 5 aren’t far behind. Samsung has not updated those devices just yet.

One UI 9 includes a few notable changes, including:

My FanCam: Automatic video tracking & reframing of a subject

Generative and Editable Cards on Now Brief

Warranty and Care details in Settings menu

More Galaxy AI features: Now Nudge, Creative Studio, Interpreter, Document Scan, Voice Recorder

Privacy & security features: Security Brief, Privacy Alerts, Scam Detection

If the update isn’t ready for you yet, it should be very soon. For those on older devices, it may take a few more weeks.
