title: The $2,000 Duo: Who Is Apple’s First Folding iPhone Actually For?
snippet: Whether you’re a fashionista, a power user or a tech nerd, the Duo is a pretty specific device with a high starting price.
fullText:
Apple’s first swing in the foldables market, the iPhone Duo, has already made a huge splash before it’s even available to buy. 

The foldables segment has been overrun by Android devices, and all eyes have been patiently waiting for Apple to make its move. And the Duo’s design confirms the popularity of Samsung’s Galaxy Fold 8 and Google’s original Pixel Fold: Shorter and wider seems to be the sweet spot, as opposed to the more traditional taller folding phone designs we see with something like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. 

But this is Apple we’re talking about, and the iPhone Duo is more than just an iOS version of the Galaxy Fold and Pixel Fold — it has a lot going for it. We had a lot of things to say about it during our hands-on with the device, and while personally, it seems like the best foldable I’ll never buy, it certainly will be delivered into the pockets of some discerning customers who want the Apple level of polish (or who can’t stand green message bubbles).

			

More from CNET

So who needs the iPhone Duo? Who is it best suited to? We know that the latest iPhone 18 Pro Max is for photography enthusiasts and those who want the best battery ever in an iPhone, but the Duo doesn’t provide that. It’s an oddly-shaped but good-looking device that fills a new space in Apple’s lineup. 

Is the iPhone Duo actually for anyone in particular? There are a few crowds that are more likely to gravitate toward this foldable over others. Your grandparents likely aren’t going to run out and grab the Duo, but here’s who likely will. 

Read More: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone Duo: Comparing Apple’s New Pro Phone Against Its First Foldable

Early adopters, power users and professionals

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

There are likely plenty of Apple fans who have been waiting for its first foldable, but a lot of people also likely won’t pick up a first-generation device, preferring to wait until the second or third version so that Apple works out any kinks. (On the other hand, Apple has patiently waited and watched the foldable market, so its first swing might not feel like a first-generation foldable full of finicky foibles at all. It’s probably going to be great.)

But there will be some early adopters and tech enthusiasts who won’t care and plan to get this phone anyway.

Power users and those looking essentially for a foldable iPad Mini are going to love the iPhone Duo. You’ll likely be able to resize apps side by side, similar to how you would on any iPad, making it a dream for those who want an iPad experience with an iPhone form factor that fits right in your pocket. Still, we’ll need to see just how well multiple apps work on the inner screen simultaneously. It might not be as elegant as you’d get on an iPad, but it’s close. 

The other group that might really want to get their mitts on the Duo is the professional crowd. The larger inner screen makes way for easier work apps that would be more cumbersome than even the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Editing Excel or Google Sheets spreadsheets, Google and Word docs, checking emails and sending work chats will be a far smoother experience on the wider display. Throw in a wireless keyboard, and you might have a pocket iPad-like productivity suite of your dreams.

Fashionistas 

Apple products are synonymous with style, and this is a crowd that will happily gravitate toward this phone. 

The new “it” item will be in the pockets of celebrities and content creators who want to make sure they’re seen with Apple’s newest device. It’s also an expensive phone, like all foldables, making it a status symbol that maintains the cool and pretentious vibe that Apple products give off. 

The sexiest Kindle replacement

The iPhone Duo has a typical but useful foldable feature of showing a preview of what the rear cameras are shooting to help with selfies.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Avid readers may also want to pick up the iPhone Duo, since it’s virtually the perfect e-reader size. Not only that, but you’ll also get access to the App Store, which doesn’t limit you just to Amazon’s Kindle Store or e-reader apps. 

That type of flexibility on top of the power of iOS and the A20 Pro chip makes this a killer Kindle or e-reader replacement. While it is very expensive to replace a Kindle, its style, form and functionality would make it a worthy consideration for some people.

If your priorities are camera features, battery life and durability, your first choice shouldn’t be the iPhone Duo. What you’re looking for is the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It checks all of those boxes, and you shouldn’t be swayed by the novelty of the Duo. 

It’s not that the Duo isn’t alluring, but it’s both nearly double the price of the latest iPhone 18 Pro handsets and likely significantly less durable. The iPhone Duo costs about as much as a new iPhone 18 Pro and an iPad combined. 

Like most foldables, the iPhone Duo doesn’t ship with issues, just compromises. That’s something that really needs to be considered when making your purchasing decision. This device is a marvel of engineering, wrapped in luxurious style, but 90% of people spending money on new phones are not going to buy this one.

title: Rocket Money’s Rowan is a financial AI assistant you’ll actually want to text
snippet: We have all watched AI assistants become a permanent fixture on our phones over the last few months, yet finding...
fullText:
We have all watched AI assistants become a permanent fixture on our phones over the last few months, yet finding one that genuinely takes everyday chores off your plate is still surprisingly rare. Most general-purpose AI chatbots are great if you want to brainstorm ideas or summarize an article, but they hit a wall when it comes to practical, real-world tasks like managing your personal finances. 

You can describe a theoretical budget to a standard chatbot and get plenty of generic feedback, yet that chatbot cannot keep an eye on your live accounts, start a bill negotiation, or cancel a subscription for you.

That gap between talking and doing is exactly why Rocket Money built Rowan. Designed as an AI-powered personal financial assistant that lives right in your text messages, Rowan proactively watches your money, looks after your budgeting and finances, and does the actual legwork to help save you money so you don’t have to.

When evaluating any new AI tool, the biggest question is what happens behind the scenes after you send a prompt. Most AI assistants can only talk about your money, whereas Rowan is directly connected to your finances and built to take action.

	

Just as importantly, Rowan isn’t a standalone experiment from a brand-new company trying to figure out personal finance on the fly. Rowan has Rocket Money behind it, meaning it runs on the exact same platform that more than 10 million members already use every day. When you ask Rowan to help lower a bill or drop a recurring service, it taps directly into the established subscription cancelation and bill negotiation operations that Rocket Money has been running for years.

It also brings that capability to you without asking you to build a brand-new habit. Because Rowan lives entirely in your text messages, there is no new app to download and no complicated interface to learn. Rowan doesn’t replace the main Rocket Money mobile app, either; instead, it serves as an additional, conversational way to use Rocket Money straight from the messaging inbox you already check throughout the day.

A proactive partner that reaches out first

Most personal finance tools are passive by design, waiting silently on your phone until you remember to open them up and dig through your recent activity. Rowan flips that dynamic by reaching out to you first whenever something in your accounts needs your attention.

On a regular basis, Rowan texts you a weekly spending summary that provides updates on your recent finances and budgeting, complete with a detailed breakdown of where your money went and a heads-up on any areas of concern. In between those weekly check-ins, Rowan keeps a close watch on your day-to-day activity. It texts you automatically when an account balance is getting low, alerts you the moment a new subscription is detected on your statements, and lets you know when prices are increasing on your existing recurring bills.

Because it lives in your texts, checking in on your money becomes a natural two-way conversation. Whenever a question pops into your head, you can text Rowan to get instant financial updates. You can quickly categorize recent transactions right through text, ask about cancelable subscriptions you might want to clear out, or ask how much money is genuinely safe to spend right now based on your current income and upcoming expenses.

Offload financial chores with a quick text

Getting an alert about a price increase or a forgotten subscription is helpful, but Rowan’s real value shows up when you ask it to take things off your plate. Rowan can start work on your behalf so that the only thing you have to do is send a text.

If you spot a recurring service you no longer want, you can simply text Rowan to cancel that subscription. If a monthly service bill is creeping upward, you can text Rowan to start a bill negotiation on your behalf. Of course, because canceling subscriptions and negotiating bills requires coordinating with providers behind the scenes, these actions don’t happen instantly. Rather, your text kicks off the workflow so Rocket Money can step in and handle the follow-through for you. For everyday organization, you can even text Rowan to set a financial reminder, such as asking it to remind you to pay your credit card on the 15th, keeping your monthly routine on track without cluttering up your calendar.

Pricing and how to get Rowan

Available to users in the United States, the core Rocket Money app is free to download and comes with free basic features, including balance alerts, subscription management, spend tracking, basic budgeting, and bill negotiation. To unlock everything the standard app can do for your finances, you can upgrade to Rocket Money Premium, which uses a “pay what you think is fair” approach currently set between $7 and $14 a month.

Rowan is not part of the free app or the standard Premium tier. To get access to Rowan, you will need to subscribe to Rocket Money Premium+, a separate plan available for a flat $15 per month. Upgrading to Premium+ gives you everything included in Rocket Money Premium, plus full access to Rowan right in your text messages.

Most general-purpose AI chatbots are great if you want to brainstorm ideas or summarize an article, but they hit a wall when it comes to practical, real-world tasks like managing your personal finances.

You can describe a theoretical budget to a standard chatbot and get plenty of generic feedback, yet that chatbot cannot keep an eye on your live accounts, start a bill negotiation, or cancel a subscription for you.

title: Xbox Introduces New Pocket-Size Nano Controller
snippet: Game on the go: The Xbox Nano controller is smaller and lighter than an iPhone 18 Pro.
fullText:
You can jam a phone in your pocket, sure, but good luck stuffing a regular Xbox game controller in there. On Wednesday, Microsoft announced the release of the Xbox Nano controller, the console’s smallest yet. It’s just over 5 inches long, weighs 3.5 ounces and is lighter and shorter than most modern smartphones.

For comparison, an iPhone 18 Pro is 5.9 inches long and weighs 7.4 ounces. A current standard Xbox One wireless controller is just over 6 inches long and weighs 9.9 ounces without batteries.

Microsoft says the Nano controller has all 18 standard gameplay inputs, referring to the physical buttons and triggers on the controller, and they match up with the layout on the standard version. A programmable Action Button can be customized to support features such as taking screenshots, capturing gameplay and other shortcuts.

			

More from CNET

The Xbox Nano controller comes with a rechargeable battery and can connect to compatible devices via Xbox Wireless and Bluetooth.

The new Xbox Nano controller, right, is shown next to a larger, standard-sized Xbox controller.Microsoft

“While there are third-party mini Xbox controllers, they’re almost all wired,” says Josh Goldman, CNET managing editor for computers and gaming. “The Xbox Nano supports official Xbox Wireless without the need for an additional wireless adapter, plus it has Bluetooth. This makes it not only a great option for taking over to a friend’s house for gaming, but for travel in general, so you can use it for playing on a phone or tablet, too.”

The Xbox Nano controller is priced at $50, and US gamers can preorder now on the Xbox site. It will be available in other markets, including Australia, Canada and the UK, beginning in November. Pricing and availability vary by country.

The Xbox Nano controller and two months of Microsoft’s Game Pass Ultimate will be included with the purchase of select Samsung TVs this holiday season. (We review Game Pass here, calling it pricey, but a useful add-on for gamers.) The Xbox app is available through the Gaming Hub built into Samsung TVs. Another holiday offer will include the Nano controller and two free months of Game Pass Ultimate for those purchasing a Meta Quest headset.

title: Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis
snippet: The founders detailed how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.
fullText:
Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis. The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

“There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that’s somewhat potentially conservative,” Goldie said on stage. “So we don’t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans to focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

“I think the way everything is shifting is that humans bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI,” Goldie said. “And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that’s something that recursive does for chip design.”

The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, “donut-shaped” arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.

They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.

The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

“If it takes six months or a year or two years to design a new chip, then you really have to be extremely selective about the chips that you design,” Goldie said. “But if you can design a chip in like a week, and then say for manufacturing, you can design custom chips for all sorts of different types of applications in like space and AR, VR, and biological computing, it makes sense financially to do that, and we can be more energy efficient.”

title: Meet the five companies competing in the Startup Battlefield finals at Disrupt 2026
snippet: It’s time to unveil the five companies that will be competing in the Startup Battlefield finals.
fullText:
Over the past two days, 20 startups have been pitching on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, presenting live demos and answering tough questions from our expert judges. Now it’s time to unveil the five companies that will be competing in the Startup Battlefield finals.

This year’s Battlefield spanned four categories — space and physical AI, energy and manufacturing, health tech and life sciences, and enterprise and security — and our finalists are working on everything from miniature human organs to fighting scams to computing in space. 

The finals will kick off tomorrow (Thursday) at 11:30 am Pacific — you can watch them on stage at Disrupt or on the livestream here. The founders will be presenting for another panel of expert judges who will pick the winner; that winner gets to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000, equity-free.

Here are the finalists:

Apate.ai

Apate deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, with different ages, genders, and accents, speaking various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

Flox Intelligence

Flox Intelligence has built a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently than the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away. Instead, it uses edge devices with perception systems trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away.

Intero Biosystems

Intero Biosystems is developing human intestinal organoids — lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, as another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. Its organoids differ from simpler models that replicate only part of the gut. They contain multiple cell and tissue types found in the human intestine, which the company believes makes them a more human-relevant model for testing drugs and other compounds.

Industrial Next

Industrial Next builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context, and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks, without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor. In fact, some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones. 

Satlyt

Satlyt is building software designed to allow many satellites to share the work of large computing jobs in space. The startup has already flown its software on two demonstration missions, with an initial focus on finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft. Those spacecraft typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise, with communication, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings. The next goal: to show that it can create a shared computing cloud between two satellites.

title: XREAL 1 Pro+ has exactly the right hardware upgrades at the same $599 price
snippet: Ahead of its Android XR-based Aura launching later this year, XREAL is giving its flagship One Pro a “Plus” upgrade without raising the price. more…
fullText:
Ahead of its Android XR-based Aura launching later this year, XREAL is giving its flagship One Pro a “Plus” upgrade without raising the price.

XREAL 1 Pro+ delivers upgrades that, after my experience with the existing generation, are exactly what I would have picked as pain points to address. 

That starts with the display itself. XREAL is nearly doubling the brightness of the display to 1,200 nits as well as introducing AI-powered HDR. While the 700-nit brightness of the older model was plenty bright in dark environments, I did find that it had trouble holding up, say, if my neighbors on a flight decided to have the window open. The 1,200 nit upgrade should go a long way there, and I’m already impressed in some brief testing at home.

The display gets dedicated “Standard,” “Movie,” and “Reading” modes, too, to tailor the display to what the user is doing. 3D conversion also now supports 60Hz, up from the previous 30Hz limit. 

	

The biggest physical upgrade is to the nose pads, which now have a larger air cushion design that, in practice, is a major improvement in regards to wearability. XREAL One Pro often got a bit uncomfortable on my nose after a few hours, but this upgrade makes it a whole lot better. 

XREAL 1 Pro+ is available starting today for $599, keeping the same price as the existing model.

title: Report: HomePod mini 2 to release on October 30 with these upgrades
snippet: In just a couple days, Apple should be unveiling its long-awaited new lineup of new Home products. That includes an updated HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, the brand-new smart home hub called ‘HomeView’, as well as a new lineup of smart home accessories, in collaboration with LG. Here’s what to expect with the HomePod mini 2. more…
fullText:
In just a couple days, Apple should be unveiling its long-awaited new lineup of new Home products. That includes an updated HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, the brand-new smart home hub called ‘HomeView’, as well as a new lineup of smart home accessories, in collaboration with LG. Here’s what to expect with the HomePod mini 2.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the new HomePod mini should equip the S10 chip, up from the current S5 chip. This isn’t quite the latest silicon, but it’s still a massive step-change from the outgoing model.

With the S10 chip, the HomePod mini will be able to offer Siri AI features – a first for any of Apple’s Home products. It’ll also “extend” your HomeView throughout your house, with voice control and music playback all being able to sync up to your HomeView. Of course, the updated Apple TV and HomeView will also support Siri AI.

The new HomePod mini will come in a fresh array of colors, including pink, green, and blue – on top of the traditional midnight and white.

Outside of the S10 chip, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to offer Apple’s N1 networking chip to serve as a Thread and Matter radio, as well as offering Wi-Fi 7 support. Currently, the HomePod mini only offers Wi-Fi 4.

Pricing and release date

	

While pricing isn’t necessarily clear, it’s worth noting that HomePod mini increased in price from $99 to $129 back in June with Apple’s wave of memory-related price hikes. I personally expect pricing to stay the same, as Apple likely anticipated the upcoming hardware when it set them. Only time will tell, though.

As for release date, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that the second-generation HomePod mini should arrive in stores on October 30th, alongside the new Apple TV 4K. The HomeView, on the other hand, is expected to slip into mid-November. You can read more about the HomeView here.

title: Apple just closed the day above $5 trillion for the first time
snippet: Apple today became the second company ever to close with a market valuation north of $5 trillion, following NVIDIA’s landmark achievement in October 2025. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple today became the second company ever to close with a market valuation north of $5 trillion, following NVIDIA’s landmark achievement in October 2025. Here are the details.

Apple counters tech selloff

Apple’s stock closed at $342.96 today, up 0.5% on the Nasdaq. Although modest, the gain was enough to push the company’s market capitalization past the $5 trillion threshold, ending the day at $5.01 trillion.

Today’s result was particularly notable as most of the tech sector operated in the red, with Oracle closing down 8.83%, Meta down 3.27%, Nvidia down 3.16%, Microsoft down 1.8%, Amazon down 1.74%, and Google down 1.68%, to name a few.

Although Apple closed above the $5 trillion mark for the first time, this was not the first time it had reached that valuation. As The WSJ noted, today marked the seventh time Apple crossed the $5 trillion threshold during intraday trading, but the first time it managed to stay above it through the closing bell.

Apple’s stock performance on October 14, 2026

During intraday trading, Apple’s stock reached $347.07 per share, just 0.31% below its record high of $348.15.

Today’s milestone comes on the heels of a series of major product announcements from Apple, including the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, the iPhone Duo, and, just yesterday, the new Apple HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple TV 4K.

It also comes ahead of the company’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings report on November 2, which will offer a clearer picture of how Apple has navigated rising component costs and the impact of its recent hardware price increases.

Be that as it may, Apple has seen its stock rise roughly 5% since John Ternus took over as CEO on September 1 (or 8.2% if you count the August 31 closing price of $316.85), with today’s milestone further underscoring investor confidence in the company under its new leadership.

title: Google’s Demis Hassabis Puts a Hopeful Spin on AI’s Environmental Impact
snippet: The DeepMind co-founder addressed AI’s role in scientific inquiries and the positive outcomes he expects in addressing climate change.
fullText:
Google DeepMind chair and co-founder Demis Hassabis took the main stage at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Wednesday morning to speak to global ministers, media and delegates about innovations in science and math, frontier AI and – taking a hopeful tack – the potential for AI to address climate issues. 

“I actually think with the help of AI, that’s what’s going to end up giving us the technology to tackle the climate question,” he said.

During his chat, Hassabis briefly mentioned this week’s rollout of Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon model and the debacle around OpenAI’s claim to have solved the Navier-Stokes equation, one of history’s most difficult mathematical problems. But perhaps the most interesting aspect of his chat was what Hassabis did not say: AGI was not mentioned once. 

			

More from CNET

In May, I attended the Google I/O event in Mountain View, California, and listened to Hassabis speak at length about the power of artificial general intelligence – the hard-to-pin-down concept of AI that matches human intellectual capabilities – calling it the “foothills of the singularity” and estimating that achieving AGI is on the horizon. 

Five months later, a status report on progress toward AGI seemed to have slipped his mind. 

Instead, Hassabis opted to use his discussion time (a 20-minute slot following Executive Vice President of the European Commission Henna Virkkunen) to outline how AI excels in disciplines such as mathematics, coding and games like Go and those from Atari. He contrasted its success in those areas with its ability physical and natural sciences – physics, chemistry, biology, engineering – which require “real-world loops” of human creativity and judgment, intuition and curiosity in creating hypotheses and developing lines of inquiry.

In 2024, Hassabis and DeepMind colleague John Jumper, along with University of Washington scientist David Baker, won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for their work on an AI model that can predict protein structures 

“I think that’s the hardest thing in science is actually asking and articulating the right question,” Hassabis said. “That’s even harder than finding the answer.”

AI and the climate crisis

Before exiting the stage in Dublin, Hassabis was asked about AI’s significant sustainability problem. The massive push to build sprawling, energy-hungry data centers is spurring a surge in demand for fossil-fuel power plants, a key driver of the climate crisis.

Rather than acknowledging the stresses that data centers are exerting on our energy grid and natural resources, he expressed optimism about the potential for using AI to drive breakthroughs in green technology, clean energy and models for predicting natural disasters like floods, fires and hurricanes. 

“The most important thing is that the AI systems we’re building, if we build the right types, should be able to help with things like climate modeling and weather modeling,” Hassabis said. 

“Looking further forward,” he said, “AI systems will help with new sources of energy — fusion plasma containment for fusion reactors, new materials like superconductors, better batteries and better solar materials. I actually think that with the help of AI, that’s what’s going to end up giving us the technology to tackle the climate question.”

Editor’s note: Macy Meyer’s travel costs for the International AI Summit were covered by Enterprise Ireland. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: Formlabs Just Announced the First Resin Printer Aimed at Safe Home Use
snippet: Formlabs is bringing its walled garden to home users, which may be a very big deal.
fullText:
Resin printers are very cool, but difficult to recommend for home crafters. When most people think about 3D printers, they think about filament and a printhead that moves around in front of you to create something. Some of this is due to availability and cost, but the biggest reason that kind of printer has become the most popular is safety. Resin printers, which use light to create a 3D shape inside a container of liquid resin, are historically best used in workshops and creative studios over a shelf in your home. Not only is the resin not safe to get on your hands, but most also produce fumes that are not safe to inhale for extended periods of time. As a result, the software driving these machines is generally less user-friendly as it’s not aimed at casual home use.

Today, the team at Formlabs is announcing the Form Studio 1, a $699 resin printer promising a home-friendly user experience and a collection of resins that don’t put off those unhealthy fumes.

	

			

	

			

									

						Form Studio 1					

							

		

Formlabs’ most affordable printer to date is a clear attempt to expand beyond the more industrial settings you would previously find these printers, without sacrificing the things that make other printers from this company stand out. Form Studio uses a backlight system with 28 LEDs with their own lenses to more accurately place light where it’s needed, which is a significant departure from the traditional LCD system seen in most affordable resin printers. The resin itself is loaded into the tank through the unique Formlabs cartridge system, allowing the printer to accurately tell you how much resin is left in the tank as well as allow for cartridge swapping to keep a print going when resin runs low. In terms of print speed, Formlabs promises the Form Studio is capable of printing at 130mm per hour when using its proprietary resin.

			

More from CNET

The real star of the show here, in my opinion, is the resin that is safer to use in your house, as well as the printer accessory that helps it even further. Formlabs’ Alpha Resins carry the UL Greenguard Gold certification for the low-emission quality, and the resin itself gives off very little odor. While a full review from CNET is still underway, I can say from early testing that odors from this printer are practically nonexistent when using the provided resin. When you combine that with the $180 VOC extractor accessory, it paints a clear picture of where this printer is designed to be safely used.

Our first print on the Form Studio 1, with its dedicated resin cartridge

Speaking of accessories, Form Studio has a ton, and they vary quite a bit in price. The flexible build plate and resin tanks are easy to swap in and out, so you can have multiple at the ready to rapidly switch resins in the printer and not have to pour anything back into a bottle. You can also upgrade to a flexible platform that makes getting the print off the plate way easier, as well as a pro-level resin tank for resins with higher curing temperatures. But my personal favorite launch accessory is the combination wash and cure station for resin prints. This combination unit takes up just about the same amount of space as the printer itself, and allows you to quickly clean and cure a resin print without making a mess or complicated drainage needs. It’s also only $200, which is incredible for what you get.

Starting today, Formlabs has opened up orders for what it’s calling the Founders Edition of the Form Studio with a few options. For a limited time, the printer will be available in four colors, with the option to upgrade to the flexible build plate for $750. If you choose to go with the standard edition, you can still grab that $700 price, but the flexible plate really is worth the extra money. Accessories for Form Studio are also available now, including resins for this printer starting at $29 for a one-liter cartridge. And don’t forget to check back, we will be conducting a thorough review of just how home-friendly this printer is soon.

title: Google Home bug turns your smart home device list into a mess
snippet: A bug in the Google Home app has left device lists messy for some users, with no obvious way to fix it for the time being. more…
fullText:
A bug in the Google Home app has left device lists messy for some users, with no obvious way to fix it for the time being.

Over the past week, a number of users have run into a problem in the Google Home app that turns the device list into nothing but clutter. 

The way the Google Home app’s “All Devices” page is supposed to work is by grouping linked devices into their assigned rooms, and then show anything that’s not assigned in a room to a generic “Linked to you” section.

That section is the problem right now. Users have found for roughly a week, and we’re seeing the same behavior, that Google Home is listing all of their devices under the “Linked to you” section, whether they’re assigned to a room or not, resulting in a bunch of extra clutter and making it nearly impossible to track down any devices you hadn’t assigned to rooms.

	

“Linked to you” isn’t supposed to include devices already in your room groups

This is almost certainly a bug and not an intentional change, but there seems to be no way to fix it at this point, as devices in the list still show their assigned room groupings in the settings menu.

Meanwhile, Google has so far only acknowledged the issue in recommending that affected users reach out to support. 

New Google Home app updates tend to roll out every few weeks, so it’s very possible a patch will clean up this mess sometime soon. Let us know in the comments if you’re running into this problem.

title: Colossal Biosciences announces new AI platform to help accelerate de-extinction efforts
snippet: Colossal announced a new AI platform to help accelerate its de-extinction efforts and Peter Diamandis has launched a new fund to back startups who use it.
fullText:
Colossal Biosciences announced Wednesday a new AI platform to help accelerate its efforts to bring back extinct species, TechCrunch can exclusively report. 

The platform, called GenoMorph, uses advanced 3D morphology, comparative genomics, and developmental biology to identify genes that could be edited in de-extinction projects with limited gene data. The company is using it as part of its effort to bring back the dodo bird, for which there are limited genomes to work with. 

For example, the company is working with only one dodo genome compared to the 100 genomes it has been able to obtain as part of its woolly mammoth de-extinction project. DNA from the woolly mammoth is more plentiful because the colder climates the animal lived in preserve the DNA better than the tropics where the dodo lived, the company said.

“Normally, scientists can compare many genomes to understand which genetic differences are responsible for certain traits,” Colossal CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm told TechCrunch. “We don’t have that luxury with ancient DNA from extinct species whose DNA is severely limited, and we can only get a small number of complete genomes.” 

To build GenoMorph, Lamm said the company collected a bunch of developmental data from “chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons,” and combined it with the “genetic information and 3D skull measurements from more than 70 bird species.” He said it took more than a year of work to build this platform, which also builds on the company’s years of work in de-extinction. 

“The AI learns which regions of DNA are active as different birds develop their beaks and facial structures, and uses that information to predict which genetic switches may have given the dodo its iconic appearance.” He said to think of the platform as a “treasure map for the dodo genome,” where, rather than searching through a bunch of potential genetic differences, GenoMorph can help the Colossal team find only the genetic differences that matter. 

Image Credits:Colossal Labs

“So far we’ve identified approximately 2,300 promising DNA editing targets for the dodo cranial facial morphology that we can now test in the lab,” he continued. He said GenoMorph will help the company tackle one of its biggest bottlenecks in trying to de-extinct animals — finding out which changes actually make an extinct species unique. But Lamm said scientists also need to test whether those edits can create the physical traits they need. 

“We’ve developed a new system that uses lipid nanoparticles to deliver gene-editing tools directly into developing bird embryos,” he said. This will help the team see how certain genetic changes impact the development of a bird “without having to wait through an entire breeding cycle that requires birds to reach sexual maturity.” 

The company also announced Wednesday that its Nicobar pigeon colony now has 36 birds and that it has successfully created the essential cells that become eggs and sperm. 

“Because the Nicobar pigeon is the dodo’s closest living relative, those cells are a critical part of our strategy for creating birds that carry dodo traits,” he said. Next, the company is hoping to prove what GenoMorph predicts in a lab. “What’s most exciting is that we’re reaching a point where the different technologies we’ve been developing are starting to converge together and help other projects we are working on in a completely different part of the tree of life,” Lamm continued. 

When asked whether it was safe to edit genes this way, Lamm said the point of developing a technology like GenoMorph is to make genetic engineering “more precise, controlled, and testable.” He said the product doesn’t edit genes itself, but helps their team identify which genetic changes are worth investigating. 

“Identifying a potential edit doesn’t mean we immediately introduce it into an animal or assume it’s safe,” he continued. “The more precisely we can identify and validate these changes, the more informed our decisions become throughout the process.” 

Meanwhile, Colossal Biosciences’ latest technology has already obtained a vote of confidence from XPRIZE founder Peter Diamandis. Diamandis, who is an investor in Colossal, announced on Wednesday that he has founded a new VC firm, NeoGenesis Capital, to back companies using Colossal Biosciences’ programmable biology platform across health, agriculture, and conservation.

title: Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17
snippet: Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update. more…
fullText:
Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update.

What’s new in Android 17 on Samsung Galaxy?

One UI 9, Samsung’s Android 17 update, continues the trend of evolution more than overhaul. The update introduces some slight design tweaks, more AI-powered features, and other changes built on the redesign that debuted in One UI 7 and was iterated in last year’s Android 16-based One UI 8. 

Some key changes in One UI 9 include:

Warranty & Samsung Care status in the Settings menu

Broader support for Now Nudge

My FanCam automatic video cropping based on a select subject

More Quick Panel (quick settings) customization

AI privacy alerts

Upgrades to Samsung DeX

New lock screen clocks that can adapt to your wallpaper

Samsung Galaxy devices with Android 17 – The full list

While Samsung hasn’t confirmed an exact schedule for its One UI 9 and Android 17 rollout for Galaxy devices, there are updates now rolling out in parts of the globe. Below you’ll find a regularly-updated list of every Samsung Galaxy device that has received a stable Android 17 update so far.

	

Galaxy S devices with Android 17

Galaxy S26

Galaxy S26+

Galaxy S26 Ultra

Galaxy S25 (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25+ (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25 Ultra (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy S25 Edge (limited availability)

Galaxy S24 (limited availability)

Galaxy S24+ (limited availability)

Galaxy S24 Ultra (limited availability)

Galaxy Z devices with Android 17

Galaxy Z Fold 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy Z TriFold (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Fold 6 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 6 (limited availability)

Galaxy A devices with Android 17

Galaxy A57 (limited availability)

Updating…

One UI 9 changelog

Here’s the full changelog from Samsung for One UI 9, as listed for the Galaxy S26 series. Some features may vary by device.

Galaxy AI

Enhanced Now nudge

Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.

Focus on someone important

My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.

Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you

In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.

See useful information during calls

See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.

Productivity and multitasking

More customizable quick panel

You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.

Privacy, security, and device protection

Warranty and care

The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.

Lock down your phone quickly

It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.

Location access transparency

Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.

Stronger security and privacy protection

Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.

AI privacy alerts

Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.

Samsung Health

New look for Samsung Health

Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.

Customize your Health home screen

Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.

Log health data quickly

It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.

Advanced trend analysis

Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.

Monitor changes in your sleep vitals

Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.

Manage your heart health

Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.

Track your cardio load

See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.

Check your fitness index

Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.

Keep your ears safe

The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.

View your cycle and body rhythm

Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.

Bixby

Activate Bixby with a gesture

Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.

Manage your conversations

Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.

Bixby on the Home screen

Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.

Accessibility

Discover new Accessibility features

Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.

Text spotlight for easier reading

Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.

Physical keyboard shortcuts

Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.

Mouse keys enhancements

New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.

Replace swipe with single tap

The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.

Select to speak

Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.

Improved TalkBack updates

TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.

Even more improvements

New Lock screen clock

The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.

Samsung DeX enhancements

It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.

title: Apple gets a $360 price target from JP Morgan despite iPhone demand concerns
snippet: Just days after Apple’s stock took a hit over reports of iPhone 18 Pro production cuts, JP Morgan has raised its AAPL price target by $20. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Just days after Apple’s stock took a hit over reports of iPhone 18 Pro production cuts, JP Morgan has raised its AAPL price target by $20. Here are the details.

iPhone Duo to help offset staggered release window

Last Friday, Nikkei Asia reported that, according to “multiple people familiar with the matter,” Apple had told select suppliers to cut component production for the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.”

The report sent Apple shares down roughly 2.5% in early trading, although the stock has recovered much of that loss and closed at $340.97 today.

That said, JP Morgan released a new investor note today (via AppleInsider), arguing that the reported cuts are consistent with Apple’s usual production patterns and don’t necessarily point to an unexpected drop in demand.

The report also comments on Apple’s staggered iPhone launch schedule, with JP Morgan expecting the iPhone Duo to offset the sales shortfall caused by the absence of the regular iPhone 18, which is expected to hit shelves early next year.

Interestingly, earlier today, a separate report from China’s Securities Times claimed that Apple had increased its iPhone Duo orders by 30%, potentially bringing its production for the remainder of 2026 close to 10 million units.

Looking ahead to the December quarter, JP Morgan expects Apple to sell 8.5 million iPhone Duo units. JP Morgan also projects a roughly 2% decline in iPhone revenue year-over-year, but a 2% increase in Apple’s overall revenue.

The firm also continues to flag supply constraints and broader economic pressures that could affect consumer demand.

All in all, JP Morgan raised its AAPL price target from $340 to $360, while maintaining its Overweight rating on the stock.

fullText:
We broke the news this week that a next-gen Google TV Streamer is incoming, but it also arrives as Google’s smart home hardware strategy faces a tough spot and new competition.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Google’s smart home efforts have been a bit sporadic over the years. 2021 seemed like a turning point as the company rebooted its Nest camera lineup, but it was followed by a good bout of silence. That was broken up by the occasional new camera, streaming device, and the Google Home Speaker earlier this year, but it’s all felt rather unfocused and unpredictable.

And that leads into this week’s news: Google has a new TV Streamer coming.

	

This next-gen release is pretty similar on paper, though with the additions of far-field microphones, presence sensing, and a new remote. 

Next-gen Google TV Streamer in the works with microphones, presence sensing, & new remote

Sounds good! 

But, at the same time, it feels like Google should have much bigger priorities in its smart home ecosystem. Those aforementioned 2021 Nest cameras are still in need of refreshes. The 2K updates for the wired cameras have been welcome upgrades, but I do wish my battery-powered models had the same quality. The Nest Hub Max is way overdue for an update at this point, and I’d argue that should have been the priority over a new audio speaker. Google Home has done a great job over the past couple of years at building out a third-party ecosystem of smart home devices, but the first-party hardware has been lacking, and there’s not enough tight integration with most third-party hardware to bridge the gap.

So while I’m all for a new Google TV Streamer, I’m also struggling to feel like this is the release we should be seeing right now. 

Especially in the context of this week’s other news. Apple is making a big smart home play. On top of the “HomePad” smart display, the company is teaming up with LG for some second-party hardware with deep integration. Putting aside that Google has really dropped the ball on its massive lead in the smart display space, integrations like these are exactly what I wish Google Home saw more of. Walmart cameras, the Yale smart lock, and the First Alert smoke alarms are a good start, but there’s so much room for more.

As a fan and a genuine user of Google’s smart home ecosystem, I really feel like Google is leaving so much out there right now. Just me? Let’s discuss!

This Week’s Top Stories

Amazon did the thing!

Well I never thought this day would come. After well over a decade of Fire Tablets that were inherently limited, Amazon this week announced new “Alexa” tablets that have the Google Play Store installed. Wild times folks, wild times.

Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store

Google Wallet updates

An assortment of Google Wallet updates are out, including more ID support and a new design. Plus, it sounds like car key support for certain GM vehicles is not too far off.

Google Wallet for Android adds 12th digital state ID

Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android

Pixelated has video – no, this is not a drill!

Our podcast, Pixelated, has long been audio-only, but this week’s episode features a video component and a tier list of every Pixel released to date!

title: Google Antigravity is now built into Gemini app for macOS
snippet: As part of today’s Gemini 4 Argon rollout, Google is making a big update to the Gemini app for macOS by integrating Antigravity. more…
fullText:
As part of today’s Gemini 4 Argon rollout, Google is making a big update to the Gemini app for macOS by integrating Antigravity.

Antigravity is Google’s agent-first development platform, with version 2.0 introduced at I/O 2026. It was previously a standalone app for Mac, Windows, Linux, and most recently Googlebook (Android). Since May, Google has been updating Antigravity at a rapid pace, with major updates coming on a weekly basis, or even every few days.

Google is now bringing Antigravity directly into the Gemini app on macOS. You’ll see a new Liquid Glass pill for Antigravity in the top-right corner, with the same button letting you exit. This launches the full experience found in the dedicated application.

Gemini 4 Argon’s upgraded coding capabilities are cited as the reason for this integration. This lets users code apps, web experiences, and more from one app. As of today, the new model requires AI Pro and above in the Gemini app, but Antigravity access requires AI Ultra.

	

Meanwhile, the Gemini app for macOS has been updated with the new “Chat” and “Task” switcher, with the latter being the new name for Gemini Spark. It appears below the prompt box, while the navigation drawer also sees a big update. Search is now in the top-right corner of the panel. There’s a new Scheduled view that shows both Spark tasks and Scheduled actions.

Additionally, @ (mention) is now how you access Skills, replacing the / (slash) command. In the side panel, “Customize” lets you access Skills and Connectors, which is the new name for Connected Apps.

Make sure you’re running the latest version of the Gemini app for macOS.

title: Apple Tried Hard to Sell Me on the HomeView as a Seamless Smart Home Experience and Succeeded
snippet: I’m not easily impressed when it comes to smart home hubs. Here’s why the HomeView is different.
fullText:
I test smart home devices for a living, but even I find it challenging to use and manage the ones in my home. I have Hue bulbs, Govee lamps, Dreo smart ceiling fans, TP-Link plugs, Eufy cameras, Whisker smart litter boxes and robot vacuums, among many other devices, all “bolted” together, with an Amazon Echo Show 8 and Alexa integration layer to interact with them. The result is….functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.

Apple promises that its HomeView will be different. I spent over an hour at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York City, where I got to view and interact with the HomeView across a variety of scenarios and environments. I’m not someone who’s easily convinced that a new smart screen is the solution to my problems, but after seeing the Apple HomeView in action, I’m on board.

	

			

	

									

						Preorder the Apple HomeView					

									

						Apple HomeView					

							

No third-party apps required is huge: Everything goes through Apple Home

Yes, the HomeView has a clock view.Ajay Kumar/CNET

The HomeView’s biggest and most compelling appeal is that you don’t need to download, install and set up an account with a third-party app for each and every smart home device you own.

			

More from CNET

With most smart home products, you’re lucky if they integrate with the voice assistant you normally use. Once set up, in the best circumstances, you need only to interact with their app when its connection or functionality breaks (and it will), and then you’ll need to dig into settings to find out why and fix it. Sounds awful, right?

If you’re the average person trying to connect and navigate different smart home devices for the first time, the setup prospect is daunting, as the 10-plus third-party smart home apps on my phone can attest. It’s hard to overstate how big a barrier to entry Apple has just removed by exiling third-party apps from this process.

In the case of the HomeView, I watched an Apple representative instantly find, pair and register a new smart home device on both her phone and the HomeView as she carried on a casual conversation with me, not missing a beat. Everything was managed through the Apple Home app. It seemed to work like pairing new AirPods or a HomePod. I didn’t have time to dig into the process before being shepherded to the next demo, but what I saw was one of the most compelling things I’ve seen in the smart home world: an easy, intuitive setup.

It should work with all the new Apple Home collection devices from LG and Schneider Electric, as well as Matter and Apple Home accessories. This isn’t an exhaustive list, and I expect most devices, including those from Amazon and Google, should work as well.

Face ID recognition and personalized profiles make a big difference

From the side, the HomeView gives off strong iMac G4 vibes.Ajay Kumar/CNET

Personalized profiles for a smart home hub are an underrated feature, and their current implementation is pretty poor. Echo devices let you set up multiple profiles for family members and even guests, but God forbid you have to navigate the Alexa app to set what a guest has access to or trust that the voice print actually works. Despite having plenty of voice records for my wife and me, our Echo never seems to be able to differentiate between us.

With the HomeView, you have Face ID integrated, and in the brief time I had, it worked quickly without any bugs. An Apple representative showed me how they envision the HomeView being used in a nightstand setup in a bedroom, an environment where you want privacy and don’t want a stranger having access to your entire smart home.

The HomeView registered the owner and the correct profile immediately and pulled up relevant information, such as a calendar, scheduled events, and preferred home screen and customization options. The same carried over to the other HomeView devices Apple had set up in its simulated home environment, with the exterior HomeView offering a security camera view while limiting access for guests, while granting them certain features like temperature control or Safari access.

It can register up to six people by face and set up personalized profiles for each. While Apple didn’t go into detail or confirm this, I imagine that these include child and family accounts where you can set up parental controls. 

The 7-inch square Liquid Retina display works well for a kitchen setup

The HomeView can keep your coffee and grinder company on the counter.

I keep an Echo Show and an Apolosign smart calendar in my kitchen. One helps with recipes and timers, while the other lets my wife and me coordinate meetings, appointments and important events. Both take up too much space on our kitchen counters because we don’t like how they look wall-mounted (more on that below).

The HomeView comes with a 7-inch square Liquid Retina display. I heard several people in the demo areas complain that it was too small. On the contrary, I think the size and shape are actually perfect for a smart home screen, especially one in my narrow galley kitchen with limited countertop space. 

The square screen makes it easier to view and scroll through recipes, and it’s also hands-free while you’re cooking, adjustable and tiltable to suit your needs. You can easily share recipies from your iPhone directly to the HomeView by tapping it or accessing it directly through Siri AI and Safari. The recipes are also optimized to show you step-by-step screens that guide you through the process for those of us who aren’t great at following directions. Timers are also easy to access and set.

The base also keeps the screen directly off your dirty countertops. Apple placed it next to a fancy-looking espresso setup in a demo kitchen, and it looked great without being overwhelming. By contrast, my Apolosign calendar looks like a giant eyesore and immediately draws the eye of everyone who walks in and shows them our full schedule.

Smaller footprint and better functionality in my kitchen? Sold. 

Wall mounting looks remarkably good and not like you nailed a tablet to your wall 

When you buy a HomeView, you can choose between one ready to mount on a wall or one with a speaker base.Ajay Kumar/CNET

I like the idea of a smart home hub on my wall, but I hate how it looks in practice. I briefly considered mounting our Android-powered smart calendar to our kitchen wall as a central hub for our devices. Not only was it unsightly, but it also looked like we’d just taken a tablet and nailed it to our wall, with an ugly, dangling power cable off the bottom.

Apple showed me several examples of mounted HomeViews in different settings, and they all looked great. In Apple’s case, they’re professionally installed with a hidden, wired power connection in the wall, which the company recommends if you’re planning to use the HomeView as your main smart home dashboard for temperature control or as a security screen by your entryway, for instance. But if you don’t want to cut into your wall, you can also use an external adapter and cable to a nearby wall outlet. 

For a wired install, you basically have three options. You can use the Schneider Home Power PoE wired mount, which provides hardwired power and Ethernet for $130, or a regular Power Mount AC Wired for $80, with installation by a licensed electrician. The last option, if you want to self-install is to use a Power Mount with a USB-C Wall connector and a separate 20W power adapter, for $60, though this leaves an external cable dangling. 

I like the look of a seamless wall-mounted HomeView enough to consider a professional install, especially since I plan to use it as my always-on smart home dashboard. 

Don’t underestimate the FaceTime panel for older family members

The HomeView can be used for FaceTime video calls.

I’m not a big video call person, but as my parents get older, they default to video calls. Those calls are often shaky and low-quality on the selfie cameras of whatever ancient device they’re using. Apple’s FaceTime demo for the HomeView makes its use case particularly clear. You can get your older relatives a HomeView, even set it up for them, and they can use Siri AI to video call you as needed without needing an iPhone or iPad.

I want to note that the audio on the tabletop version of the HomeView is significantly more impressive than I expected, with easily audible, room-filling sound for both video calls and music. Not the robust bass or clear lyrics I expected from a tabletop device. A full-size HomePod will deliver better sound quality, but it far outstrips an iPad for video calls or music. 

It also has easy Find My integration. Apple representatives demonstrated the feature multiple times, showing how you can ask Siri AI to find a missing phone, remote or AirPods case. It worked without a hitch each time and notably, without requiring you to reach for a phone. 

I also watched as the Apple representative demonstrated how the HomeView autoframed and autofocused on the video caller, and it did a good job of avoiding focusing on me as I lurked over her shoulder. (Hey, it’s my job to test these things!) Again, this is the sort of small but important quality-of-life feature that makes the HomeView more usable than its older competitors.

The smart displays I’ve tested don’t work that well. Is the HomeView really different?

									

						Preorder the Apple HomeView					

									

						Apple HomeView					

							

I’ve used a lot of smart home screens that have promised a seamless home hub experience, including the Amazon Echo Show 8, Google Nest Hub, and various Android-powered smart calendar options like Apolosign and Skylight Calendar. While all of them worked, none did so well enough that I thought setting them up and managing them was particularly easy. Demoing the HomeView was a much smoother experience than I was expecting. Naturally, there were some hiccups — Siri AI didn’t always cooperate or register voice commands, but that may have been due to the loud environment, and nothing ever goes perfectly in a demo.

But overall, I was impressed with what I saw, and I can easily see the HomeView working for my own smart home. If it can pull off the miracle of integrating my disparate third-party apps and hodgepodge of systems together in one seamless interface for just $299, well, that’s an easy sell for me.

I test smart home devices for a living, but even I find it challenging to use and manage the ones in my home. I have Hue bulbs, Govee lamps, Dreo smart ceiling fans, TP-Link plugs, Eufy cameras, Whisker smart litter boxes and robot vacuums, among many other devices, all “bolted” together, with an Amazon Echo Show 8 and Alexa integration layer to interact with them. The result is….functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.

Apple promises that its HomeView will be different. I spent over an hour at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York City, where I got to view and interact with the HomeView across a variety of scenarios and environments. I’m not someone who’s easily convinced that a new smart screen is the solution to my problems, but after seeing the Apple HomeView in action, I’m on board.

title: Why the Apple Home Collection will accelerate smart home adoption
snippet: I think it’s sometimes easy for geeks to forget that we live in a tech bubble with our fellow geeks. Many of us here have been using smart home technology for more than a decade now, some even for many decades. I’ve seen a lot of bemused comments on the Apple Home Collection, with people asking why anyone would want to pay significantly higher prices for devices which don’t seem to offer any added benefit. But I think this is absolutely a bubble effect … more…
fullText:
I think it’s sometimes easy for geeks to forget that we live in a tech bubble with our fellow geeks. Many of us here have been using smart home technology for more than a decade now, some even for many decades.

I’ve seen a lot of bemused comments on the Apple Home Collection, with people asking why anyone would want to pay significantly higher prices for devices which don’t seem to offer any added benefit. But I think this is absolutely a bubble effect …

HomeKit was a start, but not enough

In the very early days, smart home technology involved a great deal of soldering and programming. The tech gradually grew more accessible and fully wireless devices controlled by smartphones was the first major step change. All the same, configuring new devices was far from trivial, initially requiring a whole bunch of companion apps for products made by different manufacturers.

Apple’s attempt to change all this was HomeKit. The idea was that everything could be configured and controlled via a single app, with the HomeKit label guaranteeing compatibility. It also brought voice control to devices which previously required us to use an app.

The reality was still rather different from the vision, however. Some HomeKit devices still needed to be initially configured using a third-party app before they would appear in Apple’s Home app. Some of the setup processes made me feel like an unpaid network engineer.

Additionally, relatively few manufacturers bothered to make HomeKit-compatible products. Both the Amazon Alexa and Google Home ecosystems were far more commercially successful.

Matter and Thread helped

The launch of the Matter and Thread standards helped significantly. It meant manufacturers only had to support these new industry standards in order to ensure compatibility with each of the three big smart home ecosystems.

Matter also enabled a simpler setup process, again helping to make the technology more accessible to the mass market. Once more, however, the practical impact was limited.

Apple Home Collection

Many techies have been wondering what all the fuss is about with the Apple Home Collection. There are no new product categories, and there are equivalent but lower-cost options for each of the new devices.

	

But for non-geeks, the setup process really is completely different. Essentially, Apple has made configuring one of these devices as simple as pairing a new set of AirPods. Just like AirPods, you need only bring one of the new devices close to your iPhone, with CNET’s Ajay Kumar commenting on just how simple it appears to be.

I watched an Apple representative instantly find, pair and register a new smart home device on both her phone and the HomeView as she carried on a casual conversation with me, not missing a beat. Everything was managed through the Apple Home app. It seemed to work like pairing new AirPods or a HomePod. I didn’t have time to dig into the process before being shepherded to the next demo, but what I saw was one of the most compelling things I’ve seen in the smart home world: an easy, intuitive setup.

We shouldn’t underestimate just what a big difference this will make to normal people. I have definitely had non-tech friends be impressed by my smart home, but none of them rushed out to emulate it. I really do think this is going to represent the next step in mass market adoption.

If you’re a normie who likes the idea of a smart home but has been put off by the apparent complexity, I think we may now have reached the point where many are willing to make the leap.

That’s my view; how about yours? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Google Play adding ‘personal library’ to access your vibe-coded Android apps
snippet: Google today announced a slew of Play Store updates across vibe-coding, game discovery, social features, and more. more…
fullText:
Google today announced a slew of Play Store updates across vibe-coding, game discovery, social features, and more.

The biggest update is Google Play’s embrace of vibe-coded Android apps. Since May, Google AI Studio has allowed you to generate Android apps and quickly deploy them to your phone using ADB.

Google is now going a step further by letting you “launch personal apps on your own device” via the Play Store. A “Your personal library” section allows you to access apps across multiple devices for an easy restore and install experience. This is rolling out starting today in the US and other select markets.

The Play Store will soon let you privately share your apps with select users. These generated Android apps are kept “secure, private, and separate from the public store catalog.” It’s intended for small-scale sharing, with these apps going through a security review.

	

In the future, Google Play will let you “graduate to a professional developer account with the same Trust & Safety reviews and high-quality standards.”

Game Finder is the next big update and starts with your “Gamer DNA.” This is an “analysis of how you play and preferences you’ve shared.” You can specify “games, genres, mechanics, and more to finetune.” Gamer DNA will let you “easily find games that match your taste.” It’s rolling out initially in the US with more markets coming soon.

Plus, see how players with similar Gamer DNA are engaging with a title, find out how many people you follow are playing it, read user review summaries and learn which games are trending and why. 

This will be joined by Game Playlists that let you curate and soon share a collection of titles.

The Play Store is boosting social competitions with Sprints, or “high-energy, 48-hour micro-challenges” that involve matching with groups of two to five players for “fast-paced contests.” The Sidekick in-game overlay is also adding “30-second Playback” clips for sharing.

Elsewhere, Google Play is expanding Sports Topic Pages that show live scores and compatible streaming apps to the Premier League, Champions League, La Liga, Liga MX, and Major League Soccer. Ask Play can now generate app comparisons that highlight “key differences and user sentiment.”

title: New Apple TV 4K vs previous model: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple just launched a brand new Apple TV 4K (pre-order here), the fourth generation of the product. Here’s how the new Apple TV 4K compares to the previous, third-gen model from 2022. more…
fullText:
Apple just launched a brand new Apple TV 4K (pre-order here), the fourth generation of the product. Here’s how the new Apple TV 4K compares to the previous, third-gen model from 2022.

Performance: A19 chip vs A15 Bionic

The new Apple TV 4K has an A19 chip, the same chip that debuted in the iPhone 17 last year.

The third-gen Apple TV 4K from 2022 includes an A15 Bionic chip that first shipped in 2021. So any sort of chip upgrade would have been a big one, but A19 is an especially sizable leap with several years worth of improvements.

Apple says the new chip “delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance,” which results in “greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations.”

A19 also has a new, dedicated AV1 decoder which enables “more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth.”

Siri AI, plus hands-free Siri interactions with far-field mics

Siri AI debuts in the new Apple TV 4K, but Apple says it’s also coming to the second and third generation models. Presumably Siri AI will be more responsive on the latest hardware with A19, but it’s great that users won’t have to upgrade just to get the new Siri.

Apple says Siri AI supports features like “personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions.” Some example queries include:

“What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?”

“Where was Pluribus filmed?”

“Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?”

“Play the show Alinda recommended.”

One exclusive upgrade with the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is that it includes a three-microphone array with voice isolation built right into the box itself for hands-free interactions.

This enables you to say “Siri” or “Hey Siri” to interact with the assistant. You’ll no longer have to press the button on the Siri Remote, though that’s still an option too.

Upgraded Siri Remote with Precision Finding

The Siri Remote has been upgraded to include Find My support with Precision Finding. 

If you’ve ever used Precision Finding to locate a lost AirTag or another device, you’ll know how valuable this experience should prove for the Siri Remote.

When you lose the Siri Remote, you’ll be able to get guided, step-by-step directions to its location. And thanks to a new built-in speaker, you can even play a sound on the remote to help you find it.

You can order the new Siri Remote here for $59, it’s compatible with older Apple TV 4K models so you won’t have to buy a whole new Apple TV to get it.

New four-speaker surround sound feature with HomePods

If you have several HomePods in your house, or plan to invest deeply in the Apple Home ecosystem, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K has a new surround sound feature.

Using either HomePod mini 2 or HomePod 2, Apple TV 4K will support a four-speaker surround sound experience. Apple says, “The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space.”

You can also mix and match HomePods, as long as they’re in matching pairs. For example, you can use a HomePod 2 front pair and a HomePod mini 2 rear pair—or opt for four of the same model.

Internal storage: 128GB standard vs 64GB

Apple used to sell Apple TV 4K in two models: one with 64GB storage and a more expensive 128GB model.

With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, 128GB is the standard storage configuration. There are no options to pay more for higher storage. It’s still unclear how necessary the extra storage is, but perhaps we’ll see tvOS 27’s Smart Downloads feature resurface soon.

Connectivity upgrades

There are several connectivity improvements with the new Apple TV 4K. On the wireless front, you get the following:

Wi‑Fi 7, up from Wi-Fi 6

Bluetooth 6, up from Bluetooth 5.0

Thread (previously limited to 128GB model)

	

It’s expected that these upgrades are due to the inclusion of Apple’s N1 wireless chip, though that hasn’t officially been confirmed.

Additionally, Gigabit Ethernet is now included standard on all models. Previously, it was excluded from the base 64GB model that most people bought.

New Apple TV 4K is now available for pre-order for $299.
