title: IDC: Apple gains ground as China’s smartphone shipments plunge 15.4% in Q3 2026
snippet: According to a new report from IDC, Apple’s share of smartphone shipments in China grew during Q3 2026, despite a 4.3% year-over-year decline in iPhone shipments. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to a new report from IDC, Apple’s share of smartphone shipments in China grew during Q3 2026, despite a 4.3% year-over-year decline in iPhone shipments. Here are the details.

Apple gains ground as China’s smartphone shipments plunge 15.4%

In a new report released today, IDC says that rising component costs and retail prices continue to weigh on the broader Chinese smartphone market.

According to IDC, Apple accounted for 17.8% of smartphone shipments in China during Q3 2026, up from 15.8% in the year-ago period. The gain came despite a 15.4% year-over-year decline in overall smartphone shipments in China, with Apple itself seeing a 4.3% year-over-year decline and a 15.1% drop from the previous quarter.

This means that while Apple lost ground, it didn’t lose as much as most of its competitors, thus increasing its overall shipment share.

And speaking of Apple’s competitors, Huawei was the uncontested winner for the quarter, with a massive 17.3% year-over-year increase in shipments, bringing its market share to 21.1%, up from 15.2% in Q3 2025. However, its shipments still declined 17.6% from the previous quarter.

Other than Huawei, Lenovo was the only other brand in China’s top 10 to record year-over-year shipment growth, at 1.1%. On a quarter-over-quarter basis, however, Lenovo, Honor, and Samsung all recorded increases, with Samsung posting a whopping 106.5% jump.

On the other end of the spectrum, Wiko saw the biggest year-over-year decline among the top 10, with shipments plunging 74% in Q3 2026, bringing its shipment share down to 0.8%, from 2.6% in the year-ago period.

Here’s IDC on these numbers, which it notes are preliminary (translation ours):

Despite the overall market downturn, Huawei maintained its strong performance throughout the year, supported by its diverse product lineup and relatively restrained price increases. Its shipments recorded double-digit year-over-year growth.

Apple’s newly released iPhones received a better-than-expected market reception. However, shipments declined slightly year-over-year due to fewer models available this year.

Other major Chinese smartphone brands faced significant challenges but continued to demonstrate varying degrees of resilience under pressure.

Among them, Honor was the only major manufacturer to record quarter-over-quarter shipment growth, suggesting a potential rebound.

IDC says it expects component costs “ to remain elevated over the next several quarters,” which will in turn keep increasing device prices and stretch replacement cycles further as consumers “accept and adapt to higher prices.”

The company doesn’t expect cost pressures to subside “through much of 2027, with the market likely to continue experiencing significant declines.”

title: Galaxy phones reportedly ‘yield no profit at all’ when sold as Samsung cuts production
snippet: A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%. more…
fullText:
A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%.

Korean media, MoneyToday, reports that Samsung is cutting Galaxy smartphone production by up to 30% through Q4 2026. Where original forecasts expected Samsung to produce around 270 million smartphones in 2026, the company may just barely surpass 200 million at this point.

The reason for the reduction is, of course, the surging price of memory. 

	

Despite Samsung’s major role within the memory market, Samsung Mobile still has to deal with the same downsides as other manufacturers. The report points out that 12GB of RAM has jumped in price by 175% since last year and, in Q3 and Q4, it’s expected to rise by around 20% compared to the previous quarter alone. Samsung’s Q4 is generally a bit quiet as the lead-up to 2027 flagships looms and as other launches start to age out.

	

The big kicker here is that Samsung is apparently making “no profit at all” when it sells a Galaxy smartphone. This is presumably a layered statement, as one would imagine that more expensive devices like the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Galaxy Z Fold 8 still manage some level of profit, but even if it’s just a general statement about the whole lineup, it certainly explains Samsung’s recent price hikes. Samsung’s mobile division is expected to mount a 19 trillion won loss in Q3 2026, the report brings out, which is around $14 billion USD.

AI is just great, isn’t it.

fullText:
Update, 5:56 p.m. ET: The public beta is now available as well.

Apple is rolling out the fourth developer beta for macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, ahead of the official release in the coming weeks. Here’s what to expect.

Apple rolls out macOS 27.2 developer beta 4

Apple appears to be back to its weekly cycle of the 27.2 beta, after a two-week gap between developer betas 2 and 3.

The company is now rolling out macOS 27.2 beta 4 to developers, which is on the lighter side of user-facing features. The biggest addition to the system so far is Siri AI’s support for five additional languages, following its English-only initial rollout last month with macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Siri AI in macOS 27.2 Golden Gate will add support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, as Apple promised during the Surprise and Shine event.

One particularly interesting addition to macOS 27.2 beta 3, released last week, was the discovery of new gesture recognition tools in several built-in apps, which could be laying the groundwork for Apple’s upcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro.

Apple is expected to unveil its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro later this month, with an announcement currently rumored for October 27. The company is also expected to introduce a new iPad mini with an OLED display, alongside updated iMac and entry-level MacBook Pro models powered by the M6 chip.

Back to today’s beta, its release build is 26B5112a, which indicates this might be the last release before the first RC. We are digging through the system and will report back if we find any noteworthy tidbits.

Installing macOS 27.2 beta 4

Here’s how to install the first macOS 27.2 beta 4:

Back up your Mac

Open System Settings

Go to General ⇾ Software Update

Click the ‘i’ icon next to Beta Updates

From the dropdown menu in the top-right, select the macOS Developer Golden Gate Beta

Hit ‘Done’

title: Xreal’s New High-End Display Glasses Get a Brightness Boost
snippet: I’m wearing them now, and the display improvements have won me over, even compared with my current favorite, the Viture Beast.
fullText:
The quality of plug-in display glasses has gotten seriously good lately, if you can put up with the idea of resting your monitor on your face. The price for good glasses has been dropping (down to $299 for some notable ones), but the pricier top-end models have advantages.

The new $599 Xreal One Pro Plus glasses, available now, offer a few subtle upgrades to last year’s model. I’ve been trying a pair out and the experience is largely the same, just a bit better (namely, brighter).

The lenses on these wearable displays still stick out a bit. (I also have prescription inserts added on them here.)Scott Stein/CNET

What’s new: Brightness, a few new visual modes

The previous Xreal One Pro display glasses were one of my favorite pairs around, along with the Viture Beast ones. In the past, Xreal’s design was thinner and lighter than Viture’s, but they had a notably dimmer display. That’s been fixed now with the One Pro Plus, which have 1,200 nits of brightness (versus 700 for the One Pro display glasses). There are also a few more visual settings, including “Reading,” which seems to move the virtual display a bit closer.

			

More from CNET

The One Pro Plus also have a smoother AI 3D conversion mode that turns any 2D image or video (or connected game) into 3D. The effect runs at a smoother frame rate than before, but the conversion still feels imperfect and gimmicky and compromises the frame rate too much compared with leaving it off.

But the rest of these glasses are similar to their predecessor. They still need to be tethered via USB-C cable to whatever laptop, phone or game console you have around, and they still project their displays down from the top of the glasses through half-mirror lenses that make the display feel overlaid in front of your eyes. They’re not any more portable or differently designed than before, and still resemble odd sunglasses. (They do pack up easily into an included case, though.) They have the same onboard chip that can pin displays in place when you turn your head, along with the same ability to change the size and perceived distance of the virtual display, including widescreen modes for connected computers.

The included nose pads are slightly more comfortable, and the arms can still bend at different angles for a proper fit.

Connecting to Steam Deck is still my favorite thing to do with these types of glasses.Scott Stein/CNET

Wearing the Xreal One Pro Plus

I’ve been wearing the One Pro Plus with prescription lens inserts while writing this story on a MacBook, and the differences are subtle. But I appreciate the extra brightness, and the electrochromic dimming seems to block out room light even better. Together, those improvements make the glasses much more effective in brightly lit rooms or outdoors.

I also watched some of the indie horror movie Buddy on my iPhone, and the more vivid display made the glasses feel like a more effective personal cinema.

I played Star Wars Galactic Racer on Steam Deck with these on my face, too, and had a blast. The display is crisp and vivid, although after swapping back and forth with the Viture Beast, I prefer the Beast slightly for its larger-feeling display.

The audio on the speaker arms sounds fine, but isn’t any better than the Xreal One Pro’s audio. When I wear them, I prefer to use AirPods for audio.

The Xreal One Pro Plus (left) versus the Viture Beast (right). The Beast glasses are clearly a bit chunkier.Scott Stein/CNET

I liked the Viture Beast for their bright, micro-OLED display and their stepped-up screen resolution, which has an aspect ratio that works better for gaming (1,900×1,200). The 1,250 nits on the Beast are pretty close to Xreal One Pro Plus, though.

My issue is that Xreal has so many display glasses options now that it’s getting confusing, including a pair made with Asus, a more affordable pair released earlier this year and a mixed reality computer-glasses system called Xreal Aura that was made with Google, costs $1,279 and is arriving later this fall.

With the One Pro Plus, Xreal has made the best display glasses I’ve ever worn next to Viture Beast, and their smaller on-face feel is more comfortable. But if you’re looking to see what glasses tech has in store next, you might want to see what the Xreal Aura offer. I’ll be reviewing them soon.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											I started with CNET reviewing laptops in 2009. Now I explore wearable tech, VR/AR, tablets, gaming and future/emerging trends in our changing world. Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.

title: Flock CEO defends surveillance technology amid national backlash: ‘We shouldn’t pause progress’
snippet: At TechCrunch Disrupt, Flock CEO Garrett Langley defended his company's surveillance technology despite growing privacy concerns, arguing that its crime-fighting benefits outweigh the risks of abuse.
fullText:
Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. 

“If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking on stage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday. 

During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to cancelled contracts and even layoffs. Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns.

In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return.

A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity, according to some.

It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent.

For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained.

“Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.”

But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others.

“We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said. 

CEO: ‘Flock is far from perfect’

Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people.

Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader.

“He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said.

Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff.

“If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps.

But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers.

“I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were.

For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong.

“I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added.

title: Microsoft and Japan took down a cybercrime network behind over a billion scam messages
snippet: We've all gotten a scam text about a nonexistent parking ticket or a fake package delivery, but hopefully you'll start seeing fewer of them. Microsoft says it helped dismantle a marketplace for scammers sending phishing messages like those around the world. Through an investigation with Japan's National Police Agency, it tracked scam activity back to a marketplace called YAM Store and a pair of phishing kits, CoGUI and Iron Man: Since January 2026, YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared to … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Stevie Bonifield

 

is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

We’ve all gotten a scam text about a nonexistent parking ticket or a fake package delivery, but hopefully you’ll start seeing fewer of them. Microsoft says it helped dismantle a marketplace for scammers sending phishing messages like those around the world. Through an investigation with Japan’s National Police Agency, it tracked scam activity back to a marketplace called YAM Store and a pair of phishing kits, CoGUI and Iron Man:

Since January 2026, YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared toward Microsoft customers alone. These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators.

According to Microsoft’s report, scammers could buy stolen or fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts on YAM Store and use the phishing kits to send scam messages. Microsoft says YAM Store also hijacked real organizations’ expired web domains and created websites for nonexistent organizations, which it used to get Microsoft accounts it could resell.

The Iron Man platform was also offering over 2,300 templates scammers could use to impersonate organizations like banks and police departments. Microsoft says it disabled over 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and blocked over 100,000 web domains being used for impersonation and fraud. With health sector cybersecurity non-profit Health-ISAC, Microsoft also seized and redirected web domains that were powering all three platforms.

title: Gudea leverages AI to help organizations prevent social media crises before they erupt
snippet: Every day, conversations unfold across social media and websites around the world. A seemingly insignificant post—whether it involves AI-generated misinformation, hate speech, or a damaging rumor—can quickly snowball into a much larger public controversy. Gudea, a company that tracks how stories and rumors spread online that describes itself as the “storm tracker for the internet,” […]
fullText:
Every day, conversations unfold across social media and websites around the world. A seemingly insignificant post—whether it involves AI-generated misinformation, hate speech, or a damaging rumor—can quickly snowball into a much larger public controversy.

Gudea, a company that tracks how stories and rumors spread online that describes itself as the “storm tracker for the internet,” is using AI to help organizations spot trouble brewing online before it turns into a crisis.

Unlike traditional social listening platforms, which only track metrics such as mentions, hashtags, and impressions, Gudea aims to show organizations who is driving a conversation, how information is moving, how quickly a story is gaining traction, and where it could be headed. Rather than simply tallying posts, its AI analyzes behavior, relationships, and the pathways through which information travels across more than 500 mainstream and fringe websites and platforms, including X, Reddit, and TikTok.

Instead of simply telling a company that mentions are rising, Gudea aims to provide the context behind that growth so decision-makers can determine how and whether to respond.

Gudea pitched its mission Wednesday afternoon on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company made the case that companies need to take a more proactive approach to protecting their reputations.

“These big industries don’t understand that there are things they can do proactively to defend their reputation and their brand,” CEO and founder Keith Presley said. “A lot of the chief communications officers and chief media or marketing officers, they’re using legacy tools to try to figure out what’s happening. Those tools were only ever designed to tell you the number of hashtags or number of impressions.”

Gudea was founded in 2023 by Presley, Jonathan Sperber, and James Thomin. Presley brings more than 15 years of experience spanning political campaigns and defense, including building the infrastructure for Andrew Yang’s presidential campaign. Sperber, the company’s chief strategy officer, has a background in disinformation research. Thomin, Gudea’s CTO, holds a Ph.D. in chemical engineering and has spent roughly two decades working in AI and machine learning.

Presley called the company’s path to becoming a startup unusual.

“We’re one of those weird startups where I never wanted to do a company,” he said.

The team began with the George Washington Initiative, a nonprofit established after the 2020 election. The organization adapted strategies and tactics that the intelligence community has used overseas to disrupt online networks tied to groups such as Al Qaeda and ISIS. It applied them to domestic information campaigns.

The goal was to identify the online environments where information campaigns were taking shape and disrupt the pathways that allowed those narratives to reach wider audiences.

However, the team found that existing tools didn’t show how information was actually moving across people, groups and platforms. That gap became the opening for Gudea.

Three years after its founding, Gudea has nearly 40 clients. According to Presley, its customer base includes a Fortune 50 telecommunications company, a Fortune 50 retailer, “one of the world’s largest AI labs, one of the world’s largest bands,” public relations and crisis communications agencies, and government agencies.

With the rise of generative AI, Presley believes that the need for Gudea’s technology has only grown, as the company looks to expand its customer base.

AI tools have dramatically lowered the cost and effort required to generate content and coordinate online campaigns. What once required a larger organization can increasingly be carried out by a single person with a laptop and access to the right software.

“When we first started in 2021, and then as a company in 2023, we maybe saw one out of four things we looked at have inauthentic activity around it,” Presley said. “Now it’s probably nine out of ten things that we look at have this inauthentic activity.”

Looking further ahead, Gudea plans to expand its ability to understand where narratives originate and how they spread. One major upcoming initiative is geolocation for narratives. Slated for next year, the technology is intended to allow users to identify where conversations are happening with far greater precision, down to the city-block level, Presley explains.

The company also wants to give customers greater access to the tools behind its analysis. For example, a company could eventually run an advertising campaign through Gudea’s AI model before launching it and get a better idea of whether the strategy is likely to produce a negative outcome or not. 

Last week, Gudea announced that it had raised $7 million in seed funding in a round co-led by Mudita Venture Partners and Silicon Road Ventures. The investment brings the startup’s total funding to approximately $15 million.

title: FBI Arrests OpenAI Employee Suspected of Planting a Surveillance Bug
snippet: Espionage in AI labs poses a national security threat, according to US intelligence and security officials.
fullText:
The FBI arrested an OpenAI employee and charged him with planting a surveillance device in an executive conference room to record the company’s plans for its artificial intelligence, the company and FBI confirmed on Tuesday.

The US Department of Justice identified the employee as 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian citizen and legal permanent resident of the US, who joined OpenAI’s product team in July 2025. He was fired and arrested on Oct. 9 on suspicion of violating US law by using “an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” The charge comes with a possible five-year prison sentence and a $250,000 fine.

In a statement, Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, said that the incident underscores the importance of US success in AI development as “a national security prerogative.” 

			

More from CNET

The complaint, filed in the Northern District of California, says Alfozan allegedly placed a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage.” It was wrapped in toilet paper and stuck into a TV port. A second recording device was found in a bag Alfozan allegedly left in a printer room along with his wallet and ID.

This is one of the recording devices found in OpenAI’s conference room, according to the affidavit filed with the court by the FBI.OpenAI/FBI

The conference room where he allegedly planted the bug could be reserved only by executives and their assistants — Alfozan did not have access — and was frequently used to discuss proprietary research and hold meetings with government and industry officials. OpenAI said it has evidence Alfozan planned to place additional surveillance bugs to secretly record company meetings.

The ChatGPT maker says it discovered the first bug on Sept. 30 and alerted the FBI. During the 10 days between the discovery and arrest, the company says it took steps to contain the security risk. The company says it has not seen evidence that the safety of its products or customer data has been compromised.

“We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

This image included in the FBI’s affidavit shows a man looking behind a TV.OpenAI/FBI

AI and national security

OpenAI’s own AI was used to analyze forensic images of the device and assess changes in its data. In a bizarre detail that borders on a marketing pitch, OpenAI posted on X that its frontier AI was used to help investigators. There are no additional details on how its AI was used, but we may learn more later, as the investigation is ongoing.

This incident is one of the first public instances of an espionage case against an AI lab. In 2024, former Google engineer Linwei Ding was found guilty of stealing the company’s AI plans for Chinese rivals, though his conviction was partially overturned in August. 

In the intense, cash-fueled worldwide competition to make the most advanced AI, a case of apparent industrial espionage isn’t surprising. What is noteworthy is how the government is responding: Washington is continuing its campaign to ensure that AI companies are seen as critical national infrastructure.

“Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is critically important, and FBI views it as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in an X post.

The federal government has become more involved with AI policy and with the labs creating the tech in recent months. The US’ voluntary, largely ceremonial AI Accord announced this month had many Big Tech leaders agreeing to develop AI responsibly in the wake of renewed public concern triggered in part by multiple incidents of AI agents breaking into places they shouldn’t have been able to access. 

President Trump has consistently championed an “innovation first” strategy to ensure the US beats China, at the expense of AI regulation. His administration has highlighted “national security considerations” that come with AI. The Department of Defense has previously sided with AI labs, saying in a filing in a lawsuit brought by Memphis communities against Elon Musk’s xAI that the data centers powering AI are essential to military and national security activities. 

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Opera Air gets a minimalist makeover with a focus on distraction-free browsing
snippet: Opera is relaunching its Opera Air browser today with a redesign that is both conceptual and practical for a more focused browsing experience. Here’s what that means. more…
fullText:
Opera is relaunching its Opera Air browser today with a redesign that is both conceptual and practical for a more focused browsing experience. Here’s what that means.

Opera Air relaunches with renewed focus on distraction-free browsing

In early 2025, Opera announced Opera Air, which the company described as “the first web browser built around the concept of mindfulness.”

Since then, the company has been refining not just Opera Air but the entire family of browsers it offers, including Opera One and Neon.

Today, Opera is relaunching Opera Air with an update that builds on its minimalist design and overall experience, and “keeps distractions to a minimum to give people more room to focus on what matters.”

Here’s Opera:

Air starts simple, with a clean interface and additional tools available when wanted. Messaging and social media apps can also be added to the sidebar.

The redesign also gives Air a new visual look. Refreshed wallpapers use open spaces, perspective, and natural textures, automatically adapting to Light and Dark themes.

Less on the surface doesn’t mean less underneath. Air comes with a built-in ad blocker for faster, less cluttered browsing and a free VPN for added privacy and protection online.

In keeping with the original idea for Opera Air, today’s update still includes Soundscapes, organized into four categories, that combine music and ambient sounds to help users focus or relax.

Ambience brings sounds such as Sea Waves and Spring Forest, while five new Soundscapes feature original music composed specifically for Opera Air. Among them is Hyperfocus, a more energetic track designed for settling into a task and staying there.

And speaking of focus, Opera Air also offers a set of features that help users take a break and regroup before resuming their browsing session.

That includes customizable break reminders that bring up breathing exercises, also divided into four categories (Destress, Refresh, Box Breathing, and Relax), as well as neck stretches.They can also be accessed from the sidebar, alongside Soundscapes.

Opera Air is free and available for macOS and Windows, and you can learn more about it here.

title: Google Messages adding ‘enhanced protection mode’ as Android works to combat phone scam
snippet: For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Google is announcing new Android features to help combat messaging and phone scams, including enhanced protection mode in Google Messages. more…
fullText:
For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Google is announcing new Android features to help combat messaging and phone scams, including enhanced protection mode in Google Messages.

Google is introducing an “enhanced protection mode” for its Messages app. Billed as providing the “most powerful and intelligent defenses” against complex scam threats, this mode starts with Scam Detection leveraging Private AI Compute. Google Messages will use “cloud Gemini models to evaluate complex message context and understand a scammer’s intent more quickly when you’re in a conversation with an unknown sender.”

This secure cloud analysis augments and extends our existing on-device detection, allowing us to identify novel and sophisticated attacks, actively uncovering and stopping abusers who try to hide their tracks

Private AI Compute, which is used by Pixel Screenshots and other apps, encrypts data and processes it in a secure space that Google cannot access for any other purpose.

The existing link protections work to flag malicious and phishing websites. With enhanced protection mode, on-device Gemini Nano uses “real-time web signals to evaluate whether an unfamiliar link is trustworthy before you tap.” This feature is available on the Pixel 10+, Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Z Fold 8. and “other select devices.”

	

The final feature adds redesigned warnings that “give you extra time and clearer context to pause before tapping links sent from numbers not saved in your contacts.”

This feature was previously only available on devices in select countries or on devices with Android Advanced Protection enabled 

Enhanced protection mode is an opt-in setting that is rolling out over the “coming weeks.”

Meanwhile, Google is expanding on-device Scam Detection for chat notifications beyond Pixel to HONOR, Infinix, iQOO, itel, JOVI, Motorola, OPPO, OnePlus, realme, TECNO, vivo, and Xiaomi devices. 

On the phone scam front, automatic screen-share privacy that hides sensitive info (like passwords and banking information) in native apps will soon apply to Chrome and WebView on Android 15+ devices.

Google will block apps from “quietly enabling call forwarding in the background” to combat one-time passcode theft. This call forwarding protection will be available starting in early December on Pixel and other select devices.

If a scammer attempts to trick you into manually typing an MMI forwarding code on your phone’s dial pad, Android proactively warns you before it can take effect.

title: Amazon’s always-listening Bee wearable can now help you buy stuff
snippet: Last year, Amazon bought Bee, a relatively unknown startup with a $50 always-listening AI wearable that summarized every conversation you had. fullText:
Last year, Amazon bought Bee, a relatively unknown startup with a $50 always-listening AI wearable that summarized every conversation you had. Today, the e-commerce giant is announcing two new Bee devices — and a new subscription to go with them. First is the $74.99 Bee Frontier, an updated version of the original Bee device. And coming soon is the $99.99 Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-shaped gadget that snaps magnetically onto the back of a smartphone.

Both devices are framed as gadgets to help you stay present in the moment. They listen to your daily conversations and then provide summaries, transcripts, insights, and to-dos based on what happens throughout the day. Conceptually, they’re similar to other AI note-taking gadgets like Plaud NotePin and Limitless AI. Users can also integrate Bee devices with services like Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, Apple HealthKit, and photos. Doing so lets Bee’s AI take some actions on your behalf, like drafting emails or sending calendar invites based on your conversations.

The main difference between the two products is form factor. The Bee Frontier can be worn as a Fitbit-like band on the wrist or as a clip-on pin. It’s been slightly redesigned from the prior model so that the recording button is more prominent, and it’s now available in three colors. Like the previous version, it has dual microphones, a recording indicator light, and roughly seven days of battery life on a single charge. It also has an IP67 water resistance rating.

Meanwhile, the Eclipse is meant as a non-wearable alternative and is envisioned for more professional use cases. Its larger size allows for a bigger battery, getting 21 days on a single charge. It, too, has a recording indicator light.

While these devices are free to use, Amazon is also introducing a Bee Pro subscription for $11.99 a month. The free tier gets users conversation summaries, recaps, and 14 days of memory. The subscription gets users “unlimited” summaries, suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, conversation templates, third-party app integrations, and a desktop app. But the big marquee feature for the subscription is Amazon and Alexa Plus compatibility.

The Amazon integration is opt-in, and doing so will enable the device to surface shopping suggestions based on your conversations. For example, if your spouse asks you to buy cat litter, you might see a product card reminding you of that on your Amazon homepage or an Amazon button linking out to the product in the Bee mobile app. The Alexa Plus integration is meant to be a hands-free way to access your various Bee summaries and insights.

It’s an interesting time for Amazon to introduce these products, given the recent backlash against so-called surveillance tech. On that front, Amazon told The Verge in a press briefing that Bee devices encrypt transcripts, summaries, and to-dos via its “Private Compute” security architecture and don’t store audio recordings. Bee devices can also be programmed to automatically stop recording if no sound is detected after a certain period of time. As for whether transcripts are attributable, that depends. Upon setup, Bee’s AI is trained on the individual user’s voice. All other speakers are not automatically identified unless you ask them to also allow Bee’s AI to train on their voice. Whether that’s enough to assuage any privacy concerns, well, that depends on your definition of a recording.

The Bee Frontier is available starting today for $74.99 in black, green, and lavender. The Eclipse is “coming soon” for $99.99 and is available in black, pink, yellow, and silver.

title: Bloomberg: New iPad mini with OLED display will be significantly more expensive than current model

fullText:
The current iPad mini sells for $599 in its starting 128 GB configuration. Apple is set to introduce the next-generation iPad mini later this month and — while the starting storage may increase — interested buyers should start probably bracing for a price rise.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says he is hearing that the new iPad mini will be “considerably more expensive”, floating a new price closer to the $799 mark.

If that turned out to be the case, it would represent a $200 jump compared to the current iPad mini baseline, and slot it above the 11-inch iPad Air starting price in the current lineup. 

Of course, Apple will argue that you are getting more product for that money. The new iPad mini is expected to feature an OLED display for the first time, with a new chassis design including thinner bezels. 

The new iPad mini is also getting upgraded speaker system and a much more powerful chip upgrade. We believe it will be powered by the A20 Pro chip, the same chip as found in Apple’s high-end iPhone 18 Pro models.

However, it remains unclear whether the OLED display in the new iPad mini will be technically comparable to the iPad Pro’s industry-leading tandem OLED panel. There have also been conflicting reports about whether it will support 120Hz ProMotion.

The new iPad mini should be announced at a media event later this month, alongside new OLED MacBook Pros. But first, on Tuesday, Apple will host a ‘Welcome home’ event where it will unveil a new smart home strategy, including its first smart home display product.

title: Apple reportedly gearing up for strong iPhone 18 sales
snippet: While the iPhone 18 Pro is out, the entry-level model has been held back until early next year. That’s likely because the company wanted to maximize early production capacity and memory availability for the Pro model, alongside the iPhone Duo. But even this far ahead, one leaker has suggested that supply-chain orders indicate Apple is optimistic about demand for the base model … more…
fullText:
While the iPhone 18 Pro is out, the entry-level model has been held back until early next year. That’s likely because the company wanted to maximize early production capacity and memory availability for the Pro model, alongside the iPhone Duo.

But even this far ahead, one leaker has suggested that supply-chain orders indicate Apple is optimistic about demand for the base model …

Apple broke with tradition this year in launching only the Pro models of the new iPhone lineup, that is, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The base model iPhone 18 was nowhere to be seen.

There are likely a couple of reasons for this. First, the memory shortage meant that the company probably wanted to ensure there was enough supply for both the two iPhone 18 Pro models and the iPhone Duo.

Second with the iPhone Duo a more complex device, production demands are likely greater, even for a model likely to sell in relatively modest numbers thanks to the high price. For that reason, Apple may have wanted to give its manufacturing partners some breathing space by not launching the standard iPhone 18 at the same time.

Apple begins its production runs significantly ahead of iPhone launches in order to build up stock ready to meet initial demand. Production of the iPhone 18 is expected to begin at the end of November.

Leaker Fixed Focus Digital (FFD) says that inventory levels indicate that the company is gearing up for a significant stockpile of devices. This presumably refers to component orders placed within Apple’s supply chain.

The standard version of iPhone 18 is scheduled for production at the end of November, and judging by the inventory levels, the stockpile is quite substantial.

9to5Mac’s Take

Order levels within Apple’s supply chain are not necessarily a reliable indicator of production volumes. Apple prefers to have multiple suppliers for as many components as possible in order to negotiate the best possible pricing as well as protect against any issues experienced by individual manufacturers. It’s possible that FFD has visibility into a single supplier that happens to be favored by Apple at this point in the run-up to production. 

For this reason, we shouldn’t read too much into this report. However, the leaker does have a decent track record, so let’s call it an interesting indication that Apple may be expecting strong demand for the upcoming iPhone 18.

fullText:

title: Half of United flights have Starlink Wi-Fi – here’s how to check yours
snippet: United Airlines first introduced Starlink Wi-Fi on its flights starting early in 2025, the airline says nearly half of its flights currently offer the high-speed satellite internet service. It’s now introduced a new way to let you check whether your flight has the service … more…
fullText:
United Airlines first introduced Starlink Wi-Fi on its flights starting early in 2025, the airline says nearly half of its flights currently offer the high-speed satellite internet service. It’s now introduced a new way to let you check whether your flight has the service …

The airline says that it intends to hit 100% Starlink coverage by the end of next year, while current installation rates depend on the fleet. For mainline aircraft flying long distance routes, the current figure is 37%, while United Express regional jets have significantly greater coverage at 68%.

United already has more Starlink-equipped planes than any other airline in the world and is installing it on about 20 aircraft per week with plans to complete installations by the end of 2027. More than 250,000 United customers on average fly on a Starlink-equipped plane every day onboard more than 2,500 flights – nearly half the airline’s daily departures.

Starlink is now active on more than 635 United mainline and United Express aircraft and the airline has already flown more than 37.7 million passengers on Starlink-powered aircraft across more than 538,000 flights, powering 14 million devices.

United already notifies you about the availability of Starlink Wi-Fi in preflight emails and texts, but it’s now introduced a tracker in case of any equipment changes on your route. Airlines do sometimes need to swap aircraft at relatively short notice to account for issues like technical faults and flight cancellations that leave planes incorrectly positioned for their next scheduled flight.

Simply go to this tracking link within two days of your departure, entering your flight number and departure date. If you check further ahead, the tracker will show you the percentage likelihood based on recent flights on the same route, but it’s only within 48 hours that you’ll get a generally reliable answer.

title: YouTube begins rolling out GIF support for comments very slowly; it’s for a reason
snippet: It’s been less than a month since YouTube said it planned to let users post GIFs in the comments section. The time has come, and this is just the beginning of a gradual rollout. more…
fullText:
It’s been less than a month since YouTube said it planned to let users post GIFs in the comments section. The time has come, and this is just the beginning of a gradual rollout.

	

Reddit is being inundated with r/YouTube reports of users seeing GIFs in the comments under videos on the YouTube app. The conversation around the ability to post GIFs under a video is louder than the feature itself. It looks like YouTube is pushing this update in a gradual rollout, since a number of posts online center around not having the feature, but seeing them posted by other users.

YouTube said this would be coming last month, noting that users would be able to post a GIF under videos and Shorts. Any GIF posted will come from a library within the app, according to the company’s announcement. It’s unclear if users will be able to upload their own animated files.

What’s also unknown is how gradual this rollout is. Plenty of users don’t have the option, and it isn’t limited to Premium subscribers, it seems. Fortunately, YouTube is making this available slowly for the time being. Once it gets going, it’s not hard to imagine what a YouTube with a GIF-filled comments section would look like. It’s possible one may never see text in a comment again.

	

YouTube also announced other features when it broke the news about its new GIF comment system. The YouTube app will let users set custom feeds based on quick prompts, and Ask YouTube will get additional features centered around product comparisons. All three features are slated for “this Fall,” so it might not be much longer before YouTube comment sections are filled with GIFs instead of text.

title: Ambani’s Jio seeks to raise $3.2B in what could be India’s biggest IPO
snippet: Jio plans to use most of its IPO proceeds to repay debt as it expands beyond telecom.
fullText:
Jio Platforms, the digital arm of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is seeking to raise as much as $3.2 billion in what could be India’s biggest initial public offering. The listing will test public-market appetite for a company that attracted more than $20 billion from global investors, including Google and Meta in 2020.

On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19.

At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering.

In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion (about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion, while Google committed $4.5 billion.

Jio’s IPO is set to overtake Hyundai Motor India’s ₹278.7 billion ($3.3 billion at the time) offering in 2024, the country’s biggest to date, even if its shares are priced at the lower end of the range.

Since launching in 2016, Jio has grown into India’s largest telecom operator, with more than 524 million subscribers as of March 31, ahead of Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It initially drew customers with free data and cheap plans, though its prices are now comparable to those of its rivals. Over time, Jio has grown beyond a telco and expanded into broadband, cloud services, and other digital businesses.

Jio’s IPO comes as Elon Musk has stepped up his criticism of Ambani, accusing him of trying to keep Starlink out of India. The accusation comes more than a year after Jio and rival Airtel signed deals with Musk’s SpaceX to distribute Starlink’s satellite internet service in India, subject to regulatory approvals. Indian authorities have rejected Musk’s claims.

In the quarter ended June, Jio’s revenue rose nearly 12% from a year earlier to ₹391.7 billion (about $4.1 billion), while its net profit climbed 9% to ₹77.6 billion (around $816 million), per its IPO prospectus (PDF).

Jio has set aside shares worth up to ₹25 billion (about $263 million) for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders and another ₹5 billion ($53 million) for employees, who will receive a discount of ₹54 per share.

Of the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion ($2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remaining proceeds going toward general corporate purposes, per the prospectus.

title: Hey Google, where is the next Nest Hub?
snippet: Apple’s long-rumored smart home display is finally here and it begs the question – why hasn’t Google released a new Nest Hub in half a decade? more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-rumored smart home display is finally here and it begs the question – why hasn’t Google released a new Nest Hub in half a decade?

Following the explosive popularity of smart speakers, 2018’s Google Home Hub helped usher in a new step forward with smart displays, combining the always-listening hotwords with additional functionality in visual responses, video streaming, live camera feeds, and more. It was a pretty immediate hit that was eventually rebranded as the “Nest Hub” and later spawned two sequels: the larger Nest Hub Max and the second-gen Nest Hub.

And that’s where we’ve been for five years now.

Half a decade later, Google’s smart display efforts have been completely silent. Outside of bringing Gemini for Home to smart displays in the exact same capacity as smart speakers, virtually nothing has changed on a Nest Hub in the past few years. Just look at our coverage over the past couple of years – no new features, no groundbreaking changes of really any kind. Google impressively replaced the underlying operating system without anyone really noticing, but functionally, it’s just status quo.

	

That’s not to say status quo isn’t still good. The Nest Hub experience still checks a lot of boxes. Visual responses to voice commands is at the center, with easy controls for your smart home and doorbell previews also being core to it all. Top that off with casting of video apps (great for the kitchen), setting timers, and the Nest Hub Max’s ability to double as a Nest Cam, and it all gets the job done. There’s a reason that myself and millions of other Nest Hub buyers still use these devices. 

But did Google really hit a wall so hard that not only nothing has changed on the software side, but hardware has just been completely stagnant? Maybe, but it’s hard to believe if so, especially as Amazon has been plugging away with new form factors and ideas for its Echo Show series for years now – the bigger Echo Show 15 with Fire TV is a great example; I’d love a tiny Google TV for parts of my home that can’t justify a “real” TV.

Fast forward to today, and now we’ve got Apple’s entry to the market. “Homeview” is a little 7-inch display on an iMac-like pedestal that also mounts itself to the wall. At its core, there’s not a ton here beyond what you get on a Nest Hub. Visual responses to voice commands are the central functionality, with Apple also picking up Nest Hub Max’s ability to recognize individual users and adjust the software accordingly. Where Apple builds on it is with faster software – Nest Hub, even at launch, has always been a laggy mess – and a reboot of its smart home efforts with other new hardware in tow. It’s really just a ton of Apple’s usual polish to integrations and apps, just in the form factor of a Nest Hub.

But again, it begs the question; where is Google in all of this? 

Google hasn’t ignored the smart home space over the past few years, with its own smart home reboot coming in 2021’s Nest Cam revival and further releases since, as well as a complete reinvention of the Home app to better serve as a hub for not just Google’s ecosystem, but a deep catalog of compatible smart home devices. And there’s been a lot of good on that front, with the more recent effort to use Gemini helping to clean up what was a crumbling experience in Assistant. It’s still not perfect, but Google’s ecosystem has all of the right parts to back up a smart display. 

The last time Google acknowledged smart displays was around when the Google Home Speaker was announced. Roughly a year ago this week, in fact. At the time, Google Home chief Anish Kattukaran called the smart display the “ultimate form factor” for the smart home. And yet, it’s now Apple that’s delivering on that promise before Google.

Google seems to have something in the works, with “Google Home Display” showing up in code earlier this year, but nothing has come of it yet. 9to5Google readers pitched their ideas for the product, including keeping the Pixel Tablet’s detachable display and generally improving the performance and the display quality, the latter being things that Apple’s Homeview display absolutely do.

	

Google’s lack of action is going to hurt it pretty directly here. Apple’s launch isn’t cheap at $300, but for iPhone users, it’s a pretty easy sell. Just like how the Nest Hub was an easy sell as a smart home controller that displayed your pictures, that’s all Apple has to say to sell its own. Amazon’s Echo Show has a bigger uphill battle because, frankly, who wants to invest in Amazon’s ecosystem, but Google at least served as a nice middle ground for everyone. Out-of-the-box integration if you use an Android phone, and just a step or two if you already have a Gmail account, which is true of basically everyone anyway. But, right now, Google simply doesn’t have an option. Not only does it not have a competing option, but it just doesn’t sell anything. 

What do you think?

title: Smartphone shipments dropped by 20%, lowest point in 14 years amid memory crisis
snippet: RAMageddon continues to have wide effects throughout the tech industry, with a new report revealing that the smartphone market has just hit its lowest point in well over a decade. more…
fullText:
RAMageddon continues to have wide effects throughout the tech industry, with a new report revealing that the smartphone market has just hit its lowest point in well over a decade.

Counterpoint Research reports that global smartphone shipments dropped by 20% in Q3 2026, reaching the lowest numbers in the past 14 years. The last time smartphone shipments were this low, Samsung’s latest release was the Galaxy S3. 

Yikes.

The drop has not only impacted overall shipment figures, but also the share of the market that major smartphone brands take up. Chinese brands including Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo all make up a smaller share of the overall market in Q3 2026 compared to the same time the prior year, with Samsung continuing to hold the top spot at 23% of the overall market and Apple at 22%, up from 19% and 18%, respectively.

	

Counterpoint says that Samsung’s overall shipments only dropped by 3%, with the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s success playing a major role in the company’s quarter. Meanwhile, a recent report claims that Samsung makes no profit when it sells Galaxy phones at this point.

Apple, meanwhile, saw a 22% year-over-year decline with the absence of its base iPhone 18. Oppo and Vivo both saw drops of around 20% while Xiaomi dropped shipments by 30%.

title: Will HomeView support third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says
snippet: Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says. more…
fullText:
Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says.

Apple HomeView’s support for third-party apps will be limited

Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment.

That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls.

However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps.

According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.”

Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release.

While the produt page says:

Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas.

The press release, however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours):

Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby.

Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV.

Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView.

	

According ot Wired, “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.”

So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps.

We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back.

title: The ‘renewable’ iPhone Duo display layer may help buyers justify the price
snippet: The iPhone Duo starts at $1999 for the 256GB model and rises to an eye-watering $3199 for the 2TB version – but a “renewable” inner display layer may help buyers to justify spending so much money on a phone. Apple has addressed the biggest problem experienced with folding phones to date via a surprisingly affordable option … more…
fullText:
The iPhone Duo starts at $1999 for the 256GB model and rises to an eye-watering $3199 for the 2TB version – but a “renewable” inner display layer may help buyers to justify spending so much money on a phone.

Apple has addressed the biggest problem experienced with folding phones to date via a surprisingly affordable option … 

One of the biggest problems of Android folding phones has been a crease that is visible when new and that tends to become even more so after repeated folding and unfolding over time. Apple reportedly put a huge amount of work into a hinge and display design intended to minimize this effect, and early hands-on sessions confirm that the crease is barely visible when new.

Despite this, however, it’s still likely that some visible degradation of the inner layer will occur over time. Indeed, the company has acknowledged this, with hardware lead Kate Bergeron saying that the company has worked hard to help it “wear in as long of a manner as we can.”

That’s a potential problem with a device so expensive it’s likely that most buyers will want to hold on to it for far longer than a typical iPhone, but Bergeron also revealed that this inner cover layer is replaceable once the crease does finally become more visible.

It’s actually replaceable, which is a really nice thing for the customer, that you can peel off that layer and get a new one.

We learned at the time that a replacement costs just $19 with AppleCare, and we now know that the price without is $49. For a machine costing $2k and up, that’s a surprisingly affordable way to make the inner display look like new again. Anyone thinking they might justify the price by holding on to the phone for a number of years may very well find this the deciding argument.

What’s your view? Does this renewability make the price of the device more palatable? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Oppo confirms list of devices getting its Android 17 update, rollout starts this month
snippet: Oppo has officially revealed ColorOS 17, its Android 17 update, to global markets this week and, along with that, confirmed a list of devices poised to get the update. more…
fullText:
Oppo has officially revealed ColorOS 17, its Android 17 update, to global markets this week and, along with that, confirmed a list of devices poised to get the update.

ColorOS 17 is Oppo’s Android 17 update, and it has two main focuses – smooth performance, and AI. It’s also packed with Liquid Glass design elements, as if that should surprise anyone at this point. 

Oppo calls its Liquid Glass copy “Flow,” with the “Luminous Rendering Engine” powering animations that react to your touch. Oppo says:

ColorOS 17 reimagines how you interact with the system. It senses the pressure and direction of your touch, responding with fluid, elastic motion and nuanced lighting effects that make every interaction feel truly alive. With the all-new Unified Rendering Architecture, transitions between elements are more seamless and refined than ever.

Oppo says that ColorOS 17 is also faster and more reliable, touting 55% “more stable app launches” and 25% better app retention in memory. 

	

As with anything else in 2026, AI is a big part of the update, with Oppo continuing to build out features like AI Mind Space (similar to Pixel Screenshots and Nothing’s Essential Space), adding “AI Mind Pilot” as an agentic AI service, “AI Mind Suggest” as a proactive flight companion, an “AI Photo Agent” is a prompt-based photo editor.

Oppo says ColorOS 17 will start rolling out globally this month – October 29, to be exact – with over a dozen devices set to be updated before the month’s end and many more to be updated through the first quarter of 2027.

iCloud+ is best known for adding iCloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding its suite of benefits for subscribers. Here’s everything new for iCloud+ added in the last few weeks.

iCloud+ additions include HomeKit Secure Video upgrades, free Apple TV and Arcade for many, higher AI usage limits, more

If you subscribe to iCloud+ or Apple One, you’re probably getting more benefits than you realize.

	

Beyond extra storage, iCloud+ includes features like Hide My Email, iCloud Private Relay, full Apple Invites access, and more.

Here’s everything new for iCloud+ subscribers added in the last few weeks:

HomeKit Secure Video upgrades: Ahead of new Home products launching this week, Apple has upgraded HomeKit Secure Video in several ways. iOS 27’s powerful new features include 4K support, generated video descriptions, clip searching, and noteworthy clips.

Custom Email Domain: If you run a small business or want to use custom emails for your family or for any other reason, iCloud+ lets you set up personalized addresses for domains you own. You were previously limited to three personalized email addresses, but now you can create up to 10 per domain.

Apple TV and Arcade added in 100+ countries: It doesn’t apply to the US, but iCloud+ subscribers in more than 100 countries now get Apple TV and Arcade thrown in at no additional cost. It’s a huge upgrade for many users that makes the service more of a no-brainer in supported territories.

title: Flock CEO says its microphones detect ‘just gunshots’ — its website says different
snippet: Langley’s comments come amid mounting scrutiny of Flock from privacy advocates, including the ACLU, and members of the public who are concerned about the misuse of its technology.
fullText:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said the company’s gunshot-detection microphones detect “just gunshots,” but Flock’s website paints a far broader picture of what other ambient audio also gets picked up.

Speaking onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, the co-founder of the surveillance company defended Flock’s audio-collection product called Gunshot Detection, which listens for gunshots and other ambient audio across nearby neighborhoods to provide “earlier awareness” to potential public safety events.

Flock’s website says that the company’s audio systems can pinpoint gunfire instantly, while also being able to “detect street takeovers early to stop chaos before it escalates,” and “identify severe crashes in real time so help arrives faster.” It also says they can “expand awareness beyond gunfire with alerts for car crashes, fireworks, and sideshows.”

The company’s Gunshot Detection feature, announced last year, faced immediate pushback. In announcing the feature, Flock said the technology would listen out for sounds of “screaming.” Privacy groups condemned the company for listening for human voices, prompting the company to amend its website to instead say “sounds of human distress.” Flock later said it pulled the ability to detect “distress” altogether from its customers who tried it.

During the interview, Langley pushed back against what he described as misinformation about his product, arguing that many of its critics misunderstand how its products work. The comments come as public opinion continues to shift against Flock and other license plate reading companies amid growing unease about mass surveillance — sentiments that were visible in San Francisco, where protesters gathered to voice their opposition outside the venue as Langley took the stage.

Image Credits:TechCrunch (screenshot)

“Most people don’t call 911 when they hear a gunshot, and so that’s why we built the product,” Langley told TechCrunch editor-in-chief Connie Loizos onstage. “And then some of our customers said, ‘Oh, we have these in parking lots. It would be great if we could get alerted if someone was being abducted, if someone was being harmed.’”

Langley said that the idea seemed logical, so the company prototyped it and rolled it out to a couple of customers, but said that some people then had a lot of concerns. Langley conceded to making mistakes but that he was listening to his customers.

“There’s only a couple customers that were prototyping it with us, and we said, ‘OK, great, it’s just going to do gunshots, plain and simple.’ If a gun goes off, we’ll notify, and if not, that’s all it’s going to listen to,” said Langley.

When asked about the contradiction between his remarks and the company’s marketing materials that say the audio systems can detect more than gunshots, he responded, “It’s just gunshots.” 

When reached by TechCrunch, Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said: “Flock’s gunshot detection technology is primarily used to detect gunfire but is also capable of detecting fireworks, sideshows, and potential car crashes. CEO Garrett Langley’s remarks were intended to emphasize that Flock’s Audio Detection technology is not designed to monitor conversations or analyze speech and does not currently detect human screaming or distress.”

An FAQ section of the website notes that “in addition to gunshots, Flock Gunshot and Audio Detection can detect fireworks, sideshows, and other disruptive community events.” It goes on to state that the company’s “detection library is continually expanding to include emerging threats that are relevant” to customers’ specific needs. 

Langley stated that the number of Flock’s microphones is comparable to ShotSpotter, which as of 2024 had about 25,000 microphones, per reporting by Wired.

Langley’s comments come amid mounting scrutiny of Flock from privacy advocates, including the ACLU, and members of the public who are concerned about the misuse of its technology, with some going so far as destroying the surveillance cameras. The remarks also come as Texas and Florida have moved to end their relationships with Flock, and Amazon’s Ring has ended its partnership with the company.

Aisha is a consumer news reporter at TechCrunch. Prior to joining the publication in 2021, she was a telecom reporter at MobileSyrup. Aisha holds an honours bachelor’s degree from University of Toronto and a master’s degree in journalism from Western University.

title: LineageOS support finally comes to Pixel 10 and 10a lineup
snippet: After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a. more…
fullText:
After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a.

Over a year since its release, it’s great news that Pixel 10 owners now have the option to flash LineageOS on their devices, but the long wait is likely due to circumstances beyond the Lineage team’s control.

Google has made it harder for ROM projects in recent years, making it harder for projects like Lineage and Graphene, as the company is no longer sharing device trees and driver binaries. This coincided with the launch of Android 16, and so it has likely stalled some of the development for the last generation of hardware.

On top of that, delays to public kernel downloads for Pixel devices haven’t been ideal.

	

Some of this likely accounts for the delay in LineageOS builds for Pixel 10. At least the good news is that builds are now available for download on the same day LineageOS 24 was announced. This latest version is the Android 17 build for the custom ROM and comes with a number of changes to take better advantage of the enhancements added in early June 2026.

This release includes a whole host of Material 3 Expressive changes to the default app suite with a brand new “Canvas” image editor. Security patches are accounted for up to October 2026, meaning you are fully secure if you do prefer an AI-free experience with Lineage on your Pixel 10.

It’s worth noting that Pixel 10 Pro XL, 10 Pro Fold, and Pixel 10a builds are not yet live, but nightly Pixel 10 and 10 Pro builds are live right now.

title: Apple TV 4K and HomeView: The best and worst of $299
snippet: Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful. more…
fullText:
Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful.

HomeView for $299 feels like an invitation to try a new product category

HomeView looks like a hit. Without actually seeing or hearing it, the verdict is still out. What we can judge now is the pitch. 

In classic Apple fashion, the company is hardly the first to deliver a smart display. Yet HomeView appears to have the polish and consideration that an iPhone user would expect.

At $299, it seems Apple is pricing HomeView more as an invitation to try a new category of product. I’m intrigued.

Apple TV 4K for $299 feels like Apple already knows the customer

Then there’s the Apple TV 4K. At $299, it feels priced more like specialized hardware. Unlike HomeView, Apple TV 4K has a price history.

In 2021, Apple sold two Apple TV boxes: Apple TV HD for $149, and Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) for $179.

Both boxes ran tvOS with an App Store, but customers didn’t love that 4K support costed nearly $200.

By the end of the following year, Apple TV 4K (3rd generation) arrived in two flavors: 64GB with no Thread or Ethernet for $129, or 128GB with Thread and Ethernet for $149.

This was viewed as a great cost correction compared to the previous generation. Better hardware and a better price? That sounds too good to be true.

But it was true for a while. Then Apple raised prices on a number of existing products in June. You may recall Apple TV 4K being one of the more painful price jumps, both due to the percent increase and the age of the hardware.

The $129 model jumped to $199, and the $149 model jumped to $249.

Today’s Apple TV 4K replaces the $249 model with an even higher $299 price.

We’re now back to the original Apple TV starting price from 2007. Boy, what a relief when Apple switched from local storage to streaming with the vastly different Apple TV (2nd generation) puck for $99.

Apple TV 4K the best experience, but it’s for fewer people now

Anyway, things are different in 2026. You can literally buy a 65-inch 4K LED TV with the Apple TV app (and all the other streaming apps) built-in for $299.

Where does that leave the Apple TV 4K? It’s increasingly positioned not as a way to add streaming apps to your TV, but as a very particular way to bring the full Apple experience to your TV.

But did Apple get the feature set for the price right?

Adding mics to the box itself is a nice touch, especially since other set-top boxes already do this. There’s also the chip upgrade.

Another big new feature is support for creating a home theater experience beyond stereo speaker output with a pair of big HomePod speakers and a pair of new HomePod mini 2 speakers. That’s a $1300 experience between the set-top box and four speakers.

Personally, I’ve stayed on the Apple TV 4K (2nd-gen) from 2021 without any complaints. I don’t know how much I’ll use Siri AI from my TV, but having it come to the box I already own is a nice surprise.

A specialized home theater experience isn’t a priority in the budget right now, so I’m plenty happy with my 55-inch 4K LED that costed me $168 on sale from Hisense. It’s not the absolute best TV I’ve ever owned, but it’s plenty enough for me. Attaching a $299 Apple TV 4K to it would almost feel wrong.

	

But if a premium home theater experience is at the top of your priorities and cost isn’t a concern, Apple TV 4K at $299 is a sure upgrade over built-in TV experiences for Apple users.

For now, I’m just grateful that I’m getting most of that experience from a purchase made years ago.

Hopefully there’s an Apple TV option in the future that feels less overpowered and overpriced needs and budgets like mine in the future. At this point, even a version without the $59 Siri Remote in the box would feel more palatable.

Share your thoughts in the comments.
