title: OpenAI Sued Over Children’s Data Used to Train ChatGPT
snippet: The lawsuit says ChatGPT continued to chat with a 12-year-old, even rating her looks.
fullText:
OpenAI built ChatGPT into the world’s most profitable chatbot, but two Hawaii plaintiffs say it unlawfully scraped data from millions of children along the way. Now, they want a share of the company or its cash equivalent in return.

The lawsuit, Jane Doe v. OpenAI Foundation, was filed on Tuesday by a parent on behalf of her two children, a 12-year-old girl and a 16-year-old boy. They allege that OpenAI has used data from millions of children who signed up for ChatGPT accounts without getting their parents’ permission. OpenAI’s terms of use state that, “If you are under 18, you must have your parent or legal guardian’s permission to use the Services,” but the suit says that children can still sign up for accounts, and OpenAI never verifies consent.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

			

More from CNET

The lawsuit also says that OpenAI “grooms” kids to share highly personal information about their health, relationships, photos of their faces and bodies, voice recordings, dreams, emotions, fears and insecurities. 

“Children are an open book to ChatGPT, which methodically strips out every page of information they have,” the lawsuit argues.

By flattering children, validating their feelings and asking provocative questions, ChatGPT “conditions children to trust ChatGPT even more than they would a sibling, friend, teacher, or parent,” the complaint argues. OpenAI does this to amass enormous amounts of data on kids to train AI models and construct profiles of children, the lawsuit says.

The plaintiffs want the lawsuit certified as a class action, meaning anyone in the US who was under 18 when they used ChatGPT can join it if that status is approved.

As compensation, the plaintiffs demand that OpenAI pay equity or a cash equivalent “in proportion to the number of tokens each child contributed to OpenAI through ChatGPT.” Tokens are how AI companies calculate chatbot usage. A 75-word chat is worth about 100 tokens, OpenAI says.

“OpenAI has touted its desire to share with the public some of the vast wealth created by its AI models,” the lawsuit says. “This lawsuit provides OpenAI a chance to do so — starting with its many child victims.” 

Indeed, earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlined a public wealth fund that would distribute AI revenues to people, partly to encourage them to invest in AI companies.

A representative for OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new lawsuit is one of dozens filed against OpenAI in the past few years. Some accuse ChatGPT of contributing to user suicide, self-harm and mental health crises. Another group of lawsuits alleges that OpenAI failed to alert authorities about a user’s flagged ChatGPT activity before they killed several people at a school in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada. Other complaints say OpenAI used copyrighted material to train its AI models.

ChatGPT knew a user was only 12

The lawsuit filed this week detailed several exchanges between the 12-year-old girl plaintiff (referred to as “MC1”) and ChatGPT. At one point, the girl said she was only 12, but the chatbot continued the conversation, even though OpenAI says users must be 13 and obtain parental consent to use ChatGPT.

Even though the girl initially asked about dinner ideas and homework help, over time the chats came to involve personal details about health, appearance and emotions, the lawsuit states. In one chat, the girl asks, “Why is everything making me angry now? … Every time my mother tells me something or tells me to do something, it gets me really annoyed and mad.” ChatGPT then gives some possible reasons for her constant anger and, after the girl again says she’s 12, the bot replies, “Thank you for telling me that (heart emoji). Being 12 actually adds some important context.”

The lawsuit also says the girl often shared selfies with ChatGPT and asked for comments about what she perceived as issues with her appearance, such as chubby cheeks, pimples and her thoughts that she might be “ugly.”

She also asked ChatGPT to “rate” her looks, to which the bot replied, “YESS I can do a fun rating-style breakdown! Like facial features, hairstyle, overall vibe, styling, symmetry, etc. … send me a photo, and I can do it!” The lawsuit alleges that, over time, ChatGPT began mimicking the girl’s chat style, using similar language, words and emoji.

“By design, ChatGPT purposely extracted this information from MC1, so that OpenAI could use it to train its LLMs and build a personalized dossier on MC1, which OpenAI will retain indefinitely and later use for advertising,” the lawsuit alleges.

Earlier this month, watchdog group Common Sense Media called ChatGPT for Teens, which launched in August, an “unacceptable risk” for teen users. According to Common Sense Media, the chatbot failed to alert parents when children discussed suicide, self-harm or eating disorders, and instead of helping teens build critical learning skills, it frequently just handed them homework answers.

OpenAI said that ChatGPT for Teens will alert parents when kids discuss “high-risk” topics and will also serve as a collaborative partner in helping children with homework and test preparation.

Congress must act, says advocate

The lawsuit’s allegations are another example of the AI industry’s “move fast and break things” mentality, says Donna Rice Hughes, president and CEO of the digital child safety organization Enough is Enough. She says the industry’s guardrails and policies are not strong enough to protect children.

“When an AI platform enables a 12-year-old to upload pictures of herself to have the chatbot ‘rate’ her looks, that’s not only deeply troubling, it’s abusive,” Hughes told CNET.

Hughes called on Congress to pass several AI child safety bills, including the Youth AI Privacy Act, CHATBOT Act, Children’s Artificial Intelligence, Toy Safety Act of 2026 and the Guard Act. These legislative measures have stalled after being passed out of their committees.

Hughes also said that even though parents should not be solely responsible for how AI affects their kids, they should consult www.InternetSafety101.org for suggestions on protecting their children in the AI era.

title: The best feature of Apple’s HomeView might be its simplicity
snippet: Apple’s HomeView smart display seems tailor-made for the kitchen. (That aluminum base looks like it will hold up better than my now off-white kitchen HomePod.) I'm just going to come right out and say it. I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it's the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple's first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? No. But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? Absolutely. A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. And yes, its features replicate many of the things you already do on the devices you use all the time. B … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
I’m just going to come right out and say it. I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? No. But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? Absolutely.

A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. And yes, its features replicate many of the things you already do on the devices you use all the time. But that’s kind of the point. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with.

The HomeView’s footprint is smaller than that of most smart displays I’ve tested.

My iPad-in-the-wall experiment lasted several unsuccessful years.

I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. It wasn’t great. I’ll have to test HomeView, of course, but my initial impression is that this could be a much better solution for those use cases.

Most iPads are more expensive, have worse speakers, and do not like to be plugged in all the time (I present my sad, warped iPad Mini as tribute). An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching.

The HomeView can be wall-mounted.

Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. This means it’s always where you expect it to be, which matters when you want to adjust the thermostat or can’t find your phone and want to check your calendar. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion.

Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me

And while many people are fine using their personal phones and tablets to interact with the digital world when at home, and don’t want yet another device with a screen on their countertop or wall, the millions of Echo Shows, Google Nest Hubs, Skylight Calendars, and the like in homes today are a good indicator that there’s interest in this type of interface.

As Apple’s uncharacteristically chaotic launch video shows, HomeView targets a new demographic for the company: busy, Apple-centric households. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. I’ve occasionally used the drop-in feature on Echo smart speakers to get her attention, further proof of the advantage of always-on home devices.

The HomeView uses Siri AI (which requires an AI-capable iPhone) to provide useful personal information.

HomeView has user profiles, but anyone in the home can control devices like smart lights. (But that’s one really big button…)

I see HomeView as filling the awkward space where families don’t want phones at the dinner table or on the kitchen counter, but still want to check what time Zoey’s soccer game is or look up the origin of French toast (yeah, just kidding). This inevitably ends with one person pulling out their phone, which gives everyone else implicit permission to do the same.

Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). Siri AI’s much-hyped “personal context” capabilities, in which it can scan your text messages and emails and serve up relevant information to up to six members of your household, also give it an edge here.

The HomeView has a variety of customizable faces.

I asked Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, why Apple chose now for its biggest smart home push yet. She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.

As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.”

— Lilian Rincon, Apple

Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. She also pointed to its new conversational abilities. “It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”

Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. Based on the demos I saw, and my time using Siri AI on the iPhone, when you ask it to do something, it does it without peppering you with follow-up questions. Rincon confirmed this is by design. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. “For us, it isn’t about that. We’re there to get it done, take an action for you, show you what you need to get done, and then really get out of the way.”

The Home control widget on the HomeView can show live views of security cameras.

My first reaction to hearing about HomeView’s smart home features, which are basically just what the Apple Home app on your phone can do, was disappointment. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. I’m still waiting on that.

On reflection, I’m okay with this — for now. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights.

Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing.

HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? My family.

Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen.

HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

title: Apple-1 sets a new record at $1,148,200 after a rejected upgrade
snippet: An Apple-1 computer sold at auction has set a new record of $1,148,200. The same machine last sold in 2013 for $686,000. It comes complete with a letter which, thankfully, the original owner ignored … more…
fullText:
An Apple-1 computer sold at auction has set a new record of $1,148,200. The same machine last sold in 2013 for $686,000. It comes complete with a letter which, thankfully, the original owner ignored … 

The machine is known as the “Hatfield” Apple-1, after the name of the original owner, Fred Hatfield. The motherboard was signed by Steve Wozniak, and it came with a letter signed by Steve Jobs.

Thankfully for Hatfield, he rejected the offer made in that letter, which was to trade in the machine for an Apple II. Steve made the offer after Hatfield wrote to Apple complaining about the limited software options for the machine.

The fact that the machine is in full working order and can be traced back to its original purchaser added significant appeal, but the increase over the price achieved back in 2013 points to their continuing appreciating value.

title: Hiyd is a health tracker that attaches to the watch you already wear
snippet: Former Apple engineers figured out how to get a biometric sensor to attach to your watch without any magnets or adhesives.
fullText:
If you’re a watch enthusiast, you probably don’t want to exchange your prized timepiece for a bulky fitness tracker. But Hiyd founder Salah Batroukh doesn’t think people should have to sacrifice fashion for function.

“We don’t think that health tracking needs to be this overly conscious decision where you have to change something about the way you look,” Batroukh told TechCrunch. “That’s the ethos of the entire company. Our plan is to build out this product ecosystem of invisible health tracking.”

Hiyd’s first device to make health tracking look cooler is a small, slim disc that attaches to the back of your watch via microsuction, a material technology that allows the sensor to sit flush under your watch without magnets or adhesive. That way, it won’t leave any residue or mess with the mechanics of watches that keep time using magnets.

“Microsuction is essentially a textured silicone, with hundreds of tiny pockets per square inch molded into a pliable sheet. So when you press on it, it pushes air out of all those pockets, and you end up with a vacuum — just like traditional suction cups but scaled down incredibly,” Batroukh explained. “It works incredibly at stopping shear forces, but a little bit of prying allows it to pop right off, which is ideal for us. It’s also incredibly thin at just 0.3 mm with our manufacturing processes.”

Image Credits:Hiyd

According to Batroukh, the sensor, which measures 2.7 mm thick and weighs 7 grams, collects biometrics similar to those of leading wearables, including heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep staging, movement, calories burned, and VO2 max estimations, then syncs to an iOS or Android app. In order to fine-tune the sensor, Hiyd’s team is filming themselves doing various activities, then labeling those datasets to train its AI.

“We go for a walk and say, ‘This is somebody walking, this is somebody jogging, this is somebody running,’” he said. “The one thing that AI is really good at is data analysis, so we can basically fit a lot of heuristic analysis into our sets really quickly.”

On its app, Hiyd is also working to incorporate nutrition tracking. The goal isn’t to count calories, but rather to help users glean insights about how their eating habits impact their sleep quality or workout performance.

“What we will do is say like, ‘Hey, on days where you work out at 10 p.m. instead of 10 a.m., your sleep quality is actually worse,’ and that’ll be specific to you,” he said. “Or it’ll say, ‘Hey, we think you had a less deep sleep last night because you had a slice of cake before you went to bed, and the sugar affected it.’”

Image Credits:Hiyd

Batroukh spent about seven years as a manufacturing design engineer at Apple, a company synonymous with iconic hardware. But he wanted to know if he could design something great without the support of a global brand and a multitrillion-dollar market cap.

“One of the reasons I left Apple was a lot of the products became a little bit more about being an Apple product, rather than being something for the customer,” he said. “[Hiyd] gives me the opportunity to do the exact opposite.”

Batroukh is joined by fellow founders Omar Shakir, an experienced mechanical engineer who is the startup’s CTO, and Mahamad Charawi, who is its head of software. (Charawi previously co-led the Y Combinator-backed startup Laudspeaker through its sale.)

Hiyd is bringing its tiny sensor to the big stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where the company is competing as one of the top 20 companies at Startup Battlefield on Wednesday. (Don’t miss out on the action.) In November, the company plans to launch a Kickstarter. So far, over 16,000 people have made deposits to secure Hiyd’s first units.

title: iPhone Duo Repair Prices Will Fold Your Bank Account Without AppleCare
snippet: Thinking of saving a little money when buying Apple’s new foldable phone? A mishap could cost up to $1,500 in repairs.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo starts at expensive and goes up to exorbitant for its higher-capacity configurations, and if something happens and you need a repair, the costs could be substantial without AppleCare coverage.

The base 256GB storage option is priced at $1,999, but if you want to max out Apple’s new foldable phone with 2TB of space, it’ll cost $3,199. That’s pricey by iPhone standards, compared to the iPhone 18 Pro that begins at $1,199, though in line with the retail prices of Android folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Adding AppleCare coverage on top of the iPhone Duo’s price is an ongoing cost in addition to the price of the phone, but in terms of potential repairs, it does make sense. Because if you don’t fork out for a plan, and the inner display of your iPhone Duo gets crunched, expect to pay $999 to get it replaced, according to Apple’s support documentation. These are prices for repairs made directly by Apple, not third-party services.

			

More from CNET

The range of repairs starts at a modest $49 for “cover layer damage” and jumps all the way up to $1,499 for “other damage,” though it’s not clear what the latter entails. Here’s the breakdown:

Cover layer damage: $49

Back glass damage: $199

Battery service: $229

Rear camera damage: $229

Outer display damage: $379

Outer display and back glass damage: $509

Inner display damage: $999

Other damage: $1,499

AppleCare Plus with Theft and Loss is priced at $20 per month or $200 per year until canceled and includes “unlimited repairs for accidents like drops and spills” and theft and loss coverage for up to two claims every 12 months. It also features Express Replacement Service, which gets you a new iPhone Duo instead of waiting for a repair.

Alternatively, the AppleCare One service costs $20 a month until canceled and applies AppleCare Plus to up to three devices. It also adds a third theft-and-loss coverage event in the 12-month span.

If something happens to your iPhone Duo under AppleCare, the repair pricing ranges from zero for battery service to $149 for theft or loss. The list of repair services doesn’t match up exactly to the ones noted without coverage. Here’s what Apple details as estimated costs:

Battery service: $0

Cover layer damage: $19

Back glass damage: $29

Outer display damage: $29

Inner display damage: $99

Other accidental damage: $99

Theft or loss: $149

Keep in mind these are the amounts provided by Apple’s services. If you’re purchasing the iPhone Duo through a wireless carrier, it might have different warranty options.

iPhone Duo preorders kick off on Friday, with the first shipments and store availability set for Oct. 23.

We’re looking forward to testing not just how well the iPhone Duo works, but how resilient Apple’s most complex iPhone will be. In the meantime, be sure to check out our first hands-on impressions of Apple’s first foldable and ask yourself if the iPhone Duo is really for you.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Jeff Carlson
						

						

							Senior Writer						
					

											

								

											Jeff Carlson writes about mobile technology at CNET, from cellular phone plans to devices and emerging technology.

title: OpenAI agrees not to use alleged Apple trade secrets amid ongoing lawsuit
snippet: Bloomberg reports that during a hearing today, OpenAI voluntarily agreed not to use Apple’s alleged trade secrets while the legal battle between the two companies plays out. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that during a hearing today, OpenAI voluntarily agreed not to use Apple’s alleged trade secrets while the legal battle between the two companies plays out. Here are the details.

Apple scores second win in a row against OpenAI

Earlier today, OpenAI filed a new motion in the lawsuit in which Apple accuses the company of stealing trade secrets, alleging that a former employee who left OpenAI to return to Apple took more than 100 confidential files related to its unreleased hardware.

Soon after, the parties in the lawsuit appeared at a hearing where, as reported by Bloomberg, Judge Edward Davila indicated he was “highly likely” to grant Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction against OpenAI.

The short backstory on the injunction is the following: after Apple filed its trade secret misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products, the company also sought a preliminary injunction to prevent the defendants from accessing, using, or disclosing its confidential information while the case proceeds.

Apple also sought expedited discovery, requesting early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and employee testimony to support its case for an injunction. Many of those requests were granted yesterday.

Back to today’s hearing, Judge Davila’s indication that he was “highly likely” to grant the injunction prompted OpenAI to voluntarily agree “not to use trade secrets that Apple Inc. claims were stolen,” as Bloomberg put it.

As part of the agreement established today, OpenAI also committed to collecting forensic images of devices from 14 employees “that may contain Apple’s confidential information,” says Bloomberg.

Judge Davila will have the authority to enforce the agreement, meaning OpenAI could face court-imposed sanctions if it fails to comply with its commitments.

However, the judge also reportedly pushed back against some of Apple’s demands, describing its request to inspect every device and repository that might contain its trade secrets as a “huge ask.”

In response, Apple’s attorney, John M. Desmarais, said the company would limit its inspections to a small group of former employees, adding that OpenAI doesn’t have “400 bad apples,” but rather “a few bad apples and know who they are.”

title: HomePod mini 2 vs HomePod mini: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple unveiled HomePod mini 2 yesterday (pre-order here), exactly six years after the first HomePod mini debuted. Here’s everything new in HomePod mini 2 compared to the original model. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled HomePod mini 2 yesterday (pre-order here), exactly six years after the first HomePod mini debuted. Here’s everything new in HomePod mini 2 compared to the original model.

Siri AI vs old Siri, plus microphone change

HomePod mini 2 is getting Siri AI support, bringing similar capabilities found in iOS 27 to Siri on your HomePod. This includes broad world knowledge, the ability to have rich, natural conversations, and music discovery upgrades. Additionally, personal context support means you can ask about a song you were recommended by a friend via Messages, get key information stored in your email, and more.

The original HomePod mini will not support Siri AI, leaving it stuck on the old Siri

Siri AI won’t be available right when HomePod mini 2 ships, but it’s expected to arrive as a software update next month.

Additionally, while it’s unclear if performance will be impacted, HomePod mini 2 has three far-field microphones for interacting with Siri, down from the four offered in HomePod mini.

New S10 chip vs S5

The original HomePod mini has a very dated S5 chip, which is unsurprising since it’s a 6-year-old device. But the new HomePod mini 2 runs a much more modern S10 chip.

S10 is the main reason HomePod mini 2 supports Siri AI while the original model doesn’t. Beyond that though, Apple doesn’t offer specific details on performance improvements to expect. However, it’s possible the audio experience will be upgraded. Per Apple’s press release:

Powered by the Apple S10 chip and advanced computational audio, [HomePod mini 2] analyzes music in real time to optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance.

Apple doesn’t explicitly say that the computational audio will be an improvement over what the previous model offered, but it’s certainly possible. We’ll have to wait for reviews to know for sure.

Sound Glow

Sound Glow is a new feature that makes the top of HomePod mini 2 come to life in response to the music it’s playing. Per Apple:

With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.

Apple ecosystem features: Mac default speaker and Apple TV 4K surround sound

HomePod mini 2 includes two exclusive Apple ecosystem features not available on the original HomePod mini. One is for Mac users while the second involves the new Apple TV 4K.

Mac: HomePod mini 2 can be set as the default speaker for your Mac, either as a single speaker or a stereo pair. The original HomePod mini can only be used as a Mac speaker via AirPlay, so the connection isn’t as consistent and permanent.

Apple TV 4K: If you have the new fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, you can use a new HomePod surround sound feature for your TV. With surround sound, your Apple TV can use four HomePod mini 2 speakers for its audio output. You can also mix-and-match with the larger HomePod 2, for example with two HomePod 2 devices as front speakers and a HomePod mini 2 stereo pair as rear speakers.

Design updates: New colors and Siri animations

It goes without saying, but one key difference between HomePod mini 2 and the original model is the new lineup of colors.

HomePod mini 2: Blue, Green, Midnight, Pink, White

HomePod mini: Blue, Midnight, Orange, White, Yellow

Green and pink are the standout additions, but the new blue differs from the prior color too.

Additionally, HomePod mini 2 features a new design for animations on the top of the device. Essentially, Siri AI’s fresh color scheme replaces the old Siri appearance from the original HomePod mini.

Wireless connectivity upgrades

HomePod mini 2 comes with upgrades in both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth standards:

HomePod mini

Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax)

Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n)

Bluetooth 6

fullText:
Last year, Kuxiu was the first to make chargers that perfectly match the Cosmic Orange iPhone. They released their 3-in-1 X40 turbo and their S4 Solid State battery pack. They both matched the orange color so well that it seemed as if they were 1st-party accessories. This year, the new hero color for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup is burgundy, and Kuxiu is back at it again with a new matching burgundy D5 5-in-1 charging station. With its premium build quality, perfect color matching, built-in cooling, and price, this charger is everything you need from a performance and aesthetic standpoint.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video below!

Kuxiu D5 specs & features

I reviewed their original D5 a few months back, and it was one of my favorite chargers of the year. Now they have brought it all back with some awesome-looking accents and features. The Kuxiu D5 is advertised as a 5-in-1 charger because it charges three devices but also features a built-in cooling fan and a diagnostics display. You get:

Qi2.2 25W wireless charging

Retractable Apple Watch charging puck

AirPods charging mat

Built-in cooling fan that can be manually turned off and on

Smart color display to give us real-time charging stats

Includes 45W charging brick and braided cable in the packaging

While it is not as compact as something like their X40 Turbo, there is still some thought put into portability and travel with this charger. The Qi2.2 charger can fold down flat into a small cube you can take wherever you need, and the Apple Watch charger retracts into the charger as well. For me, it has worked best as a permanent desk charger, but it’s nice to know that it is also portable. 

My experience

As I mentioned, I have been using the original black color for a few months as my main desk charger. It is reliable, functional, and simple to use. So when Kuxiu announced their Burgundy version, I knew I had to check it out, especially since I was looking for some Burgundy color-matching accessories for my new iPhone 18 Pro. 

Since I knew this charger was already great, I wanted to see how closely the color matched the iPhone 18 Pro, and I was impressed by how identical it was. The aluminum parts of the D5 match the Burgundy on the iPhone 18 Pro, and they add other burgundy accents across the charger’s different materials. 

Beyond the aesthetics, my favorite part is the built-in cooling fan because it adds tangible value to the setup. I am someone who constantly installs new iOS betas, tests new features, and puts my phone through situations where it tends to get warm. So, having the active cooling system built directly into the charger has been game-changing in keeping my phone efficiently cooled and helping it sustain 25W charging for longer, since it does not get warm. The fan is also dead silent, but if you do want to turn it off, you can do so with one tap. Then, of course, you have the diagnostics display that shows you all the charging stats you need to see from all the active chargers. 

Pricing & availability

The Kuxiu D5 is available today on Kuxiu’s site in the original Space Grey and their new Burgundy color. You also get the required 45W charging brick and a braided USB-C cable. It is currently on sale for $59.99. 

Final take

For under $60, I challenge someone to find me a high-quality 3-in-1 charger that offers all the features above and includes all the charging accessories you need to use it at its best. That is why Kuxiu is one of the brands I recommend the most; it’s the performance-to-price ratio that sets them apart. So if you just picked up a new Burgundy iPhone or you are in the market for a new 3-in-1 charger, I highly recommend checking this one out. My only wish is that the next version has a USB-C port so you can charge a 4th device, like a smart ring or something. Otherwise, this thing is great.

I use iPhone Mirroring every day to quickly access my iPhone directly from my Mac, and it’s even better this year. iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate were released last month, bringing three key updates to iPhone Mirroring. Here’s everything new.

macOS 27: What’s new for iPhone Mirroring 

The biggest change for iPhone Mirroring in macOS 27 is the ability to resize the iPhone Mirroring window.

As my colleague Marcus reported last week, you can now adjust the size of the iPhone Mirroring window with any iOS 27-compatible apps. Right now, that means it only works for Apple’s native iPhone apps. However, once developers start rolling out iOS 27 updates later this year, support for resizing will expand rapidly.

Previously, iPhone Mirroring on macOS only support three preset sizes: smaller, actual size, and larger. The change in macOS 27 Golden Gate and iOS 27 clearly indicates Apple is prepping for the foldable iPhone Ultra, expected to launch later this year.

iPhone Mirroring in macOS 27 and iOS 27 also has several other updates:

Control Center access

DRM video support

Previously, iPhone Mirroring did not support accessing Control Center at all. In macOS 27, you can access it with the CMD+4 keyboard shortcut or with the “View” menu in your Mac’s menu bar.

DRM video support means you can watch protected videos using iPhone Mirroring on your Mac. Previously, all DRM-protected videos would simply show a black screen when iPhone Mirroring was enabled.

macOS 27 also has a new app icon for iPhone Mirroring, just like it does for many other stock Apple apps.

title: Apple planning huge iPhone Duo demo experiences at select retail stores: report
snippet: iPhone Duo is just about two weeks away from releasing, and according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has big retail plans ahead for its first foldable iPhone, to make sure every customer gets to see it to the fullest. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is just about two weeks away from releasing, and according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has big retail plans ahead for its first foldable iPhone, to make sure every customer gets to see it to the fullest.

Apple is gearing up for a major launch with the iPhone Duo, which should be no surprise. What is a surprise though, is the amount of attention Apple is putting into making sure this launch goes as smoothly as possible.

In the newsletter, Gurman reports that the company is planning to have over a hundred demo units at some of its biggest stores:

The company is preparing a major retail push, with a huge number of demo units at its flagship stores. The Fifth Avenue location in New York City is expected to have more than 150 units across hands-on demo stations and in-store fixtures. The Apple Park Visitor Center at the company’s home base, meanwhile, will have nearly 100. Other locations, including Michigan Avenue in Chicago, the Grove in Los Angeles and the Upper West Side in Manhattan, will each have roughly 30 to 40 units.

Some of its smaller stores will only have around 20 units, which still seems bigger than usual, given the fact that there are only two colors. Given how hard it’ll be to buy a Duo at launch, allowing a lot of hands-on demos at once seems sensible.

iPhone Duo demo fixtures

Beyond the number of demo units, the company has also designed a new MagSafe stand that can hold an unfolded iPhone Duo, alongside two “standard” iPhones (likely iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.) There’ll also be iPhone Duo demo units without a security tether “along the sides of stores,” so users can demo StandBy mode and other features.

Lastly, the company is planning a new fixture for some Apple Stores that showcase the iPhone Duo opening and closing, so it’s “impossible to miss” when you walk into an Apple Store.

All in all, iPhone Duo will become the forefront of Apple Stores after its launch on October 23rd. It’ll be hard to get, so if you’re interested in owning one – make sure you’re geared up to preorder it on October 16th.

title: Apple challenges Taction’s $5.7B patent verdict, says damages were based on ‘guesswork’
snippet: Apple is asking a federal judge to overturn a $5.7 billion verdict in a patent infringement lawsuit brought by Taction Technology over the Taptic Engine used in iPhones and Apple Watches. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is asking a federal judge to overturn a $5.7 billion verdict in a patent infringement lawsuit brought by Taction Technology over the Taptic Engine used in iPhones and Apple Watches. Here are the details.

’Impermissible guesswork on a massive scale’

A few weeks ago, a jury ordered Apple to pay $5.7 billion for infringing two patents held by Taction Technology, which are related to the Taptic Engine that currently powers haptic feedback across its devices.

At the time, Apple said it strongly disagreed with the jury’s verdict and the damages awarded, which it called “entirely unsupported by the facts.”

Apple stressed its technology was “fundamentally different” from what is covered by Taction’s two patents, and announced plans to appeal.

Today, Apple filed a new motion asking the court to overturn the jury’s verdict, arguing that Taction failed to present sufficient evidence to support any damages award, let alone $5.7 billion, which the company notes is “the largest patent verdict in history, by more than $3 billion.”

Apple adds that before the trial, the court excluded the analysis by Taction’s damages expert due to flaws in how the expert calculated royalties from a previous licensing agreement, and that the expert was later barred from testifying altogether.

Apple also notes that Taction never presented evidence establishing how much its patented technology was worth. Instead, it simply asked jurors to award whatever they considered a reasonable royalty, leaving them “with no choice but to engage in impermissible guesswork on a massive scale.”

From Apple’s motion:

Taction told the jury it was “just looking for a reasonable royalty for its contribution,” […], but never offered evidence of what that contribution was worth. Instead, it asked the jury to “award a reasonable royalty that y’all think is appropriate.” […] Taction failed to meet its burden to present evidence that would allow the jury to “adequately tie a dollar amount to the infringing acts,” […]. Without any such evidence, the jury was left to speculate, contrary to the Court’s instructions and binding Federal Circuit case law.

Apple also notes that, before the award was announced, the judge told attorneys he was “not sure that the figure that appears on the verdict form is what the jury meant to convey,” raising questions about whether the $5.7 billion figure was what the jury actually intended.

In a more striking accusation, Apple argues that one of Taction’s key technical experts, Dr. Oliver, relied on a “rigged” test to support his findings of patent infringement.

In essence, both Taction patents in question describe a technology designed to produce consistent vibrations across different frequencies. Apple argues that its Taptic Engine works differently, producing much stronger vibrations at certain frequencies than at others.

The company goes on to allege that Dr. Oliver developed a new testing method specifically for the lawsuit, which measured how Apple’s electronic control system could regulate the Taptic Engine’s vibrations, rather than whether the underlying hardware met the patents’ requirements.

From the filing:

No reasonable juror could find that “the output of the transducer is highly damped” in the accused products, as required by the Court’s construction. Rather than assess highly damped output by using the test in the patent, Taction’s infringement theory rested on a legally erroneous test rigged by Dr. Oliver for this case. The only evidence of the transducer’s actual output, including Taction’s pre-filing and infringement contentions testing, was introduced by Apple and those tests showed a peaked response that Dr. Oliver conceded was not highly damped.

Finally, Apple argues that if Taction’s interpretation of its patents is accepted, the patent claims at issue would themselves be invalid. According to the company, the testing method used to establish infringement contradicts the method described in the patents, making it impossible to clearly determine what the patents actually cover.

For these reasons, Apple is asking the court to overturn the jury’s verdict, rule that Taction is entitled to no damages, and find that Apple did not infringe the (possibly invalid) patents. Alternatively, the company is requesting a new trial covering infringement, patent validity, and damages.

With Apple’s motion now filed, and the jury’s verdict not yet formally entered as a final judgment, the court will now consider whether to uphold the $5.7 billion award, overturn the verdict, or order a new trial.

What’s your take on Apple’s arguments? Let us know in the comments.

title: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
snippet: The former Steelers coach built the sprawling city brick by brick with a video game console controller.
fullText:
Football coaches have the freedom to create their own worlds on the playing field. But retired Steelers legend Mike Tomlin took a different route — manifesting his vision block by block within a massive Minecraft city. What started as a shared family project with his children evolved into a solitary, 12-year labor of love. Now, the sheer depth of Tomlin’s digital city is capturing widespread attention online.

Tomlin served as the Steelers’ head coach for 19 seasons before resigning in January, having never finished with a losing record. 

His video was released Oct. 1 and received more than 3 million views in less than two weeks. In the video, Tomlin shows off an expansive Minecraft city, complete with sports stadiums, high-rise apartments, homes and other buildings. He began working on the city about 12 years ago after watching his kids and their friends play Minecraft when they were in middle school, building it in the game’s creative mode with their help.

			

More from CNET

“I was mesmerized by what could occupy their attention for such large periods of time,” Tomlin says in the video. “I’m certainly not skilled enough in video game play or have the stick control to [play the game’s survival mode], so I got interested in this creative mode. I like to build, I’ve always had an interest in architecture, and so I started doing this creative city as a means to spend time with them.”

His kids eventually outgrew the game and moved on to different ones, high school and eventually college. That left Tomlin to work on the city by himself, which he did off and on for years while still coaching the Steelers.

“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me, some mindless entertainment,” Tomlin says. “I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and pressures of life.”

Tomlin spends the rest of the video showing viewers around the place, focusing on his basic, early-days architecture, penthouses, apartments and how he tried to design a solid urban space. He plans to release more videos to discuss different buildings, the city’s design and other elements of his sprawling city. 

How wonderfully weird

Tomlin says he wanted to build his city around this lake, and the nearby high-rise apartments have balconies overlooking the water, giving it an upscale vibe.Mike Tomlin

Leading up to the video’s release, there was no indication whatsoever that Mike Tomlin played computer games. That helped make his big Minecraft debut all the more delightful. The 54-year-old coach showed off thousands of hours of playtime in a 19-minute video, and no one could believe it. 

“12 years of Minecraft? Didn’t you know this? Did nobody know this?” asked a shocked Ty Schmidt, producer and on-air personality of the Pat McAfee show,  on an episode of the show. 

The sports world finally saw what some Minecraft fans already knew: Tomlin’s dedication to the game is unmatched.

“We’re talking block by block,” McAfee said. “He had 14 30-story buildings around a body of water that he wanted to build his city around — one block at a time! They all got patios! He had a penthouse with a shark aquarium. It was unbelievable.”

Minecraft fans, too, showed up to explore the coach’s dazzling feat. Many were surprised to learn that he built this on the Bedrock edition of the game using a video game console, beginning with PlayStation 3 before moving on to PlayStation 4 and 5. That means Tomlin didn’t have access to the mods that many builders use in the Java version of the game on PC, or the freedom that a mouse and keyboard provide. He built his city one brick at a time on a PlayStation controller. 

Tomlin was initially unaware of his viral fame. In an interview on Late Night with Seth Meyers, Tomlin said he was at a gala with his phone off when the video went live, and it wasn’t until later that his kids told him about the massive response. Tomlin had caught up by the time he appeared on Football Night in America with NBC on Sunday night. 

“I’m appreciating all of this, to be quite honest with you,” Tomlin said during the broadcast. 

How good are Tomlin’s designs?

Tomlin shows off his high-rise apartment building, where each apartment has a balcony with a gorgeous view. These were built in the early days of the server, so they’re constructed with the game’s older building materials.Mike Tomlin

The spectacle of Tomlin’s Minecraft city is one of those wholesome events that had viewers smiling all weekend, except a few Steelers fans who were probably already pretty mad about losing to the Cleveland Browns less than 24 hours after the video was released. That didn’t stop a lot of people from wondering whether Tomlin’s city is actually as good as it looks. It turns out that most of the Internet agrees that it lives up to the hype.

“From my understanding, [it’s a] phenomenal Minecraft city,” McAfee said. “Like, as I was watching it, I was like, man, the attention to detail [is outstanding].”

Noted Minecraft city builder Alpine1 was one of the first to create his own video on the topic, and he was impressed. He had some suggestions for Tomlin, recommending that the coach consider using glass panes instead of glass blocks and more sophisticated floor designs, such as installing tile floors in showers. But Alpine1 did note that Tomlin likely started building the city before many modern building tools were available to Minecraft players. 

“This is really awesome to see,” Alpine1 said in the video. “I’ve been advocating for people to build Minecraft cities for years because there’s so much you can do… and I think Mike has really captured this.”

Zach Nagel, an architecture student from the University of Cincinnati’s School of Architecture and Interior Design, also took a stab at analyzing Tomlin’s city in a separate video. He noted that Tomlin used some concepts that are actually practiced in architecture, specifically adding a penthouse with an aquarium right across the street from a full-sized aquarium. 

“Now, what Coach Tomlin is talking about here, having a central theme to the building, is a term that we use in architecture as well, the parti,” Nagel says. “If you talk to 20 architects and ask them to give a definition of a parti, you might get 20 pretty different answers. At its [simplest], a parti is a single idea or scheme that drives all of the decisions you make in a building.”

Nagel goes on to praise Tomlin for not only considering the building’s exterior appearance but also its interior design and the functional needs of the city’s fictional residents. He says that a lot of Tomlin’s design choices and approach are in line with what some architects use. 

“In another world, he could’ve totally gone down this career path had he wanted to,” Nagel says. “And I’m glad to see that Minecraft remains such an accessible tool for those who want to shape the environment around them.”

fullText:
OxygenOS, the flavor of Android for OnePlus devices, is officially going away as the brand steps out of the global market, with Oppo’s ColorOS taking over starting with Android 17. And, now, we have an official list of OnePlus devices getting Android 17 starting later this month.

To quickly summarize, OnePlus shut down its global operations in July, but confirmed software support will remain for existing devices through their promised lifespans. But that wouldn’t be on OxygenOS, with supported devices instead moving to Oppo’s ColorOS starting with Android 17.

OnePlus will continue software updates, all devices move to ColorOS with Android 17

In all reality, differences between OxygenOS and ColorOS are hard to find as Oppo’s software styling took over OnePlus’ experience years ago. 

The transition is officially underway later this month, though. 

	

OnePlus has confirmed the move with a schedule detailing when to expect ColorOS and Android 17 to land on various OnePlus devices. It starts on October 29 with the OnePlus 15 and OnePlus Pad 4, continuing to the OnePlus 15R and OnePlus 13 series the following day. title: Where Google Wallet state IDs are available on Android
snippet: States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android. more…
fullText:
States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android.

Update 10/10

How to add your state ID on Android

Open the Google Wallet app on Android 9+

Tap the “plus” button next to “View more” at the bottom

Choose “ID & personal info” and then “Driver’s license or state ID” 

Select your state and follow the instructions

The process involves taking a picture of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of yourself for verification: a “photo from this video will be submitted to your ID issuer.” 

Once approved, the ID will appear below the carousel of payment methods alongside other passes. The order can be rearranged, while you can remotely remove the ID online if your phone is missing: myaccount.google.com > Personal Info > Manage IDs.

	

Related: Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android

What Google Wallet state IDs are supported

Arizona (Rolled out October 2023)

Arkansas (Rolled out October 2025)

California (Rolled out August 2024)

Colorado (Rolled out October 2023)

Georgia (Rolled out October 2023)

Iowa (Rolled out June 2025)

Maryland (Rolled out December 2022)

Montana (Rolled out August 2025)

New Mexico (Rolled out December 2024)

North Dakota (Rolled out October 2025)

Ohio (Rolled out September 2026)

[New] Oklahoma (Rolled out October 2026)

Puerto Rico (Rolled out October 2025)

Where state IDs are coming next

Google previously said to expect support in the following places:

West Virginia (Upcoming availability announced April 2025)

Where you can use state IDs

The primary place you can use this digital ID is at TSA checkpoints in some US airports. There are two ways to do so, starting with tapping your phone at the NFC terminal. You then review the information that will be shared with the TSA and authenticate with device unlock. There’s also a QR code method that requires opening the ID in Google Wallet. 

Officially, you still have to carry the physical ID card at all times.

Some apps, like from car rental services, are beginning to accept digital IDs for identity and age verification. On mobile, if an app or website requests your age, it’s as simple as confirming (and authenticating) that you want to share this information with a system-level prompt/sheet. On desktop web, the experience involves scanning a QR code. 

Google wants to make it possible to do that “without any possibility to link back to a user’s personal identity” through what it calls Zero-Knowledge Proof. This technology will be open-sourced for anyone to use. 

Looking ahead, the IDs can be used at DMVs in Arizona, Georgia, Maryland, and New Mexico as part of “improved and streamlined customer experiences.”

	

Google is also working on letting you use digital IDs to “recover Amazon accounts, access online health services with CVS and MyChart by Epic, verify profiles on platforms like Uber and more.”

Using passport as REAL ID

Google in April pointed out how you can “use your ID pass created from a U.S. passport with TSA security for domestic travel at supported airports, even if you do not have a REAL ID driver’s license or state-issued ID.” This comes ahead of the May 7, 2025 deadline. 

To do so, open Google Wallet > Add to Wallet > ID pass. This three-step process involves taking a picture of your passport’s info page, and then scanning the security chip found inside the back cover of your passport. You also have to record a video of your face that Google will review “to make sure you’re a real person, and compare the video to your passport photo to make sure you’re the owner of the passport.”

The NFC and QR code instructions for using this digital passport ID are unchanged from above. You also have to keep the physical version on you when traveling. As a reminder, this won’t work internationally.

title: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablet finally gives the iPad lineup some much needed competition
snippet: This week, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of Alexa Tablets. They no longer run a proprietary OS with a custom App Store, and instead embrace Android with a stock feel – while offering the Play Store. It’s a big shift in direction for Amazon. The tablets also look quite beautiful, while previous Fire tablets have felt cheap. I think these have the opportunity to do quite well. more…
fullText:
This week, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of Alexa Tablets. They no longer run a proprietary OS with a custom App Store, and instead embrace Android with a stock feel – while offering the Play Store. It’s a big shift in direction for Amazon. The tablets also look quite beautiful, while previous Fire tablets have felt cheap. I think these have the opportunity to do quite well.

First and foremost, I want to make it quite clear that I’m not saying the iPad is doomed or anything remotely close to that. However, I do think the Alexa Tablet serves as a real form of iPad competition, which the iPad has generally lacked.

New Alexa tablets serve as strong competition

Amazon is putting a lot of care into these tablets that other Android manufacturers haven’t, and while these tablets come in at lower price points – they certainly punch above their weight class.

There are three Alexa Tablets to start off the lineup: an 8.7” model at $229, an 11” model at $329, and a 12” Pro model at $499. To me, the one in the middle is the most interesting.

It offers 8GB of RAM, a 90Hz display, a thin design, and a similarly sharp display. That compares to the budget iPad, which comes in $120 higher with less RAM, a lesser display, and a thicker design. Granted, the iPad has the A16 chip, which probably feels much faster than the MediaTek chip powering it. The iPad also starts at 128GB, compared to the 64GB on the Alexa Tablet. Once you upgrade the Alexa Tablet to 128GB, there’s only a $70 difference.

Hardware wise, the Alexa Tablets seem pretty competent. Obviously, Android on tablets isn’t going to be quite perfect, but given its tie in with Alexa and the fact that the tablet is priced quite well, I could see a lot of people wanting to buy these, even if they potentially would’ve considered iPads. Of course, one strong suit from Amazon is the Kindle experience, and these Alexa Tablets offer a reader mode that cuts blue light.

Wrap up

Only time will tell, but Amazon might make a pretty big dent into the tablet market with its new entries. Even the 12” Pro at $499 seems like a really worthwhile product. At the very least, I hope some strong competition means Apple will be less complacent with its iPad upgrades. For example, the iPad Air has largely only received chip upgrades since its last redesign in 2020.

	

I’m personally excited to try one of these out and truly put it to the test. Right now, Amazon also offers 20% off with any trade-in, making it an even better deal.

What do you think of these new Alexa Tablets? Would you consider getting one of these for a friend or family member during the holiday season? Sound off in the comments.

title: Gemini ‘Task’ redesign integrates Spark into the main chat app
snippet: In addition to revamping settings and the navigation drawer, Google is combining its Spark personal agent with the main Gemini chat experience. more…
fullText:
In addition to revamping settings and the navigation drawer, Google is combining its Spark personal agent with the main Gemini chat experience.

This redesign adds buttons for “Chat” and “Task” just above the prompt box. “Task” is Gemini Spark, with Google explaining that there’s now a “new home for Spark: Start new tasks anytime and keep track of them in your chats.”

Old vs. new

As part of this change, “Spark” disappears from the navigation drawer, while a new “Scheduled” page is introduced. This surfaces Spark tasks and Scheduled actions, with the feed organized by Active, Paused, Completed, and Suggested. 

	

Meanwhile, the list of conversations at the bottom is no longer called Recents. All chats and Spark tasks are combined into one history. The new filter icon lets you sort by All, Ready, Needs attention, and In progress.

Google appears to be deemphasizing the “Spark” branding with this redesign. Another example is how “Gemini Spark Settings” in the account menu has been renamed to just “Task settings.” 

This change is rolling out via a server-side update on Android. We’re not seeing it just yet on iOS or the web. Gemini Spark requires an AI Pro or AI Ultra subscription.

Announced at I/O 2026 in May, Gemini’s 24/7 personal agent is now better integrated into the overall app with this update. It’s much quicker to start a task with the experience no longer siloed off.

title: You can now join a WhatsApp call without an account
snippet: WhatsApp is making it easier to makes calls with everyone by introducing the ability for non-WhatsApp users to join a call without needing an account. more…
fullText:
WhatsApp is making it easier to makes calls with everyone by introducing the ability for non-WhatsApp users to join a call without needing an account.

Detailed in a blog post today, WhatsApp no longer requires an account for you to join a call. This works by sharing a link with another user who can then join that call through the web, and it works with calls of all sizes, whether that’s one-on-one or up to 32 people.

Calls with users invited via link remain end-to-end encrypted and all users retain the same core features such as the ability to raise their hand, share their screen, and more. And WhatsApp calls remain free with no time limits.

WhatsApp says:

	

To get started, navigate to the Calls tab in WhatsApp, select the “+” icon, create a call link, and send it to the people you want to talk to – colleagues, classmates, or tutor – without having to worry about what apps they have. Guests can open the link in their computer browser, type in their name, and join 1:1 and group calls with up to 32 people once admitted by the host. Only people with a WhatsApp account can create a call link.

title: HomeView will support video apps like YouTube, Netflix—if they say yes
snippet: Apple unveiled its new HomeView product yesterday (pre-order here), but the device’s support for third-party apps was initially unclear. A newly published Apple document, however, offers good news about HomeView supporting third-party video apps like YouTube and Netflix. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled its new HomeView product yesterday (pre-order here), but the device’s support for third-party apps was initially unclear. A newly published Apple document, however, offers good news about HomeView supporting third-party video apps like YouTube and Netflix.

Apple says third-party video apps will be available on HomeView if they also support CarPlay

Yesterday when Apple announced the HomeView, it said surprisingly little about third-party apps.

HomeView doesn’t have an App Store, so you won’t be able to download third-party apps like on iPhone. However, support for some audio and video apps was vaguely confirmed by Apple.

Today we’ve learned new details, including as relates to which video apps will be compatible. In a newly updated CarPlay Developer Guide, Apple says:

CarPlay audio and video apps also work on Apple HomeView without requiring you to make any modifications to your app. […]

Apps with CarPlay audio app (CarPlay framework) or CarPlay video app entitlements appear on Apple HomeView.

Video apps for CarPlay were newly introduced this year in iOS 27. But they require automakers to explicitly support CarPlay’s video feature—which most don’t. As a result, developers have had little reason to make their video apps compatible with CarPlay.

But HomeView will change that in a big way.

Now major players like YouTube, Netflix, and Disney+ will be able to make their apps appear on HomeView simply by adding CarPlay support.

	

HomeView now provides these developers a great reason to invest in making CarPlay-compatible apps. And that investment will benefit not only HomeView owners, but CarPlay users too.

I might be overly optimistic, but I suspect major video apps will be eager to support Apple’s new HomeView product as soon as possible. Perhaps we’ll even see several of them available before the November 13 launch.

You can pre-order HomeView starting at $289 for select models.

Typically, Apple’s fall updates for IT are around better way to manage devices, etc. This year, there was an underrated update that I think will be a real win in certain situations: remote AppleCare log collection.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

If you’ve ever opened an AppleCare support case for a hard-to-reproduce issue in your Apple fleet, you know how hard this process is. AppleCare needed a sysdiagnose and getting one meant either physically having the device or walking a user through a series of steps they’ve never done before. That process worked eventually, but it was slow, required the user to be available and willing to help, and, for remote employees or traveling executives, made it appear that IT didn’t have sufficient visibility into the logs of what was happening on the devices. The issue is that they somewhat didn’t.

The harder the issue was to reproduce, the more frustrating this was for IT. By the time you got the logs, the device had rebooted, the macOS state had changed, and you were starting over with your troubleshooting.

TriggerEnhancedLogCollection is your friend

Apple introduced two new device management commands in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS 27: TriggerEnhancedLogCollection and a cancel command. The process is straightforward. You open an AppleCare case, AppleCare provides you a token, and you pass that token through your device management when you trigger the command. The device collects the logs and uploads them directly to Apple, where they are automatically attached to the ticket with Apple.

The device also reports its status through declarative management at all times, so you can see whether log collection has started, whether it’s finished, whether it’s waiting on user consent, and if the upload is in progress. 

Interactive vs non-interactive

There are two modes for this command, and the difference matters depending on what you’re managing. On iOS, non-interactive mode is available when the device has no passcode and no accounts, so it collects and uploads logs in the background without user involvement. I think this would be applicable in kiosk/POS type settings. On tvOS and Shared iPads, non-interactive is always available.

On macOS, interactive mode is required. The user sees a notification and is prompted to consent to both the log collection and the upload. They can decline, but this is still dramatically better than the old process, but it’s not completely hands-off. The user is in the loop., but at least it’s a simple UI box..

Wrap up

Remote and hybrid work make manual log collection harder and a remote user in a different city experiencing intermittent macOS issues is one of the more challenging support scenarios an IT team can face. With this feature, the moment that Apple’s team asks for logs, you can send the command from your device management console, the device does the work, and Apple has the info it needs to work the case.

title: TrendForce warns of higher notebook prices and weaker demand in 2027
snippet: TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments could decline by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising component costs. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments could decline by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising component costs. Here are the details.

’Brands [to] face difficult trade-offs’

In a report released this week, TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments will decline in 2027, with the drop ranging from low- to high-single digits, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising costs.

TrendForce says the impact will depend on how much of the rising component costs manufacturers pass on to consumers through higher retail prices, rather than absorbing them at the expense of their profit margins.

From the report:

TrendForce’s latest notebook industry research reveals that the primary risk facing the market in 2027 is expected to shift from supply constraints to the impact of rising costs on demand. Global notebook shipments are currently projected to decline by a low-single-digit percentage in 2027.

However, if DRAM and CPU prices remain elevated, brands may be forced to pass more of these costs on to consumers. These higher retail prices could further extend replacement cycles, potentially pushing the full-year shipment decline into the high-single-digit range.

TrendForce says that notebook shipments in 2026 were supported by factors such as improved CPU availability, early purchasing by manufacturers, and replacement demand brought forward from later periods.

With some purchases originally expected in the second half of 2026 and beyond already brought forward, replacement momentum in subsequent periods is likely to weaken. Furthermore, as lower-cost inventories are gradually depleted, brands will face more direct pressure from rising CPU, DRAM, and SSD prices.

The report notes that 68% of the bill of materials for an unnamed “mainstream notebook with a manufacturer’s suggested retail price of US$900” was made up of CPU, DRAM, and SSD costs in the third quarter of 2026.

	

It adds that next year, if component costs keep rising, brands will likely have to choose between raising retail prices and risking weaker demand, absorbing the increases at the expense of gross margins, or reducing specifications, potentially making their products less competitive.

TrendForce says that DRAM supply is “likely to stay tight” next year thanks to AI-related demand, “while PC DRAM faces the risk of limited supply growth.” On the flip side, it expects NAND Flash supply constraints to “ease in the second half of 2027 with new capacity coming online. “

In 2027, brands are therefore unlikely to be able to maintain pricing, specifications, and profitability simultaneously. The extent to which they pass higher costs on to consumers will be a key factor shaping demand.

Finally, the report notes that if tariff pressures don’t increase further, manufacturers could move some notebook production back to China to reduce costs. TrendForce estimates that China’s share of global notebook production will rise from 76% in 2025 to 79% in 2026, potentially exceeding 80% in 2027.

title: iPhone Duo buyers to get a special surprise at U.S. Apple Stores, report says
snippet: According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, iPhone Duo buyers who purchase their device at an Apple Store in the US will be treated to a nice little surprise when they turn it on for the first time. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, iPhone Duo buyers who purchase their device at an Apple Store in the US will be treated to a nice little surprise when they turn it on for the first time. Here are the details.

Cool surprise in store for in-store buyers

When Apple launches the iPhone Duo on October 23, some customers who purchase the device at an Apple Store in the US will be able to have its initial setup screen personalized with their name.

According to Gurman, “Apple retail stores will have a system to customize the boot of the device,” allowing the iPhone Duo to display a greeting containing their name when it turns on for the first time. Gurman says the feature will be exclusive to the iPhone Duo, and support both English and Spanish.

Fun little touch for the iPhone Duo launch: Apple retail stores will have a system to customize the boot of the device with the buyer's name so it says "Hello, Mark" (for example) when it turns on for the first time. (US only, Duo only, English and Spanish).

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 9, 2026

It is not clear how Apple will implement the feature, or whether it will rely on Presto, the system Apple Stores already use to wirelessly update iPhones without removing them from their boxes.

	

First reported by Gurman in 2023, Presto allows Apple retail employees to turn on an iPhone, install software updates, and turn it off again, all while the device remains sealed in its packaging.

Back to the iPhone Duo, it will be available to pre-order starting Friday, October 16, with deliveries and in-store availability beginning October 23.

Apple recently announced that customers will be able to get ready for iPhone Duo pre-orders beginning October 12, and you can read more about that here.

title: Next-gen Google TV Streamer in the works with microphones, presence sensing, & new remote
snippet: 9to5Google can report that development on a next-generation Google TV Streamer is underway. more…
fullText:
9to5Google can report that development on a next-generation Google TV Streamer is underway. 

According to a source familiar with the matter, the new Google TV device retains the same general design. The width is narrower for a slightly more compact footprint. 

The big upgrade is the presence of microphones on the Google TV Streamer itself. There are cutouts on the slanted, pill-shaped surface that will listen for “Hey Google” commands. 

	

Another new hardware feature is presence sensing. Last year, TCL launched the first Google TV with that capability to turn on the Google Photos screensaver when someone enters the room. If you get close, the display shows ambient information like the time and weather.

	

Meanwhile, the new Google TV Streamer will be powered by a faster processor and offer more storage than the current model’s 32GB.

Google is also updating the included remote. The design is largely the same but with two more shortcuts joining the existing buttons for YouTube and Netflix. Additionally, the Find My Remote button remains on the back of the streaming device. 

We don’t have any information on when this next Google TV Streamer is launching. There was a four-year gap between the Chromecast with Google TV 4K and the Google TV Streamer, with the lower-end HD dongle coming in between the two. This refresh comes as Google raised the price of the existing unit by $50 in August.

title: Googlebook’s app situation is a mess, and not just because things are missing
snippet: Having been using a Googlebook for the better part of a week, there are any number of headaches I could talk about, but easily the biggest problem I’m running into thus far is the app situation. Frankly, it’s a mess. more…
fullText:
Having been using a Googlebook for the better part of a week, there are any number of headaches I could talk about, but easily the biggest problem I’m running into thus far is the app situation. Frankly, it’s a mess.

Googlebook, like Chromebook, was never going to be in a “good” place for apps. The Android-based platform sets up a more capable foundation for the future but, without a major push from Google and partners, it was always going to result in a rough start. 

And, yeah, it’s a rough start.

The “main” issue is around desktop-class apps and programs. Staples like the Adobe suite are simply not here, and there’s no easy way to replace them. Not to mention the depth of niche apps that have been built out in the Windows and macOS over the decades. At launch, Googlebook was never going to compete with that, though I’d argue that stripping away the Linux support ChromeOS did have isn’t exactly helping matters.

	

The problem I’m finding much more frustrating is around the apps Googlebook can access, and the messy situation around that.

The Google Play Store is your main way to obtain apps on Googlebook. Android apps are the preferred method and, in time, I’m sure that’ll work better than it does today. But, at the moment, Google’s stopgap to varying levels of quality for Android apps on desktop was to give five quality labels to any given app. 

Built for mobile: Hasn’t been tested for desktop

Better on the website: The web app/browser version has full features and/or better performance

Compatible with Desktop: Works with mouse/keyboard controls

Optimized for Desktop: “Adapted for a comfortable desktop experience”

Made for Desktop: “Built for desktop with specialized features and controls”

These are all applied by Google — developers have no direct control.

In my book, that’s wildly confusing for the end user, especially as the Play Store doesn’t link out to where you can use the web app for the Android apps it tries to steer you away from.

And it sadly should steer you away from some apps. 

Telegram is a great example of my frustration. The Android app is “better on the website,” and that’s incredibly true. The Android app is broken on Googlebook in a lot of ways, but the most frustrating is that the enter key doesn’t send a message. But, on the flip side, the web app isn’t that much better, as I’ve frequently run into cases where it misbehaves or even crashes. 

Slack continues to be a daily source of frustration, with the Android app being truly a terrible experience on anything other than a phone, and the web app unable to be installed. This is not some niche or trivial app, it’s something that millions rely on for daily work on their laptops. 

Spotify says that it is “Optimized for desktop” and, while it’s not bad, the phone UI doesn’t even scale as well here as it does on a foldable. It gets better when the “Now Playing” panel is expanded out, but it’s still not on par with other desktop platforms. “Optimized” just feels like the wrong word for this label. “Compatible” feels more apt for this particular example, but Google’s categories are way too specific to let that work.

“Optimized for desktop” according to who, exactly?

	

There’s no easy solution here.

Googlebook is in its early days and, while the foundation presents a better future, the “now” is a huge headache, and one I struggle to get on board with because, well why would you subject yourself to this? Good Windows laptops are easy to find. The MacBook Air is easy to find for $1,099 (cheaper than most Googlebooks!). Good, established platforms that simply don’t have these shortcomings. Why would I give that up for some Android integrations that don’t even work with my phone yet?

Sound off in the comments, I’d love to hear what you think about this problem and how it impacts your view of Googlebook.
