title: Chrome 155 for Googlebook brings expanded web app installs, integration
snippet: With Chrome 155, Googlebooks now better support web apps by allowing for expanded installation and system integration. more…
fullText:
With Chrome 155, Googlebooks now better support web apps by allowing for expanded installation and system integration.

Previously, Chrome on Googlebooks (which is the Android version with desktop-level features) “only enabled the Install option for websites specifically configured as web apps.” As seen above, pages “without an installable web manifest” just opened as a browser tab.

Google reiterates today how that was a “conscious design choice,” but it heard the community feedback.

Chrome 155 this week lets you “manually install any webpage as an app directly from the Chrome browser so that it works as an app in its own window.” To do so:

	

On your Googlebook, open Chrome.

Go to a website you want to install.

At the top right, open the Chrome menu > Save and share > Install and create shortcut…

On some websites, at the top right of the address bar, select Install.

Select Install.

To complete the web app installation, follow the on-screen instructions.

	

Additionally, Google says: “If you previously created a browser-tab shortcut for a website prior to this update, remove the old shortcut first and re-install the page using the steps above.”

Meanwhile, installed web apps that appear in the app launcher can now be “pinned to your taskbar or homescreen and run in Chrome.” They will benefit from “shared Google Account login, cookies, site permissions, and installed browser extensions.”

With this release, Chrome Settings is no longer a fullscreen interface, which has been the case on mobile but not desktop platforms. As a separate tab, “you can more easily reference a web page while tweaking settings.”

Version 155.0.8059.79 of Chrome is rolling out via the Play Store on Googlebooks. We’re seeing it on all our devices.

title: PSA: Wall-mounted HomeView may not work if you buy the wrong power adapter
snippet: Earlier today, Apple confirmed that the wall-mounted HomeView does not come with a power adapter in the box. Now, the company has published a support document detailing the device’s power requirements, including what to look for when purchasing a compatible adapter. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Earlier today, Apple confirmed that the wall-mounted HomeView does not come with a power adapter in the box.

Now, the company has published a support document detailing the device’s power requirements, including what to look for when purchasing a compatible adapter. Here are the details.

Important information for HomeView (Wall Mounted) buyers

If you’re buying the wall-mounted version of the new Apple HomeView, Apple has published a new support article with some important information.

As the company announced earlier today, the HomeView (Wall Mounted) model does not include a mount, nor does it come with a power adapter in the box.

This means that users will need to buy those separately. As my colleague Ryan explained earlier today, “Apple is selling two different mount options that start at $59, and it says a third is coming in early 2027.”

As for the power adapter, Apple explains in a new support article that the wall-mounted HomeView requires a USB-C power adapter rated for at least 20W, with support for 9V at 2.22A or higher. If those requirements aren’t met, the device may display a “Not Enough Power” warning.

	

Alternatively, depending on the third-party mount, the wall-mounted HomeView can be connected directly to a home’s electrical wiring without a separate USB-C power adapter.

Here’s Apple:

HomeView ships with a power cable and adapter. HomeView (Wall Mounted) requires a compatible third-party mount and power solution for operation, sold separately. Depending on the mount, you can use a separate power cable and adapter or connect to line power (hardwired).

HomeView: Use a USB-C cable and a USB-C power adapter that’s at least 30W and supports 15V at 2A or higher.

HomeView (Wall Mounted): Use a USB-C cable and a USB-C power adapter (both sold separately) that’s at least 20W and supports 9V at 2.22A or higher.

Apple also links to a compatible power adapter for HomeView or HomeView (Wall Mounted), and details the troubleshooting process for a HomeView showing a “Not Enough Power” message.

title: Android Auto 18.0 update starts rolling out, continues to gear up for redesign
snippet: Announced earlier this year, Google continues to set the stage for its next Android Auto redesign behind the scenes, which might be codenamed “Cielo.” more…
fullText:
Announced earlier this year, Google continues to set the stage for its next Android Auto redesign behind the scenes, which might be codenamed “Cielo.”

About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.

Google is now starting its rollout – in beta – of Android Auto 18.0. While that sounds like some milestone, the update itself is just as underwhelming as most Android Auto app updates have been. No new user-facing features we’ve spotted, and likely just some assorted bug fixes throughout. 

In a teardown, “cielo_launcher” did appear as a new asset, which might be the best indication we’ve seen that this is the codename for Google’s next Android Auto redesign. This codename has been appearing for months in Android Auto’s flags – the folks over at Android Sage mention v15.9, but we’ve seen references as far back as v15.7 in November 2025 –  but “launcher” points pretty directly at this being the replacement for “Coolwalk,” which was the codename of Android Auto’s dashboard redesign back in 2023. “Coolwalk_launcher” showed up in Android Auto’s code years ago as the dashboard was being build out.

	
	

Prior Android Auto updates mentioning “cielo” also mentioned screen layouts, which might tie into how Android Auto’s new design is set to cover more of the display and support widgets. 

Android Auto is getting a redesign that takes up your whole display, adds widget support, more

“Coolwalk” didn’t have a direct meaning, but “Cielo” is a real word in Italian and Spanish meaning “sky.” It’s unclear if that has any meaning, though.

As far as Android Auto 18.0 goes, this update is purely just building on the redesign, as there’s nothing (at least that we’ve found) that actually implies it’s imminent. Notably, there’s also the use of “Coolwalk” in the flags here too around the light/dark theme that Google has been building out for what feels like an eternity at this point, but nothing particularly suggestive of when that feature might actually debut – it’s still not live in this update.

title: OpenAI alleges ex-employee took ‘highly confidential’ device files to Apple
snippet: In a new filing today, OpenAI claims that a former employee who departed for Apple sent “over a hundred highly confidential files about at least one unreleased OpenAI device under development to his personal accounts.” Apple, however, told Reuters that it hasn’t found any evidence to support these allegations. more…
fullText:
In a new filing today, OpenAI claims that a former employee who departed for Apple sent “over a hundred highly confidential files about at least one unreleased OpenAI device under development to his personal accounts.”

Apple, however, told Reuters that it hasn’t found any evidence to support these allegations. 

This is the latest development in the ongoing trade secrets lawsuit between Apple and OpenAI. Apple filed the lawsuit in July, accusing former employees of stealing trade secrets to benefit OpenAI. In August, Apple revealed what it called “shocking evidence” based on an early forensic analysis of a laptop used by a former engineer who left for OpenAI.

In today’s filing, OpenAI says:

Based on a recent and ongoing forensic investigation arising from this lawsuit, OpenAI has learned that a former OpenAI employee (who joined OpenAI from Apple, worked for OpenAI for six months, and has now returned to Apple) , sent over a hundred highly confidential files about at least one unreleased OpenAI device under development to his personal accounts. The files at issue include detailed images of the unreleased device(s), as well as highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s). The files also include supplier information and project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports regarding coating and sealing of hardware components.

OpenAI goes on to allege that the files were sent on June 2, 2026, which was the employee’s final day at the company. The employee also allegedly “made a presentation about OpenAI’s plans to Apple’s senior leadership, including Apple’s vice president of operations in Asia.”

“ That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products,” OpenAI writes.

OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work. OpenAI has raised these issues directly with Apple, but to date, Apple has not provided OpenAI with the requested assurances that Apple is not in possession of, and has not used, OpenAI’s trade secret and confidential information.

Apple, however, says that it hasn’t found any evidence to support OpenAI’s claims. As reported by Reuters, Apple has “policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use ​confidential information from ​previous employers.”

title: I Put the Oppo Find X10 Pro’s Camera to the Test. These Are the Results
snippet: I’ve used Oppo’s Find X10 and these are my favorite example photos.
fullText:
Oppo’s latest flagship Android phone, the Find X10 Pro is set to be unveiled in the coming weeks, but Oppo kindly sent me a unit ahead of time to let me take its cameras for a spin. So I did. I’ve been on multiple walks around my home in sunny Edinburgh and have taken a variety of snaps with the phone’s multiple rear cameras.

The fun part here is that while I can show you the photos — and you can see the phone in my hand above — I’m not yet allowed to talk about any specs, including the resolution of the cameras or what technology is powering them. So instead, I’m presenting these photos just as they are, almost as a little teaser ahead of the phone’s full unveiling later in the month. I’ll have a full review ready then, along with all the information about the cameras and some comparisons against other top Android camera phones like the Leica Leitzphone.

But all of that’s to come. For now, enjoy some of my early test images taken with the X10 Pro, along with as much information as my non-disclosure agreement allows me to share. Keep in mind that all photos have been imported into Adobe Lightroom in order to be easily assessed and resized for publishing online. No other edits, including sharpening, have been applied unless otherwise stated.

			

More from CNET

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Taken with the main camera, this image is sharp, packed with detail and has natural colors. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the ultrawide camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

 I don’t think I’m breaking any rules in telling you that the phone has an ultrawide camera, so here’s a photo I took with it. It looks a little more drab than the one from the main camera, but it’s still got plenty of detail.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are various color filters, which I almost certainly can’t tell you about here, but you probably assumed it had them anyway, right? Right?! Anyway, I used one of them (I won’t say which) to take this shot, and I like the filmic vibes it’s produced.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I used a different, unnamed, color filter here and I like the punchy tones, especially from that flash of red at the bottom of the ship. 

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While this color filter is much more subtle, it gives a bold blue that contrasts nicely with the building’s orange.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot in XPan mode.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The last two generations of Oppo phones (including the superb Find X9 Ultra) had Hasselblad’s XPan mode, so I can’t imagine it’s a secret that the new one does too. This mode allows you to shoot with a wide, narrow crop that’s reminiscent of Hasselblad’s legendary XPan panoramic film camera. Those cameras are rare and expensive, so this is the closest you’ll probably get to an authentic XPan experience. I love this wide, cinematic aspect ratio.

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While I love the vibrancy of this image — and the sense of the warm evening glow — I do think the camera’s image processing has gone a bit hard with the “HDR” here, creating a less realistic-looking shot.

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

That over-processing is especially noticeable here. It’s as though the phone has desperately tried to eliminate any shadow in the image, creating a flat-looking shot that lacks the rich tones you’d expect from a good camera.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera, in Master Mode.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The Find X10 Pro isn’t alone in this regard — I find most phones seem to go too hard on image processing, and that includes the Find X9 Ultra. The way around it is to shoot in Master mode, taking control of your white balance settings and shooting in DNG raw to avoid any built-in software and AI-based processing being applied. I made my own tweaks to this image in Adobe Lightroom.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While this shot is a straight-out-of-camera image taken in the default mode. Again, I’d have to say that it looks over-processed, especially with the artificially brightened shadows.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera, in Master Mode.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I took this shot in Master Mode specifically so I could take control of the white balance and warm the scene up to emphasise that glorious morning sunshine. I took it in JPEG and have done no further editing.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the telephoto zoom camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Yes, the phone has a telephoto zoom lens, but no I can’t tell you what that zoom factor is. What I can say is that I think this shot looks good. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the telephoto zoom camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And this telephoto zoom shot also looks good, with sharp details and vibrant colors. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the telephoto lens accessory.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Like the Find X9 Ultra, the X10 Pro will be available with an add-on telephoto zoom lens to take your zoom shots even further. Here’s a white pigeon I found. While the camera struggled to get focus on the bird (getting confused by the railing in front) it eventually achieved an impressively sharp image, with natural-looking bokeh from the out-of-focus railing. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the telephoto lens accessory.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And another with the add-on telephoto lens. This time it’s a seagull on a boat, even though it doesn’t need a boat because it can fly. This seagull just wants to have everything and it’s a real shame that late-stage capitalism has influenced the local birdlife in this way. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the front-facing camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Speaking of capitalism, I’ll end on this photo of yours truly with a Leica M6 slung around my neck. Taken with the front-facing camera, this shot has nice-looking tones, both in terms of the shadows and the colors.

I like many of these early test shots I’ve taken, and I’m looking forward to spending more time with the phone over the coming weeks. It has some stiff competition – not just from the aforementioned Leica Leitzphone and the new iPhone 18 Pro, but also from its predecessor, the Find X9 Ultra, which impressed me with its photography skills when I reviewed it in June.

title: Apple and Epic clash over document production in latest App Store court filing
snippet: Epic Games is accusing Apple of “manufacturing” a pause in the legal proceedings over its proposed new App Store commission rates. Apple disagrees. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Epic Games is accusing Apple of “manufacturing” a pause in the legal proceedings over its proposed new App Store commission rates. Apple disagrees. Here are the details.

In a joint status update, Epic Games and Apple present very different accounts of Apple’s efforts to turn over internal documents explaining how it arrived at its proposed App Store commission rates.

A bit of context

As a reminder, in August, Apple proposed a new commission structure for purchases made through external App Store links.

Under the proposed structure, developers would pay commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, down from the 27% fee Apple introduced in 2024 after a court ordered the company to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods.

The court later found Apple in contempt of its order, a designation Apple is seeking to overturn before the Supreme Court, arguing that the order never forbade it from charging any commissions at all.

While the Supreme Court considers Apple’s challenge to the contempt ruling, a lower court is separately examining whether Apple can impose commissions on purchases made through external links, and if so, how much it can charge.

Apple recently tried to pause those proceedings until the Supreme Court reached a decision, but its requests were rejected by both the lower court and the Supreme Court.

As part of that process, Apple submitted its proposed 5% to 15% commission structure in August, along with evidence supporting those rates.

Under the agreement governing the proceedings, Apple was also required to hand over internal documents showing how it arrived at those rates.

The documents are meant to give Epic an opportunity to examine the basis for Apple’s proposed fees before formally responding to the court.

That’s where the latest dispute comes in, with Epic accusing Apple of deliberately delaying the proceedings and Apple rejecting those allegations.

Apple and Epic dispute evidence behind proposed App Store fees

In the joint status filing, Epic says that “[n]early two months after its production deadline, Apple has scarcely produced any documents,” adding that “Apple’s […] continued unwillingness to commit to a date certain by which it will complete its production demonstrates that Court intervention is essential.”

Apple disputes those accusations, arguing that it had already fulfilled its initial obligation to produce documents explaining how it arrived at the proposed rates.

The company also blames Epic for the delays, saying the Fortnite maker took weeks to submit additional document requests, and subsequently demanded extensive searches involving 27 individuals. Apple says it has agreed to those requests and expects to substantially complete its production by November 25.

In the document, Epic also disputes Apple’s assertions that only four senior executives were involved in determining the proposed commission rates, those four executives being Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Kevan Parekh, and Carson Oliver.

Epic argues that the decision was also informed by discussions and analyses conducted by other teams within Apple, including work on alternative commission structures in markets outside the United States. (And speaking of that, there is also a dispute over whether Epic should have access to documents concerning Apple’s international commission policies.)

Apple, in turn, maintains that the decision-making process was much narrower than the one behind its original 27% commission, and relied heavily on analyses conducted by outside experts rather than broader internal discussions.

Apple says it has already provided the business records and data that informed its proposal, and disputes Epic’s assertion that a larger group of employees must have been involved in determining the new rates.

Throughout its rebuttal of Epic’s accusations, Apple repeatedly emphasizes that it has agreed to Epic’s requests for additional documents and broader searches, arguing that the scope of those demands, and the time Epic took to make them, are responsible for the delays.

Apple also says Epic caught it by surprise by asking the court to impose a November 1 deadline for completing document production, rather than first discussing that deadline with Apple. The company makes a similar argument about Epic’s objections to the scope of the documents Apple agreed to produce, saying Epic should have raised those concerns directly before seeking court intervention.

Epic, on the other hand, says “Apple feigns surprise at every request Epic raises, as if the Parties, this Court, Magistrate Judge Hixson, and three Court-appointed special masters did not just recently complete a months-long process to extract from Apple documents Epic was clearly entitled to receive.”

For this reason, Epic asks the court to order Apple to:

“[I]mmediately begin rolling document productions and fully complete its productions on a reasonable timeline, and by no later than November 1, 2026”

“[P]roduce by said deadline all relevant documents, without regard to the artificial limitations Apple has placed on the scope of its production, as further detailed [in the document].”

title: MacBook Pro overhaul: entry-level model to gain new design sooner than expected
snippet: Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected.

Normally, when Apple introduces a new MacBook Pro design, it takes a while to trickle down. For instance, the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M1 Pro and M1 Max was introduced in 2021, but the base model MacBook Pro stuck with the 13-inch design until 2023, when it gained the 14-inch chassis with the M3 chip.

Similarly, when Apple redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2016, it wasn’t until 2019 that the entry level model gained the Touch Bar. There’s also a similar story for the 2012 retina MacBook Pro redesign.

This time around though, there’ll only be a roughly 6 month gap before the redesign comes to the entry level.

M7 entry-level with redesign

According to Bloomberg, Apple will be introducing the redesign to the entry level MacBook Pro in early 2027, shortly after debuting it in the high end MacBook Pros, rumored to be called MacBook Ultra. From the report:

Apple is also preparing a revamped entry-level MacBook Pro, code-named K104, for as early as the first half of next year. The 14-inch laptop will adopt a new design in line with what Apple is preparing for higher-end MacBooks with touch screens due between the end of this year and early next year.

It’s worth noting that there’ll also be another entry level MacBook Pro with the current design and the M6 chip, which is currently on track to debut this fall alongside the redesigned high-end MacBook Pros. 

To make things even weirder, those redesigned high-end MacBook Pros are also expected to debut with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, instead of M6 generation chips. Apple recently made a decision to abandon its plans for high end M6 chips to instead accelerate M7.

In short, it’ll look like this:

Fall 2026: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M6/old design, high-end with M5 Pro/Max and new design

Spring 2027: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M7 and new design

Fall 2027: High-end MacBook Pro refresh with M7 Pro/M7 Max

Of course, the redesign is expected to feature a slightly thinner chassis, OLED displays with touch support, and possibly even come with a Dynamic Island.

Wrap up

With the recent price hikes, this is excellent news for some people. I’m sure the redesigned 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro will likely cost over $2500, so if you’re looking to get something more in budget with the M7 chip and the redesign, you’ll only have to wait until the following spring.

	

It’s certainly unfortunate that the $1,999 price point of the entry level MacBook Pro today is what the Pro chip versions cost just under a year ago, but that’s the inevitable reality of this memory shortage.

Are you looking forward to the M7 MacBook Pro with the redesign? Let us know in the comments.

title: Googlebook improving ‘Better Together’ Android sync features, Samsung support rolling out
snippet: The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices. more…
fullText:
The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices.

There are several core features that work between Android phones and Googlebook including app streaming, notification sync, “Continue On” for compatible apps, and more. But, at launch, not everything works as expected. Some features, like Instant Hotspot, seem to work widely, but others are either inconsistent, slow to activate, or simply unavailable. One of the problems is that it takes a bit of work to fully activate these features.

In a post on Reddit, Google explains that it has started rolling out “smoother first-time setup” for these features, reducing the needed steps to actually set up these cross-device features. A bug where the QR code used to pair your phone continues to show even after Googlebook pairing is complete is apparently also fixed with this update. Google Play Services 26.37 (on the phone) is the version you’re looking for. You can check for Play Services updates through the Play Store. Cross-device Services also needs to be updated to 1.0.1346, again through the Play Store. 

Apparently, these updates also seem to enable support for Samsung devices. 

	

Missing Galaxy smartphone support was perhaps the biggest gap in Googlebook at launch, at least in terms of compatibility. Google originally said this would arrive “in the coming weeks,” a phrase that continues to be incredibly vague.

Here’s Google’s full breakdown of everything you’re looking for:

Confirm your phone runs Android 17: Your Android phone must run Android 17. To check your version, open Settings > About phone > Android version (your phone’s settings may vary). Better Together features work with Pixel and compatible Android 17 phones including Xiaomi, Oppo, OnePlus, Motorola, Lenovo, Honor, Sharp, Sony, Samsung (One UI 9.0), and more.

Check your Bluetooth and Wi-Fi: Confirm your phone and Googlebook use the same personal Google Account with both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on.

Use a private home Wi-Fi network: Hotel, cafe, office, and guest Wi-Fi networks frequently use client isolation, which blocks direct local connections between your phone and laptop. Pause any active VPNs or network DNS blockers and test on a standard home Wi-Fi network.

Update Google Play services: Google Play services must be at version 26.37 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings > Apps (or Apps & notifications)> See all apps. If Google Play services doesn’t appear, select More and then Show system. Select Google Play services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Update Cross-device services: Cross-device services must be at version 1.0.1346 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings, then Apps (or Apps & notifications), then See all apps. Select Cross-device services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Verify Continue activity sub-toggles: On your phone under Settings, search for Cross-device services > Continue activity, and confirm that Tasks, Apps, Notifications, Files & media sharing are all turned On. 

Restart both your phone and your Googlebook to ensure changes take effect.

Some Samsung Galaxy users have already confirmed that “Better Together” features are working on their Googlebooks following these updates.

Missing Samsung support was initially attributed to missing updates on Samsung’s end by some, but it sounds like everything is worked out at this point. You’ll still need One UI 9, though, which is only rolled out to a small portion of Samsung’s device catalog at this point.

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

Sound off in the comments below if you’ve been able to use any of these new Googlebook features, or if you even bought a Googlebook in the first place.

title: Googlebook’s hidden ‘Glowbar Disco’ turns your laptop’s lid into a light show — how to find it
snippet: Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank. more…
fullText:
Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank.

The Glowbar on Googlebook is a carryover from the iconic light bar on the original Chromebook Pixel. It doesn’t function quite the same, lacking the fun and useful “knock knock” gesture that Google’s original offered, but it still shows battery on plug-in, and serves as a nice accent too.

But, hidden behind the scenes is more control over the glowbar.

The “Glowbar Disco” app is an Easter egg buried deep within the OS, and even Google’s Alexander Kuscher admits it might be “too hard to find.” The app itself lets you set the Glowbar on a Googlebook to show a constant color, a preset animation, a gradient of colors, or even sync with music. It leaves the Glowbar active whenever the machine is turned on and the Disco app is open, and it’s a super fun little addition.

	

Finding the app, though, is not exactly an easy task. 

You’ll have to go to Settings > Apps then allow the search function to show system apps, then search for “Glowbar Disco.” From there you can launch the app, but you’ll need to repeat that process every time you want to access it. And, if you close the app, the effects stop.

If you ask me, this should be baked into the Settings because it is very fun. Hopefully that’ll change in time — Googlebooks certainly need a lot of updates.

title: ElevationLab pulls AirTag Silencer after backlash over stalking concerns
snippet: Following intense criticism over the obvious fact that its AirTag Silencer could facilitate stalking and other forms of misuse of Apple’s AirTag, ElevationLab has now pulled the accessory. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following intense criticism over the obvious fact that its AirTag Silencer could facilitate stalking and other forms of misuse of Apple’s AirTag, ElevationLab has now pulled the accessory. Here are the details.

A couple of weeks ago, Glenn Fleishman wrote a lengthy post over at Six Colors criticizing ElevationLab’s AirTag Silencer, which does pretty much what it says on the label.

Equipped with a piercing mechanism intended to neutralize the AirTag’s speaker without damaging the rest of the hardware, the accessory was announced on September 30 for $9.99.

Yesterday, as Fleishman noted in a new post on Six Colors, ElevationLab announced its decision to remove the product from sale, in a brief note acknowledging the obvious opportunity for misuse the accessory afforded.

The note, titled “An apology,” reads:

We launched an AirTag silencing tool recently. We have always made products we want for ourselves, and this was no different – we wanted it for AirTags on our bikes. (Some of us here have bikes more valuable than our cars.)

In retrospect though, this also has the side effect of aiding someone with bad intentions to track someone that wouldn’t get phone notifications.

We have removed the product and will use our patent on it to prevent anyone else from making one in the future.

Sincerely,

Elevation Lab

The product is also no longer listed on Amazon, although it still appears as an autocomplete suggestion in search results.

9to5Mac’s take

It is worth noting that the now-pulled product information page for ElevationLab’s AirTag Silencer noted that it worked “on multiple AirTags.”

As a longtime AirTag accessory maker, ElevationLab was certainly aware that one of the changes Apple made with the second-generation AirTag was making its speaker harder to remove, a change that could help discourage tampering and unwanted tracking.

Be that as it may, the product is no longer for sale, and it would be great if ElevationLab kept the public informed about its efforts to prevent similar devices from being sold through the promised enforcement of its patent.

title: Nintendo’s Zelda Remake Is Rewriting My Memories
snippet: After an hour of playing the new Ocarina of Time, I think I prefer it to the old one.
fullText:
I spent weeks of graduate school curled up in front of my TV playing The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on my N64. I remember the epic journey with fuzzy nostalgia that, when I load up the game on the Switch’s N64 app, doesn’t entirely pay dividends. It looks uglier now than it does in my head. As Bill Pullman said in Lost Highway, “I like to remember things my own way…how I remembered them. Not necessarily the way they happened.”

Nintendo’s $60 Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 filled me with uncanniness when I saw the first trailers. It was lush, almost weirdly rich with detail. Hyrule Castle Town almost looked like a theme park. Everyone’s faces seemed so…shiny.

But after an hour of playing the remake in an early preview session, I came away from it in a happy haze. If someone had never played Ocarina of Time before, this would feel like a whole new game. And if you have…this might end up being your new memory of it.

			

More from CNET

A beautiful rebuild

It’s a freaky thing, the idea of game remakes. It’s the same way I feel about movies being updated or remade. I like to preserve the original artifact. Nintendo has been on a roll lately, working to reboot its classic catalog into fully new versions, starting with StarFox earlier this year and now continuing with Ocarina of Time. Both were Nintendo 64 games, and both, I think, feel so new in their remade versions that they almost feel original.

And yet Ocarina is a beat-for-beat return to the original, as far as I can tell. With a few new bits, and possibly other mysteries lurking, too.

Sometimes the graphics almost feel too lush.Nintendo

I played a bit of the beginning, where Link starts off in his Kokiri forest village, where the trees actually feel like they’re pressing in now. Link can jump now and also swim in the water (I dove for some rupees). I didn’t mind the new voice acting, and the character animations won me over. It almost felt like a more immersive version of the art style in Link’s Awakening or Echoes of Wisdom, blended with Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom.

The Great Deku Tree, with its dripping root mouth, now seems more sinister or overwhelming. Every part of the game’s visuals actually feels more ramped up than even Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom, but on a smaller scale. Less overwhelming vistas, more gorgeously detailed foliage and buildings.

Running across Hyrule Field and exploring Hyrule Castle Town, talking to villagers and exploring shops, I wondered if this many characters were here before. Was it this bustling? 

Everything feels atmospherically revamped.Nintendo

I played as Adult Link, too, exploring the Forest Temple and making my way through almost all its puzzles again. I played this temple long ago (and again on the Nintendo 3DS remaster), but everything is so graphically overhauled this time that some environments just feel totally new. The stained glass windows, the cathedral-like interiors…was I here before?

You can also play the Ocarina’s spell songs by actually singing them over the Switch 2’s microphone (or by tapping buttons the old school way). I tried and felt ridiculous, but it worked. Gimmicky, but fun.

Nintendo’s whole holiday lineup of Switch 2 game releases is throwbacks: Switch Sports Resort, then Ocarina of Time. I’d love some original games too, but those look like they’re on deck for 2027 (Metroid Ravenous, and the new Kirby and the World Beyond). In the meantime, is Nintendo testing the Switch 2’s graphics chops with remakes while it works out new games for the future…or biding time until more Switch owners hop aboard Switch 2? I like what I’ve tried so far, but will it make me want to play all of Ocarina all over again? We’ll find out soon.

title: HomeView can display third-party widgets from your iPhone
snippet: Apple’s new HomeView (pre-order here) won’t have an App Store, but it will support third-party apps in some cases, including letting you run third-party widgets from your iPhone. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new HomeView (pre-order here) won’t have an App Store, but it will support third-party apps in some cases, including letting you run third-party widgets from your iPhone. Here are the details.

When Apple’s HomeView was unveiled yesterday, the company didn’t say much about its support for third-party apps. But today the device’s app story is becoming more clear.

In addition to being able to run third-party audio and video apps—likely to include favorites like Spotify, Audible, YouTube, and Netflix—Apple now says widgets are supported too.

Per Apple’s updated developer agreement:

6.4.1 iOS Application Widgets on CarPlay and Apple HomeView

You agree that Your iOS Application widget may be made available on CarPlay and Apple HomeView. Furthermore, You are responsible for determining whether Your iOS Application widget is functional and suitable to use for CarPlay, and for using the disfavoredLocations function to disfavor Your iOS Application widget if it is not. For example, iOS Application widgets that are not functional or suitable include those that require extensive user interaction while driving, or that require the iPhone to be unlocked to be used.

CarPlay and HomeView are mentioned in tandem because third-party CarPlay apps in the audio and video categories will be available on HomeView too.

But for widgets, supported third-party HomeView widgets will be much broader than just those two categories.

That’s because any iOS app can provide widgets to CarPlay, and thus those same widgets will be able to support HomeView too.

Widgets first came to CarPlay with iOS 26 last year, and include popular third-party widgets from Amazon, ChatGPT, Instagram, and more.

Based on Apple’s documentation, these iOS widgets will be available on HomeView too unless explicitly excluded by the developers.

title: Someone ported Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text to other Android phones
snippet: One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is. more…
fullText:
One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is.

Rambler on the Pixel 11 series is essentially AI-enhanced voice-to-text. The feature takes what you say and runs it through AI, spitting out a result that includes grammar and formatting while taking out filler words and times you may have tripped over your words. It’s not perfect, as not being able to see a live preview or get word-for-word output can be a little unsettling, but it’s still a huge upgrade to traditional voice-to-text.

That’s why it can be a little annoying that it’s Pixel 11-only.

A developer, though, has managed to port the feature to any other Android phone. “PixelBoard” is a split off of the Gboard app that brings support for Rambler to essentially any other Android phone. 

	
	

In a post on Reddit (h/t Artem Russakovskii), the developer explains that the project is based on the official Gboard app, just modified to unlock Rambler and other new writing tools.

The app is available for sideloading via the project’s GitHub page, but as always that’s done at your own risk. That said, we installed the app on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 to a complete success. It runs just like Rambler on a Pixel 11. Your results may vary and, again, install at your own risk! The project has other install methods available, including patching the existing Gboard installation on your phone.

It’s still unclear if Google ever plans to bring Rambler to other devices, but third-party mods like this will be the only way to do so for the time being. For those wanting to stick with a Play Store install, Microsoft’s SwiftKey acts as a fine alternative.

snippet: In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything. more…
fullText:
In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is a full-on powerhouse with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chipset, up to 128GB of RAM, and plenty of ports. But it’s one of those ports that is the most unique new features.

“Magnetic Connect” is Microsoft’s name for “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C” charging port. The USB-C port itself functions as normal with any standard cable, but the included charger is specially designed to magnetically attach akin to Apple’s MagSafe or any other number of magnetic charging connectors.

I want it.

	

The “how” here is that the charging portion of the cable uses super-strong magnets to align and latch on the charger so the port connects properly, but the charger itself also tapers the edges of the USB-C port so it can more easily slide into place. As such, that end won’t securely connect to your phone or other devices, as it needs that magnet to hold itself in place. 

	

The Verge shows it in action in a video on YouTube:

Microsoft is apparently hoping this idea will catch on and show up on other laptops, and I sure hope that’s the case! As for phones, the size of the magnets implies it probably won’t be feasible in a standard smartphone, but I really hope this idea starts showing up everywhere! Certainly I hope it at least shows up on a laptop that doesn’t cost $2,600 — Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders are open now.

What do you think?

fullText:
An overhauled Apple Health app is coming, but it looks like iOS 27.2 won’t include it.

Apple first announced the upgraded Health app in September. The company still says to expect it to launch later this year.

iOS 27.2 developer beta 1 was the first iPhone software update to include the new Health app.

Apple added it to iOS 27.2 public beta 1 and public beta 2 as well. It features new data points like health age while adding the ability to schedule lab work through Quest Diagnostics.

However, it appears Apple plans to take a bit more time to get the new Health app ready for release.

Today’s iOS 27.2 developer beta 4 release no longer includes the new Health app. Instead, the prior version is restored. The longevity section is replaced with the previous sharing section.

iOS 27.2 beta 4 notes that Health data added during the beta testing period will be retained and viewing in the Settings app. It also adds that the release is still planned for this year. 

This likely means that we’ll see iOS 27.3 beta in late October or early November with the Health app upgrade included.

title: Big Walk skipped Xbox to boycott Microsoft’s involvement with Israel
snippet: Big Walk's co-op multiplayer walking adventure has proved popular since launching in August, but Xbox players have been excluded from the fun - and now the game's creators have explained why. Developer House House said in a blog post that it decided not to release Big Walk on Xbox consoles in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which has called to boycott Microsoft, including products under the company's gaming division. Microsoft was named a priority BDS target in June last year over contracts it has with the Israeli military and government, with the boycott specifically calling out Xbox conso … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Big Walk’s co-op multiplayer walking adventure has proved popular since launching in August, but Xbox players have been excluded from the fun — and now the game’s creators have explained why. Developer House House said in a blog post that it decided not to release Big Walk on Xbox consoles in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which has called to boycott Microsoft, including products under the company’s gaming division.

Microsoft was named a priority BDS target in June last year over contracts it has with the Israeli military and government, with the boycott specifically calling out Xbox consoles and Game Pass subscriptions, gaming franchises owned by Microsoft, and any gaming accessories produced by the company. Microsoft’s involvement with Israel has also been protested by its own employees, and the company has fired staffers for participating in pro-Palestine demonstrations.

Here’s what House House said regarding its participation in the boycott:

It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to those intentions. This decision means that some people will miss out on playing Big Walk with their friends, and we understand the disappointment we’re causing. We are disappointed too.

We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets.

We’ve made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free.

Thank you for your understanding.

Big Walk is playable on Microsoft’s Windows operating system, however, as it’s available to download via Steam. We’ve asked House House why it hasn’t excluded Big Walk from Windows and will update if we hear back.

title: The iPhone Duo’s cooling system hides a clever trick inside its hinge
snippet: While a folding iPhone posed a new challenge for Apple’s thermal engineering team, they came up with a creative way to leverage the device’s hinge to their advantage. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
While a folding iPhone posed a new challenge for Apple’s thermal engineering team, they came up with a creative way to leverage the device’s hinge to their advantage. Here are the details.

iPhone Duo’s hinge features a flexible graphite pipe

PCMag recently sat down with Dan Murray, Apple’s vice president of silicon engineering, and Banafsheh Barabadi, the company’s senior manager of thermal product design, to discuss the architecture of the A20 Pro chip.

The new SoC, which powers the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, is Apple’s first iPhone chip built on a 2 nm process, following the technology’s debut with the M6 chip in the Mac mini in August.

And while the A20 Pro was designed with all three new iPhones in mind, the iPhone Duo version packs some additional capabilities. These include a second display engine to run both screens simultaneously.

From PCMag:

The iPhone Duo’s A20 Pro variant is just slightly different. “For iPhone Duo, we added a second display engine to support simultaneous operation of the inner and outer displays,” says Murray, “and with the increased CPU and GPU performance, we ensure we can deliver a smooth user experience across the displays. For the inner display, we also added support for placing the FaceTime camera behind the display.”

The report offers a really interesting, in-depth look at the A20 Pro’s thermals and the new vapor chamber Apple developed to keep them at bay. That includes what Apple calls “metal over foam,” a material that iFixit also examined during its recent teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro.

The second pillar is a new material that bridges the gap between the A20 Pro and the vapor chamber. “We call it metal over foam,” says Barabadi, and it “basically creates a direct thermal and mechanically compliant coupling between the SoC and the vapor chamber. It is highly effective in removing the heat, meeting the strict mechanical requirements of the system. It took us months of development to get the material properties exactly right to be able to use this material.”

Perhaps the most interesting tidbit from the story is what Apple did to improve the iPhone Duo’s thermal performance, particularly given the challenges of dissipating heat in a device that doubles in thickness when folded.

From the report:

“This was one of the most technically challenging aspects of our design,” says Barabadi. To surmount the issue, Apple routed a flexible graphite pipe through the hinge itself to transfer heat between the two halves, thereby increasing the surface area available for heat dissipation. “This part need[ed] to be co-engineered between our thermal team and the mechanical team. It’s a flexible material that needs to survive, as you can imagine, many hinge cycles while maintaining its thermal connectivity, and also its structural integrity throughout the product life cycle.”

PCMag’s interview with Murray and Barabadi also goes into the A20 Pro’s architecture, including the benefits of placing the DRAM next to the processor rather than stacking it on top, and you can read it in full here.

title: TimeTeller puts our internal clocks at the center of personalized medicine
snippet: German startup TimeTeller has developed a saliva test kit to help anyone understand their circadian rhythm; it aims to reduce side effects from cancer treatments.
fullText:
At-home health testing has been mired in overblown claims and outright fraud. But German startup TimeTeller, which has developed a saliva test kit to help anyone understand their circadian rhythm, is led by CEO Angela Relógio, who is the polar opposite of Theranos’ disgraced founder Elizabeth Holmes.

Relógio is a physicist-engineer and molecular biologist who spent years researching oncology, circadian biology, and systems medicine in Germany before leaving academia to build TimeTeller. She is careful about what the test can and can’t do today.

It would be easy to oversell: Relógio’s last name means “clock” in her native Portuguese, and TimeTeller has the potential to reduce side effects from cancer treatment and improve outcomes by timing treatment to each patient’s internal clock. That’s also why she’s careful to warn that TimeTeller itself operates on two timelines.

The long-term goal is to determine when cancer treatments will be better tolerated and most effective, and doing so much more granularly than just telling whether someone is a morning person or a night owl. But its direct-to-consumer kit won’t help patients figure that out on their own. “That is something that we need to calculate for every single medicine; we do that in the context of clinical studies,” Relógio cautioned.

According to Relógio, TimeTeller started accepting direct orders because of demand from longevity clinics, which focus on healthy aging and understand that individual data on a person’s circadian rhythm can be used to offer personalized advice on sleep, nutrition, light exposure, and physical activity.

TimeTeller could also apply to metabolic diseases (such as diabetes) and neurodegenerative diseases (such as Alzheimer’s), performance, and women’s health, but cancer is its core mission. It was while studying cancer that Relógio made the discovery that led her to leave academia.

She noticed that many cancer patients stopped or started their treatment because of side effects. “As a scientist, that was just impossible to watch, particularly when I was convinced that part of the problem might not only be what treatment we give, but when we give it,” Relógio said. This led her to develop the circadian rhythm test at the core of TimeTeller — which she knew had to become a company.

“I personally funded our first patent because I strongly believed that this discovery should not remain in scientific publications,” she said. The startup spun out of Berlin’s Charité university hospital but has since moved to Medical School Hamburg, which provided access to patients and funding. It also offered a fallback: backup employment for TimeTeller’s team of 10 if the company couldn’t pay them.

That’s a safety net TimeTeller may not need. Having enlisted biochemist and market access specialist Benjamin Dose as a co-founder, the startup secured a partnership with Techniker Krankenkasse, one of Germany’s largest health insurance providers. The partnership started out as a reimbursement deal in which the insurer pays back the cost of the test for a subset of cancer patients, and both sides are now ready to expand it to more of the insurer’s 12 million members, Relógio said.

Despite her caveats about the direct-to-consumer test, TimeTeller has become a solution that cancer patients can actually access. Ahead of her appearance at TechCrunch Disrupt, where Relógio appeared onstage today in San Francisco as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, she made clear that the company has broader ambitions: a future in which asking “when” is central to precision medicine, because “almost every process in our body is timed.”

You aren’t too late to join the action at Disrupt. Come for the headliners; stay to see who wins this year’s no-strings check from TechCrunch — and the attention of the hundreds of VCs in attendance.

title: Apple Maps Gets a Ticket to Austin for the F1 Grand Prix
snippet: Whether you’re in town for the United States Grand Prix or scoping out a visit, Apple Maps now has more details for Austin.
fullText:
If you’re headed to Austin, Texas, for next week’s Formula 1 United States Grand Prix, you won’t want to miss the city’s other highlights – if nothing else, you’ll need to find good barbecue. Apple is adding another dimension to the Texas capital by applying its Detailed City Experience treatment in Apple Maps, including the Circuit of the Americas track where the race is held each year.

Apple enhanced Maps’ Austin layout with detailed 3D day and night renderings of landmarks such as The Paramount Theater, Sixth Street, the Texas State Capitol building and Terry Black’s BBQ. Navigation improvements include streets with lanes (including bus and bike lanes) marked and more accurate elevation.

The race venue marks the track’s turns, shows 3D versions of the grandstands and pit building, as well as the admission entry points. It also includes flourishes such as the stars-and-stripes design of the runoff areas. (But not the World’s Largest Cowboy Hat, alas, which is still being constructed for the event.)

			

More from CNET

Enhancements to Apple Maps include race track details, notable areas of the venue and 3D versions of landmarks in the Austin area.

Apple, which is the official US broadcaster for F1 races on Apple TV, previously applied the Detailed City Experience glow-up to Monaco, which hosts one of the most storied F1 races of the entire tournament (several top racers call Monaco home), as well as the Albert Park Grand Prix Circuit in Melbourne.

The improvements to Apple Maps aren’t solely visual additions – the app on the iPhone is also an invaluable guide for getting directions and finding places of interest.

For instance, those attending the F1 race can get directions to COTA and see where roads have been temporarily closed or redirected for the event. But it will also guide you to the section where you’re seated and help you find race-specific areas such as bathrooms and first aid areas.

Although the F1 race is a big reason for visiting Austin, it’s just one of many things to do in the state’s capitol. For that weekend and the rest of the year, Apple has created a new curated guide by country music singer-songwriter Dylan Gossett. You’ll find the race track (where Gossett once worked), as well as his favorite bar, the Armadillo Den, and his favorite guitar store, Moon Music Pro.

The Austin improvements to Apple Maps are available now on Apple devices and on the web.

title: Google announces $179 Fitbit Edge tracker with display, GPS
snippet: Google is following the Fitbit Air launched in May with a second tracker that features a screen called the Fitbit Edge. more…
fullText:
Google is following the Fitbit Air launched in May with a second tracker that features a screen called the Fitbit Edge.

The Fitbit Edge features a wide, pill-shaped AMOLED screen — protected by Gorilla Glass 3 — that offers 46% more display than the Charge 6 from 2023. The 11.5mm-thick body is made from precision-crafted aluminum with nano-molding technology to allow for a 40% more precise GPS (versus Charge 6), while there’s a dedicated altimeter for elevation tracking. On the right side, you’ll find a large button for tactile control, like when swimming. This device has IP68 / 5ATM dust and water protection.

On the underside, you’ll find the sensors. The Fitbit Edge has an accelerometer, altimeter, ambient light sensor, far-field skin temperature sensor, gyroscope, heart rate sensor, multipurpose electrical sensors (ECG), and red and infrared sensors (SpO2).

The Fitbit Edge uses the same magnetic USB-C charger as the Fitbit Air. A 5-minute charge gives you a day of battery, while a full top-up takes 90 minutes. Battery life is rated at a week with the always-on display disabled. When enabled, the Fitbit Edge comes in at around 2 days. Like the Pixel Watch 5, you can open the device to replace the battery.

	

The Fitbit Edge is available in the following colors:

Matte Black Aluminum case / Obsidian Active Band

Polished Silver Aluminum case / Fog Active Band

Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Olive Active Band

Champagne Gold case / Canyon Active Band

The bands are replaceable with a new swap mechanism and four additional designs: 

$39.99 Active Sport: Made of “ultra soft silicone” with large pill-shaped cutouts

$59.99 Magnet Band: Clasp-free design with magnets embedded into the strap

$149.99 Metal Links

$49.99 Performance Loop: Stretch and micro-adjustable

Supporting Android and iOS, the Edge is running a Fitbit operating system similar to the Air. A larger screen unlocks a richer interface that takes inspiration from the Pixel Watch 5.

Google showed a dozen or so watch faces for the Fitbit Edge with analog and digital options. You can customize what complications appear via the Google Health app.

Swiping left/right from the watch face lets you access various tiles, with the order customizable. This includes Quick start (for different exercises), Focus metrics, Sleep, Heart, Cycle health, Weather, Timers, Alarms, and Music controls.

Compared to the Charge 6, music controls work with any app on your paired device, while phone notifications are also available. Quick replies to messages are limited to Android due to iOS platform limitations. You also get Google Maps navigation, but there is no Google Wallet given the lack of NFC.

	

The Exercise app lets you track over 50 types of activity with real-time guidance and workout views. The Fitbit Edge can connect to equipment with heart rate broadcasting. 

The Fitbit Edge (and the Air) feature upgraded automatic activity detection. This AI-powered contextual reasoning can learn your habits over time to add support for over 100 activities. 

You can have the Fitbit Air, Edge, and Pixel Watch 5 operate on the same account with seamless switching.

The Fitbit Edge costs $179.99 with pre-orders open today and availability on October 27. A Stephen Curry Special Edition is available for $219.99 with a custom band.

title: iPhone Air 2 is coming, here’s everything we know so far
snippet: Apple is working on a second-generation iPhone Air, and it could address several key limitations of the current model. Here’s everything we know about the iPhone Air 2, including features, release date, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple is working on a second-generation iPhone Air, and it could address several key limitations of the current model. Here’s everything we know about the iPhone Air 2, including features, release date, and more.

Will there be an iPhone Air 2?

The iPhone Air has reportedly sold worse than Apple expected. The Information reported in November that Apple had indefinitely delayed the release of a second-generation model due to those lower-than-expected sales.

Apple reportedly “notified engineers and suppliers that they were taking the next iPhone Air off the schedule without providing a new release date.”

Shortly thereafter, however, The Information updated its reporting to say Apple wasn’t canceling the iPhone Air 2 altogether and that one is still very much in the works.

iPhone Air 2 features

A second camera

One of the biggest tradeoffs of the ultra-thin iPhone Air design is that it only has one camera. This is reportedly something Apple is pushing to change for the iPhone Air 2.

According to sources including Bloomberg and The Information, the iPhone Air 2 will have a second camera on the back.

Bloomberg says it will be an ultra-wide camera, not a telephoto camera. This would align it with Apple’s base model iPhones, which also have a main camera and an ultra-wide camera.

A20 Pro chip

The iPhone Air 2 will reportedly be powered by the A20 Pro processor, up from the A19 Pro in the current model.

The A20 Pro chip will be Apple’s first 2-nanometer iPhone processor. This new fabrication process will mean the A20 Pro can offer more power and be more efficient in a similar-sized footprint.

The chip will also use another new innovation called Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module, which integrates the SoC and DRAM at the wafer level for better performance and lower power consumption.

Better battery life

Apple is also reportedly working to improve the battery life of the iPhone Air 2.

According to a supply chain leak, the iPhone Air 2 will have a 3,500mAh battery. For comparison’s sake, the first-generation iPhone Air has a 3,149mAh battery, so this is an increase of more than 10%.

Beyond increasing the physical size of the battery, the iPhone Air 2 will likely offer longer battery life thanks to the efficiency improvements of the A20 Pro chip.

It’s important to remember, however, that there are many variables at play when it comes to an iPhone’s battery life. We’ll have to wait and see the exact numbers when Apple officially unveils the iPhone Air 2.

Vapor chamber

According to The Information, the iPhone Air 2 will feature a vapor chamber cooling system. Apple first debuted its vapor chamber cooling technology in the iPhone 17 Pro, touting significantly improved heat dissipation and performance.

If Apple brings the vapor chamber to the iPhone Air 2, it means the device will stay cooler during high workloads and sustain high performance for longer periods.

iPhone Air 2: Release date

The iPhone Air 2 was originally expected to be released in September 2026 alongside the iPhone 18 Pro lineup.

Most recently, however, Bloomberg reported that Apple plans to release the iPhone Air 2 in spring 2027 alongside the new base model iPhone 18.

What do you think of Apple’s plans for an iPhone Air 2? Is Apple making the right changes and improvements? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Apple showcases iPad Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max’s role in ‘landmark fashion show’
snippet: Apple today shared a behind-the-scenes look at “From Earth to Sky,” a fashion show in Turkey that was designed with an iPad Pro and filmed using an iPhone 18 Pro Max. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple today shared a behind-the-scenes look at “From Earth to Sky,” a fashion show in Turkey that was designed with an iPad Pro and filmed using an iPhone 18 Pro Max. Here are the details.

Apple showcases ‘From Earth to Sky’ fashion show

From time to time, Apple’s Newsroom highlights interesting uses of the company’s products in projects that help illustrate the practical applications of their more advanced and professional hardware and software features.

Today, Apple shared a fascinating look at “From Earth to Sky,” a fashion show created by German-born designer Bünyamin Aydın to celebrate the 15th anniversary of Turkish fashion brand Les Benjamins.

Aydın’s creative process relies heavily on the iPad Pro and the Apple Pencil Pro, paired with apps such as Freeform and Procreate.

Aydın’s creative process seldom takes place behind a desk, so he appreciates the flexibility iPad Pro offers with its thin, light form factor and battery life that can last him up to two days. “It’s the ultimate workstation on the go,” Aydın says. “That gives me freedom.”

For this specific project, Aydın says he used Freeform to organize photographs, fabric references, and early designs into mood boards that could be shared with his team, while Procreate played a central role in designing the three custom-built hot-air balloons featured in the show.

As for where the new iPhone 18 Pro Max came in, French filmmaker Neels Castillon used the device to capture the fashion show, including footage shot with custom-built drones carrying two iPhones each.

As feeds from the whirling drones come into Castillon’s production control center, synchronizing them begins right there on location. He reviews footage and makes selections on MacBook Pro with M4 Max; its nano-texture display helps reduce glare from the sun overhead.

While the post is obviously intended to help promote the technical capabilities of Apple’s current product line-up, it also offers a really interesting look at a creative project from a world that very few of us have contact with.

Apple says its @apple Instagram account will begin showcasing “From Earth to Sky” starting today, but you can also check out a behind-the-scenes video, photos, and more details about the project here.

title: Apple’s frenetic HomeView video showed the one use-case for this device
snippet: The launch video Apple created to show off the long-awaited HomeView product couldn’t have been more different from its usual fare. While just watching it gave me a feeling of anxiety, I suspect it perfectly encapsulates the one use-case for this device … more…
fullText:
The launch video Apple created to show off the long-awaited HomeView product couldn’t have been more different from its usual fare. 

While just watching it gave me a feeling of anxiety, I suspect it perfectly encapsulates the one use-case for this device …

HomeView is cute. I said a couple of years ago that I hoped that Apple would lean into the quirkiness of the iconic iMac G4 design, and in my view the company has borrowed enough of that heritage while still making it look like a modern device. What was rather less cute was that launch video – but that’s not accidental.

I’m a minimalist who places a premium on a home which feels calm and organized, and the typical Apple product video bears a strong resemblance to what my home would look like if I had about ten times the income (space in London is expensive!). The HomeView video, in contrast, felt to me utterly chaotic.

I found it both frenetic and jarring. But I think that’s exactly the point. I’ve spent enough time in the homes of friends with teenage kids to get the sense that this is probably a pretty accurate picture of a typical weekday morning. It also depicts the one scenario I could see making sense for this device.

If you’re either single or live as a couple, then it’s hard to see too much benefit to a HomeView. It doesn’t do anything we can’t do on our own devices or on HomePods with the existing multi-user Personal Requests feature we’ve had since 2019. (And no, I don’t find the digital photo frame justification convincing simply because the display is so small.)

	

Of course, the same argument could be made about families with kids, but when you’re trying to gather everybody together around the breakfast table, then I can definitely see the appeal of having a single device in one place be the way everyone gets their digital needs met. It’s a more wholesome picture than each family member silently staring at their own iPhone.

How realistic a goal this is is something I will leave to the parents to advise, but it certainly strikes me as a valiant attempt.

If you’re a parent with teenage kids, did the video accurately depict a typical morning, and do you think a HomeView could bring everyone together in the way Apple hopes? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: MagSafe Monday: This aluminum MagSafe wallet ejects your credit card with one click
snippet: My biggest annoyance with all types of wallets is when it This aluminum MagSafe card wallet takes a different approach with a side-mounted eject button that fans your cards up with a single press, so you can grab the one you need one-handed without pulling them all out. more…
fullText:
My biggest annoyance with all types of wallets is when it This aluminum MagSafe card wallet takes a different approach with a side-mounted eject button that fans your cards up with a single press, so you can grab the one you need one-handed without pulling them all out. 

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

The eject button is the best part

Hands down, the best part of this wallet is the eject button. The side button slides to fan your cards upward so you can grab whichever one you need without removing the wallet from your iPhone. This is the reason to buy this wallet over others as its the main unique thing. If you’re the type who keeps one card in a wallet and never needs to choose between them, a basic slot MagSafe wallet is probably fine. If you’re carrying two or three cards and want to pick the right one quickly at checkout, the ejector earns its keep.

The wallet is machined from lightweight aluminum with a scratch-resistant finish, and it comes in a bunch of different colors if you want it to match your iPhone or case. The wallet uses 32 built-in magnetic strips to snap onto a MagSafe compatible iPhone. I haven’t used it long enough to know how the finish holds up, but it feels solid.

The aluminum housing claims it blocks 13.56MHz RFID frequencies, so your contactless credit cards and ID are protected from electronic skimming in airports, etc. This is worth knowing upfront: this wallet holds up to 3 cards. That covers most everyday carry setups, but if you’re someone who needs four or five cards accessible, this isn’t the right fit. Three cards, one eject button, and a metal build is the whole point here. If this held 5 cards, it would honestly be perfect.

I wish it had Find My support, but it doesnt. If Find My matter to you, you’ll need to look elsewhere, but if you want a clean metal MagSafe wallet with a fast card ejector and solid MagSafe hold, this does this job well.

Wrap up

The eject button is what makes this MagSafe wallet worth buying. This one has a mechanism that actually speeds up the process of getting a card. The RDID blocking functionality is also pretty nice as well. The Metal housing is not something I’ve used in a wallet before, so it’s been a change, but overall I like it. Again, the downside is that it’s limited to 3 cards only.

You can buy it from Amazon.

fullText:
iPhone Duo pre-orders officially kick off on Friday, but Apple is letting you prepare now. Starting today, you can head to the Apple Store Online or Apple Store app and save your exact iPhone Duo configuration.

Apple has offered this “get ready for pre-order” window for the last several years. It allows you to streamline the pre-order process by preparing key details ahead of time. This includes the iPhone Duo color, storage, and carrier options.

You can also prepare your iPhone Duo pre-order payment method. You can pay in full, finance with Apple Card, join the Apple Upgrade program, or check for applicable carrier offers.

	

If you complete this process ahead of time, you can check out in just a couple of taps when iPhone Duo pre-orders officially begin on Friday morning.

The new “get ready” option is available today and will likely run through much of the day on Friday, October 15. You’ll then have to return to the Apple Store app or website on Friday, October 16 at 5 a.m. PT/8 a.m. ET to finalize your order.

title: Logitech brings its mouse & keyboard controller to Googlebook, supports Magic Pointer
snippet: Logitech has just launched its Logi Options+ app for Googlebook, bringing support for controlling its keyboard and wireless mice to the Android-based platform. more…
fullText:
Logitech has just launched its Logi Options+ app for Googlebook, bringing support for controlling its keyboard and wireless mice to the Android-based platform.

Previously available on Windows and macOS, Logi Options+ is the app needed to control Logitech peripherals such as the MX Master mouse, various keyboards, and more. This includes adjusting the functions of Logitech’s added buttons and shortcuts, as well as updating firmware on the products.

Logitech does warn that features are “limited” at launch, but there are plenty of supported peripherals including MX Master 4, MX Keys S, Logitech Lift, Pebble Keys 2, and more.

For Logitech mice, this also ensures Googlebook’s Magic Pointer feature works. Logitech says:

	

Pair your supported Logitech device with Googlebook using the Logi Options+ App. Get the best of Gemini with features like Magic Pointer, Circle to search, personalize mouse buttons or keyboard keys, optimize pointing and scrolling experience with Options+, designed specially for your Googlebook.

Logi Options+ for Googlebook is available now via the Google Play Store.
